In 1791, he defeated Philip Schuyler, Hamilton’s father-in-law, for a seat in the U.S. Senate — a defeat that began the long enmity between Burr and Hamilton.
In the election of 1800, Burr ran for Vice President on the Democratic-Republican ticket with Thomas Jefferson. When the Electoral College produced a tie between Jefferson and Burr, the election was thrown into the House of Representatives. Despite detesting Jefferson, Hamilton used his influence to ensure Jefferson’s election, describing Burr as “a man of talents of a certain kind, but of a character altogether unfit for the trust.”
The Duel with Hamilton
Hamilton had blocked Burr’s ambitions repeatedly over fifteen years. In 1804, when Burr ran for governor of New York, Hamilton actively opposed him, and Burr was decisively defeated. Learning of a remark attributed to Hamilton describing him as “a dangerous man,” Burr demanded satisfaction. The two men met at Weehawken, New Jersey, on July 11, 1804. Hamilton, having resolved to throw away his shot, fired into the air; Burr’s bullet struck Hamilton in the abdomen, and Hamilton died the following day.
The duel destroyed Burr’s career. Indicted for murder in both New York and New Jersey, he fled to South Carolina. His subsequent schemes — including the Burr conspiracy to create an independent empire in the Southwest — led to his trial for treason in 1807. He was acquitted by Chief Justice John Marshall but lived the rest of his life in obscurity and disgrace.
Sources

Chernow, Ron. Alexander Hamilton. New York: Penguin Press, 2004.

entities/alexander-hamilton.title: Alexander Hamilton
entities/alexander-hamilton.content:
Alexander Hamilton
Born: January 11, 1755 or 1757 (date disputed), Nevis, British West Indies
Died: July 12, 1804, New York City (from wounds received in duel with Aaron Burr)
Spouse: Elizabeth Schuyler Hamilton (m. 1780)
Occupation: Statesman, lawyer, soldier, economist
Alexander Hamilton was the first Secretary of the Treasury and the principal architect of the American financial system. He founded the Federalist Party, authored the majority of The Federalist Papers, and was the most influential figure in George Washington’s cabinet. His vision of a strong central government, commercial economy, and national credit system defined the Federalist era.
Early Life
Hamilton was born on the Caribbean island of Nevis, the illegitimate son of James Hamilton, a Scottish merchant, and Rachel Faucette Lavien. His father abandoned the family; his mother died when he was a child. Working as a clerk for a trading company on St. Croix, the young Hamilton impressed his employers with his intelligence and ambition. His employers collected money to send him to the American colonies for an education.
Hamilton arrived in New York in 1773 and enrolled at King’s College (later Columbia College). He quickly became involved in the revolutionary movement, publishing pamphlets defending the cause of colonial resistance.
Military Career
At the outbreak of the Revolution, Hamilton joined the Continental Army and served as an artillery captain, seeing action at the battles of Long Island, White Plains, Trenton, and Princeton. His competence attracted George Washington’s attention, and in 1777 Washington appointed Hamilton as his aide-de-camp with the rank of lieutenant colonel. For four years, Hamilton served as Washington’s chief staff officer, handling correspondence, intelligence, and strategic planning.
Hamilton distinguished himself at the Siege of Yorktown in 1781, leading a successful bayonet assault on Redoubt No. 10. After the war, he studied law, was admitted to the bar, and served in the Confederation Congress.
The Federalist Papers and the Constitution
Hamilton was a delegate to the Annapolis Convention of 1786 and the Constitutional Convention of 1787. Though he did not agree with every provision of the proposed Constitution, he argued for its ratification with extraordinary energy. He conceived the plan for The Federalist Papers, recruiting James Madison and John Jay as collaborators, and wrote 51 of the 85 essays himself.
In the Federalist Papers, Hamilton developed the case for a strong executive, an independent judiciary with the power of judicial review, a national bank, and a government with direct authority over individuals. His essays on the executive (Nos. 67–77) provided the most thorough contemporary defense of presidential power.
Secretary of the Treasury
As the first Secretary of the Treasury (1789–1795), Hamilton implemented the financial system of the United States. His first and most consequential Report on Public Credit (January 1790) proposed funding the national debt at par, assuming state debts, and securing revenue through customs duties and excise taxes. Despite opposition from James Madison and Thomas Jefferson, Congress adopted the funding and assumption plan as part of the Compromise of 1790 (which also moved the capital to Philadelphia temporarily and then permanently to the Potomac).
His Report on a National Bank (December 1790) proposed the Bank of the United States (First Bank, 1791-1811). When Washington hesitated over the bank’s constitutionality, Hamilton produced the Opinion on the Constitutionality of the Bank — a 15,000-word argument for implied powers and broad construction of the Constitution that ranks among the most important state papers in American history.
The Report on the Mint (1791) established a decimal currency and bimetallic standard. The Report on Manufactures (December 1791) argued for federal promotion of domestic industry through tariffs, bounties, and internal improvements — though Congress did not enact its specific proposals, it established the framework for American industrial policy.
Hamilton also created the Customs Service, the Revenue Cutter Service (precursor to the Coast Guard), and oversaw the financial markets of Philadelphia. When the Panic of 1792 struck after the collapse of speculation by his assistant William Duer, Hamilton ordered the Treasury to purchase $150,000 in government securities to stabilize the market — the first federal intervention to prevent a financial panic.
Political Battles
Hamilton’s programs provoked fierce opposition. Jefferson and Madison organized the Democratic-Republican Party in response, and a newspaper war erupted between Hamilton’s Gazette of the United States and Jefferson’s National Gazette. In 1793, House resolutions introduced by William Branch Giles accused Hamilton of maladministration; Hamilton produced exhaustive reports and was completely vindicated.
During the Citizen Genet Affair affair, Hamilton wrote the “Pacificus” essays defending the American Neutrality and arguing for executive authority in foreign policy. During the Whiskey Rebellion of 1794, he urged Washington to raise a federal militia and personally accompanied the army to western Pennsylvania. He defended the Jay’s Treaty in twenty-eight “Camillus” essays.
Later Years and the Duel with Burr
After resigning from the Treasury in 1795, Hamilton returned to his law practice in New York. He remained the intellectual leader of the Federalist Party and was appointed inspector general of the army during the Quasi-War with France (1798–1800). His pamphlet attacking John Adams in 1800 split the Federalist Party and helped ensure Jefferson’s election.
Hamilton’s long rivalry with Aaron Burr culminated in the gubernatorial election of 1804, when Hamilton actively opposed Burr’s candidacy. Burr demanded satisfaction, and the two men met at Weehawken, New Jersey, on July 11, 1804. Hamilton, having resolved to throw away his shot, fired into the air. Burr’s bullet struck Hamilton in the abdomen, and he died the following day at age 49.
Sources

Chernow, Ron. Alexander Hamilton. New York: Penguin Press, 2004.
Hamilton, Alexander. Report on Public Credit. 1790.
Hamilton, Alexander. Report on a National Bank. 1790.
Hamilton, Alexander. Opinion on the Constitutionality of the Bank. 1791.
Hamilton, Alexander. Report on the Subject of a Mint. 1791.
Hamilton, Alexander. Report on Manufactures. 1791.
Publius [Hamilton, Madison, Jay]. The Federalist Papers. 1787–1788.
Irving, Washington. The Life of George Washington. Vols. IV–V.

entities/bank-of-the-united-states.title: Bank of the United States (First Bank, 1791-1811)
entities/bank-of-the-united-states.content:
Bank of the United States (First Bank, 1791–1811)
The Bank of the United States was the central financial institution established by Alexander Hamilton in 1791. It served as the fiscal agent of the federal government and expanded the nation’s money supply through bank notes and credit. Its charter was not renewed in 1811.
Hamilton’s Proposal
Hamilton submitted his proposal for the Bank of the United States to Congress on December 13, 1790. His report argued that a national bank would serve three principal purposes: it would increase the active capital of the country through the mechanism of fractional-reserve banking; it would give the government easier access to credit, especially in emergencies; and it would facilitate the payment of taxes by expanding the circulating medium.
The bank was modeled on the Bank of England and the Bank of North America. Hamilton proposed a capital of $10 million, with one-fifth subscribed by the federal government and the remainder by private investors. The bank would hold government deposits, issue bank notes that circulated as currency, and make loans to the government and private borrowers.
Constitutional Controversy
The bank bill passed the Senate easily but provoked a furious constitutional debate in the House. James Madison, now leading the opposition, argued that the Constitution did not specifically grant the federal government the power to incorporate a bank. He argued for “strict construction” — that the federal government could exercise only those powers specifically enumerated.
When President George Washington hesitated, Hamilton produced a 15,000-word opinion, the Opinion on the Constitutionality of the Bank, arguing that the necessary and proper clause of the Constitution gave the government the right to employ all means necessary to carry out its enumerated powers. This famous argument for “implied powers” and “broad construction” ranks among the most important state papers in American political history.
Washington accepted Hamilton’s argument and signed the bank bill into law. The bank controversy deepened the emerging split between Hamilton and Madison, who had formerly been close collaborators on The Federalist Papers.
Operations and Legacy
The Bank of the United States opened for business in Philadelphia in December 1791. It issued bank notes, held government deposits, and regulated the currency. Its creation also sparked America’s first securities market boom and speculation frenzy. Hamilton’s argument for implied powers was later cited by Chief Justice John Marshall in McCulloch v. Maryland (1819), establishing the broad interpretation of federal power.
The bank’s charter expired in 1811, and Congress narrowly voted against renewal. A Second Bank of the United States was chartered in 1816.
Sources

Chernow, Ron. Alexander Hamilton. New York: Penguin Press, 2004.
Hamilton, Alexander. Report on a National Bank. 1790.
Hamilton, Alexander. Opinion on the Constitutionality of the Bank. 1791.

entities/benedict-arnold.title: Benedict Arnold
entities/benedict-arnold.content:
Benedict Arnold
Born: January 14, 1741, Norwich, Connecticut
Died: June 14, 1801, London, England
Spouse: Margaret Mansfield (m. 1767; d. 1775); Peggy Shippen Arnold (m. 1779)
Occupation: Merchant, soldier
Benedict Arnold was one of the most brilliant generals of the Continental Army before his treason made him the most infamous American of the 18th century.
Early Military Brilliance
At the outbreak of the Revolution, Arnold joined the army as a Connecticut militia captain. He participated in the capture of Fort Ticonderoga (May 1775) alongside Ethan Allen — the two forceful personalities clashing but succeeding in seizing the fort and its crucial artillery.
In the autumn of 1775, Washington selected Arnold to lead an expedition against Quebec through the Maine wilderness. The march was an ordeal that became legendary: 1,100 men entered the wilderness in September; by the time they reached the Chaudiere River in November, they were a ragged, starving remnant, having been forced to eat dogs, shoes, and cartridge boxes. Arnold pushed on with fierce energy, arriving opposite Quebec with about 600 exhausted men. Though the subsequent assault on Quebec failed, Washington wrote a remarkable eulogium of Arnold, praising his “astonishing” march.
Arnold played a crucial role at the Battle of Saratoga (1777), where he led a furious charge that broke the British lines, sustaining a leg wound in the process. His wound and his temperament contributed to a growing sense of grievance that he was not receiving adequate recognition or compensation from Congress.
Treason
In 1780, while commanding West Point, Arnold conspired with the British to surrender the fortress. The plot was discovered when the British spy John André was captured carrying papers revealing Arnold’s treason. Arnold escaped to the British lines just ahead of his arrest.
He served as a British brigadier general, leading raids against American forces in Virginia and Connecticut. After the war, he lived in London and died there in 1801, largely forgotten and impoverished.
Sources

Irving, Washington. The Life of George Washington. Vols. I–III. Boston: Desmond Publishing Co., 1899.

entities/benjamin-franklin.title: Benjamin Franklin
entities/benjamin-franklin.content:
Benjamin Franklin
Born: January 17, 1706 (Old Style: January 6, 1705), Boston, Massachusetts Bay
Died: April 17, 1790, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania
Spouse: Deborah Read Franklin (common-law marriage, 1730–1774)
Occupation: Printer, scientist, inventor, diplomat, statesman
Benjamin Franklin was the most famous American of the 18th century — a printer, scientist, inventor, diplomat, and statesman. He was the only person to sign all four of the key documents of the revolutionary era: the Declaration of Independence, the Treaty of Alliance with France, the Treaty of Paris (1783), and the Constitution.
Early Life
Franklin was born in Boston, the fifteenth of seventeen children of Josiah Franklin, a soap and candle maker. Apprenticed to his brother James, a printer, young Benjamin taught himself to write by studying the Spectator and published his first essays under the pseudonym “Silence Dogood.” At seventeen, he ran away to Philadelphia, where he established himself as a printer and publisher.
The Philadelphia Years
In Philadelphia, Franklin became a leading figure of the city. He published Poor Richard’s Almanack (1732–1758), a compendium of practical wisdom and proverbs. He founded the Junto, a discussion club; the Library Company of Philadelphia, America’s first subscription library; and the University of Pennsylvania.
Franklin’s scientific experiments established his international reputation. His most famous work was on electricity: he demonstrated that lightning is electrical in nature and invented the lightning rod. He also invented the Franklin stove, bifocal glasses, and the flexible urinary catheter. His studies of the Gulf Stream and weather patterns made contributions to oceanography and meteorology.
Franklin served as deputy postmaster-general for the colonies (1753–1774), improving postal delivery times and making the service self-sustaining. He represented Pennsylvania at the Albany Congress of 1754, where he proposed the Albany Plan of Union — an early attempt at colonial federation.
London and Paris
Franklin spent much of the 1760s in London as the colonial agent for Pennsylvania (and later Georgia, New Jersey, and Massachusetts). He was examined before the House of Commons during the Stamp Act crisis and famously demonstrated the practical impossibility of enforcing the act. He returned to America in 1775 and was elected to the Continental Congress.
In December 1776, Congress appointed Franklin as commissioner to France. He arrived in Paris as America’s most famous citizen, the embodiment of New World simplicity and Enlightenment philosophy. His popularity in French society helped secure the French alliance (1778), which was decisive for American independence. He served as American minister to France until 1785, negotiating the Treaty of Paris that ended the Revolutionary War.
Constitutional Convention and Final Years
Franklin returned to Philadelphia in 1785 and was elected president of Pennsylvania’s executive council. At the Constitutional Convention of 1787, he was the oldest delegate at 81. Though his own proposals (including a unicameral legislature) were not adopted, he played a crucial role in mediating disputes and forging compromises. His closing speech urged unanimous approval of the Constitution.
Franklin died in Philadelphia on April 17, 1790, at age 84. His funeral was attended by 20,000 mourners. His Autobiography, left unfinished at his death, became one of the most widely read works of American literature.
Sources

Isaacson, Walter. Benjamin Franklin: An American Life. New York: Simon & Schuster, 2003.
Irving, Washington. The Life of George Washington. Vols. I–V. Boston: Desmond Publishing Co., 1899.

entities/charles-cornwallis.title: Charles Cornwallis
entities/charles-cornwallis.content:
Charles Cornwallis
Born: December 31, 1738, London, England
Died: October 5, 1805, Ghazipur, India
Title: 1st Marquess Cornwallis
Occupation: British Army officer, colonial administrator
Charles Cornwallis was the British general whose army surrendered at Yorktown (1781), effectively ending the American Revolutionary War.
Campaigns in America
Cornwallis arrived in America in 1776 as a major general and served under General William Howe. He fought at the Battle of Long Island and the occupation of New York City. He was pursuing Washington across New Jersey in late 1776 when Washington turned and struck the Hessian garrison at Trenton on Christmas night and then defeated Cornwallis’s relief column at Princeton.
In 1778, Cornwallis served as second-in-command to General Henry Clinton. In 1780, he was given command of the British Southern campaign. He won a decisive victory over General Horatio Gates at Camden, South Carolina (August 1780), but his advance into North Carolina was checked by Nathanael Greene’s strategy of attrition. After a pyrrhic victory at Guilford Courthouse (March 1781), Cornwallis abandoned the Carolinas and marched into Virginia.
Yorktown
In Virginia, Cornwallis fortified Yorktown, expecting the British navy to maintain his supply line. Instead, a French fleet under Admiral de Grasse blockaded the Chesapeake, while Washington and Comte de Rochambeau marched south and trapped Cornwallis. After a three-week siege, Cornwallis surrendered on October 19, 1781. He sent his second, General O’Hara, to deliver his sword to Washington, claiming illness.
Cornwallis later served as Governor-General of India and as Lord Lieutenant of Ireland.
Sources

Irving, Washington. The Life of George Washington. Vols. II–III. Boston: Desmond Publishing Co., 1899.

entities/comte-de-rochambeau.title: Comte de Rochambeau
entities/comte-de-rochambeau.content:
Comte de Rochambeau
Born: July 1, 1725, Vendôme, Orléanais, France
Died: May 10, 1807, Thoré-la-Rochette, France
Full name: Jean-Baptiste Donatien de Vimeur, Comte de Rochambeau
Occupation: French Army officer
Jean-Baptiste Donatien de Vimeur, Comte de Rochambeau, was the commander of the French expeditionary force (the Expédition Particulière) that fought alongside the Continental Army in the American Revolution. His cooperation with George Washington at the Siege of Yorktown secured the decisive victory of the war.
The French Expedition
In 1780, Rochambeau arrived in Newport, Rhode Island, with 5,500 French soldiers. His forces were blockaded by the British navy for nearly a year before Admiral de Grasse’s fleet arrived in 1781. After coordinating with Washington, Rochambeau marched his army from Newport to join Washington’s forces on the Hudson, and then both armies marched south to Virginia.
Yorktown
Rochambeau’s French troops played a crucial role at the Siege of Yorktown, manning the siege lines alongside the Americans. The French fleet’s blockade prevented the escape or reinforcement of Charles Cornwallis’s army. The surrender of Cornwallis on October 19, 1781, effectively ended the war.
Later Life
Rochambeau returned to France after the war and served as a marshal during the French Revolution. He narrowly escaped the guillotine and died in 1807.
Sources

Irving, Washington. The Life of George Washington. Vol. III. Boston: Desmond Publishing Co., 1899.

entities/continental-army.title: Continental Army
entities/continental-army.content:
Continental Army
The Continental Army was the national army formed by the Continental Congress in 1775 to conduct the war against Great Britain. Commanded by General George Washington, it served from 1775 until its disbandment in 1783.
Formation
The Continental Congress authorized the raising of the Continental Army on June 14, 1775, and appointed George Washington as commander-in-chief the following day. Washington took formal command at Cambridge, Massachusetts, on July 3, 1775.
The army was initially a heterogeneous collection of militia regiments from the various colonies — poorly armed, badly supplied, and lacking any common organization. Washington reported to Congress that the army had barely 36 rounds of powder per man. The Rhode Island troops under Nathanael Greene stood out for their discipline, but most regiments were undisciplined and inexperienced.
Development and Training
The army grew and evolved over the course of the war. After the disastrous winter at Valley Forge (1777–1778), Friedrich Wilhelm von Steuben drilled the troops in European-style tactics, producing a standardized drill manual that became the foundation of American military training. The Battle of Monmouth (June 1778) demonstrated that the Continental Army could now fight British regulars on equal terms.
Composition
The army was composed of regiments raised by the states, serving for varying terms (often one to three years). Enlistment was a constant struggle; Washington repeatedly appealed to Congress and the state governments for longer enlistments and better pay. The army included infantry, artillery (commanded by Henry Knox), and cavalry units. African Americans served in the Continental Army, though their status varied by state.
Major Campaigns

Siege of Boston (1775–1776)
New York and New Jersey campaign (1776–1777) — defeats at Long Island and Fort Washington, victories at Trenton and Princeton
Philadelphia campaign (1777) — defeats at Brandywine and Germantown
Valley Forge winter encampment (1777–1778)
Monmouth (1778)
Southern campaign under Nathanael Greene (1780–1781)
Siege of Yorktown (1781)

Disbandment
After the Treaty of Paris (1783), the Continental Army was disbanded. Many officers formed the Society of the Cincinnati. The army’s experience under the Articles of Confederation demonstrated the need for a more permanent military establishment, which was created under the Constitution in 1789.
Sources

Irving, Washington. The Life of George Washington. Vols. I–V. Boston: Desmond Publishing Co., 1899.

entities/continental-congress.title: Continental Congress
entities/continental-congress.content:
Continental Congress
The Continental Congress was the revolutionary governing body of the American colonies and later the United States from 1774 to 1789. It consisted of the First Continental Congress (1774) and the Second Continental Congress (1775–1781), after which it continued as the Congress of the Confederation (1781–1789).
First Continental Congress
The First Continental Congress met in Philadelphia in September–October 1774, bringing together delegates from twelve colonies (Georgia alone was absent). George Washington was among the Virginia delegates. The Congress adopted a Declaratory Resolution asserting the rights of the colonies, a Bill of Rights enumerating grievances, and addresses to the king and the people of British America. It also established the Continental Association, a non-importation agreement.
Second Continental Congress
The Second Continental Congress convened in Philadelphia in May 1775, after the battles of Lexington and Concord. It functioned as the de facto national government throughout the Revolution. Its major actions included:

Appointing George Washington as commander-in-chief of the Continental Army (June 15, 1775)
Adopting the Declaration of Independence (July 4, 1776)
Adopting the Articles of Confederation (November 1777; ratified 1781)
Conducting foreign policy, including the French alliance (1778)
Issuing currency and managing the war effort
Overseeing the negotiation of the Treaty of Paris (1783)

Congress of the Confederation
Under the Articles of Confederation (1781–1789), Congress was a weak body that could only “recommend” measures to the states. It had no power to tax, regulate commerce, or enforce its decisions — structural defects that Alexander Hamilton, James Madison, and others identified as fatal weaknesses in The Federalist Papers.
The Congress of the Confederation passed the Land Ordinance of 1785 and the Northwest Ordinance of 1787, establishing the framework for western expansion. It also called the Constitutional Convention of 1787.
Replacement
The Constitution replaced the Continental Congress with the United States Congress — a bicameral legislature with the power to tax, regulate commerce, and legislate directly on individuals. The new Congress first met in 1789.
Sources

Irving, Washington. The Life of George Washington. Vols. I–V. Boston: Desmond Publishing Co., 1899.
Publius [Hamilton, Madison, Jay]. The Federalist Papers. 1787–1788.

entities/democratic-republican-party.title: Democratic-Republican Party
entities/democratic-republican-party.content:
Democratic-Republican Party
The Democratic-Republican Party (often called the Republican Party in the 1790s) was the opposition party formed by Thomas Jefferson and James Madison in response to the policies of Alexander Hamilton and the Federalists. It advocated for states’ rights, a strict interpretation of the Constitution, an agrarian economy, and sympathy for the French Revolution.
Origins
The Democratic-Republican Party emerged from the growing opposition to Hamilton’s financial program in 1791–1792. Jefferson, then Secretary of State, and Madison, then a congressman, organized the opposition. They recruited the poet Philip Freneau to establish the National Gazette as a Republican newspaper. Jefferson provided Freneau with a nominal position in the State Department as a translator, enabling him to attack Hamilton’s policies. The party drew its strength from southern planters, small farmers, and urban artisans.
Ideology
The Democratic-Republicans believed that Hamilton’s system would create a corrupt moneyed aristocracy that would subvert republican government. They advocated for:

Strict construction: The federal government could exercise only those powers specifically enumerated in the Constitution
States’ rights: State governments should be the primary locus of political authority
Agrarianism: America’s future lay in independent yeoman farmers, not commercial cities
Pro-French foreign policy: Sympathy for the French Revolution and opposition to the Jay’s Treaty

Leadership
Jefferson was the undisputed leader of the Democratic-Republican Party. Madison was his closest ally and strategist. Other prominent Democratic-Republicans included George Clinton, Aaron Burr, Patrick Henry (though he never formally joined), and William Branch Giles.
Triumph
The Democratic-Republican Party won the election of 1800, which Jefferson called “the Revolution of 1800.” It marked the first peaceful transfer of power between opposing political parties and the triumph of Jeffersonian Republicanism. The party dominated American politics for the next quarter-century.
Sources

Chernow, Ron. Alexander Hamilton. New York: Penguin Press, 2004.
Irving, Washington. The Life of George Washington. Vols. IV–V. Boston: Desmond Publishing Co., 1899.

entities/edmund-randolph.title: Edmund Randolph
entities/edmund-randolph.content:
Edmund Randolph
Born: August 10, 1753, Williamsburg, Virginia
Died: September 12, 1813, Millwood, Virginia
Occupation: Lawyer, statesman
Edmund Randolph was the governor of Virginia who presented the Virginia Plan at the Constitutional Convention and later served as the first Attorney General of the United States and as Secretary of State.
The Constitutional Convention
Randolph was a delegate to the Constitutional Convention of 1787 and, as governor of Virginia, presented the Virginia Plan (largely the work of James Madison) that became the framework for the Constitution. The plan called for a powerful national government with a bicameral legislature, an executive chosen by Congress, and a national judiciary.
However, at the end of the Convention, Randolph refused to sign the proposed Constitution, objecting to what he saw as insufficient checks on federal power. He published an explanation of his objections, which became an important Anti-Federalist document. Nevertheless, he later supported ratification at the Virginia ratifying convention.
Federal Office
President George Washington appointed Randolph as the first Attorney General of the United States in 1789. When Thomas Jefferson resigned as Secretary of State in 1793, Randolph succeeded him. He served as Secretary of State during the Citizen Genet Affair affair and the Whiskey Rebellion.
Randolph’s cabinet career ended in 1795 when he was accused of improperly soliciting money from the French minister. Though the charges were never proven, he resigned and returned to private law practice.
Sources

Irving, Washington. The Life of George Washington. Vol. IV. Boston: Desmond Publishing Co., 1899.

entities/federal-city-washington-dc.title: Federal City (Washington D.C.)
entities/federal-city-washington-dc.content:
Federal City (Washington D.C.)
The Federal City — later named Washington, D.C., in honor of George Washington — was the new permanent capital of the United States, established on the Potomac River as part of the Compromise of 1790.
The Compromise of 1790
The location of the permanent capital was a bitterly contested issue in the First Congress. Northern states wanted the capital in the North; Southern states wanted it in the South. The deadlock was broken in the summer of 1790 when Alexander Hamilton brokered a compromise: Southern votes for the assumption of state debts in exchange for Northern votes to locate the capital on the Potomac River. Thomas Jefferson famously hosted a dinner at which Hamilton and James Madison agreed to the arrangement.
The Residence Act of July 1790 provided that Philadelphia would serve as the temporary capital for ten years (1790–1800) while the new federal city was being built.
Planning and Construction
The site, a tract of land ceded by Maryland and Virginia, was chosen by Washington himself. He appointed Major Pierre Charles L’Enfant, a French engineer who had served in the Continental Army, to design the city. L’Enfant’s plan called for grand boulevards, public squares, and a grid pattern superposed with diagonal avenues — designed to rival the great capitals of Europe.
Construction proceeded slowly and was controversial. The city was still largely unfinished when the federal government moved there in 1800. The Capitol building had only one completed wing, and the President’s House (later the White House) was still under construction. Nevertheless, the location on the Potomac fulfilled Washington’s vision of a capital accessible to both northern and southern states.
Sources

Chernow, Ron. Alexander Hamilton. New York: Penguin Press, 2004.
Irving, Washington. The Life of George Washington. Vols. IV–V. Boston: Desmond Publishing Co., 1899.

entities/federalist-party.title: Federalist Party
entities/federalist-party.content:
Federalist Party
The Federalist Party was the first political party in the United States, formed in the 1790s around the policies and leadership of Alexander Hamilton. It advocated for a strong central government, a national bank, commercial development, and a close relationship with Great Britain.
Origins
The Federalist Party emerged from the struggle over Hamilton’s financial program. Though Hamilton dreaded factions as “the most fatal disease” of popular governments, his charismatic personality and far-reaching policies unified his followers while opposition from Thomas Jefferson and James Madison organized the Democratic-Republican Party. The Federalists drew their strength from banking and merchant interests in New England; the Republicans from southern planters and small farmers.
Policies
Federalist policy rested on Hamilton’s financial system: the funding of the national debt, assumption of state debts, the Bank of the United States (First Bank, 1791-1811), and federal promotion of commerce and manufacturing. In foreign policy, the Federalists favored neutrality in the European wars but maintained close commercial ties with Great Britain, as demonstrated by the Jay’s Treaty.
Leadership
Hamilton was the intellectual leader of the Federalist Party throughout its existence. George Washington, though he never formally identified as a Federalist, aligned with Federalist policies. John Adams was the Federalist presidential candidate in 1796 and 1800, though his relationship with Hamilton was deeply strained. Other prominent Federalists included John Jay, Gouverneur Morris, Henry Knox, and John Marshall.
Decline
The Federalist Party split in 1800 when Hamilton published a pamphlet attacking Adams, ensuring Jefferson’s election. The party never held the presidency again after Adams’s defeat. Though it remained a regional force in New England, the Federalist Party declined steadily in influence and had effectively disappeared as a national force by 1820.
Sources

Chernow, Ron. Alexander Hamilton. New York: Penguin Press, 2004.
Irving, Washington. The Life of George Washington. Vols. IV–V. Boston: Desmond Publishing Co., 1899.

entities/friedrich-wilhelm-von-steuben.title: Friedrich Wilhelm von Steuben
entities/friedrich-wilhelm-von-steuben.content:
Friedrich Wilhelm von Steuben
Born: September 17, 1730, Magdeburg, Kingdom of Prussia
Died: November 28, 1794, Utica, New York
Full name: Friedrich Wilhelm August Heinrich Ferdinand von Steuben
Occupation: Prussian Army officer, inspector general of the Continental Army
Friedrich Wilhelm von Steuben was a Prussian military officer who served as inspector general of the Continental Army and transformed Washington’s ragged troops into a disciplined European-style fighting force.
Valley Forge
Steuben arrived at Valley Forge in February 1778, during the darkest winter of the Revolution. He had served on the general staff of the Prussian Army under Frederick the Great and brought with him the latest European military drill and discipline.
Speaking little English, Steuben began drilling the troops himself, personally demonstrating military maneuvers. He selected a model company of 100 men and trained them intensively, then used them to demonstrate proper drill to the rest of the army. His Regulations for the Order and Discipline of the Troops of the United States (the “Blue Book”) became the standard drill manual for the Continental Army.
Steuben’s training produced immediate results. At the Battle of Monmouth (June 1778), the Continental Army fought the British to a standstill in a pitched battle — something it had never done before. The discipline and professionalism that Steuben instilled were essential to the army’s eventual victory.
Later Service
Steuben served with the Continental Army through the end of the war and was present at the Siege of Yorktown. He was naturalized as an American citizen and was granted a pension and a tract of land in New York, where he died in 1794.
Sources

Irving, Washington. The Life of George Washington. Vols. II–III. Boston: Desmond Publishing Co., 1899.

entities/george-clinton.title: George Clinton
entities/george-clinton.content:
George Clinton
Born: July 26, 1739, Little Britain, New York
Died: April 20, 1812, Washington, D.C.
Occupation: Soldier, statesman
George Clinton was a prominent Anti-Federalist leader, the first Governor of New York (1777–1795, 1801–1804), and the fourth Vice President of the United States (1805–1812).
Revolutionary Service
Clinton served as a brigadier general in the Continental Army during the Revolution. He participated in the defense of New York in 1776 and commanded the American forces at Fort Montgomery, where he was wounded but successfully delayed the British advance up the Hudson.
Anti-Federalist Leader
As Governor of New York, Clinton was the leading Anti-Federalist opponent of the proposed Constitution of 1787. He argued against ratification, fearing that the new national government would overwhelm the states and undermine liberty. Under the pseudonym “Cato,” he published a series of essays opposing the Constitution — though Alexander Hamilton, James Madison, and John Jay answered these arguments in The Federalist Papers.
Clinton’s influence was such that Hamilton considered him a major obstacle to the new government. In the 1790s, Clinton allied with the Democratic-Republicans against the Federalists. His daughter, Cornelia Clinton, married the former French minister Citizen Genet Affair after Genêt was recalled.
Clinton died in office as Vice President under James Madison in 1812.
Sources

Irving, Washington. The Life of George Washington. Vols. IV–V. Boston: Desmond Publishing Co., 1899.

entities/george-washington.title: George Washington
entities/george-washington.content:
George Washington
Born: February 11, 1732 (Old Style) / February 22, 1732 (New Style), Pope’s Creek, Westmoreland County, Virginia
Died: December 14, 1799, Mount Vernon, Virginia
Spouse: Martha Washington (née Dandridge Custis), married January 6, 1759
Occupation: Planter, surveyor, soldier, statesman
George Washington was the leading military and political figure of the American Revolution and the early republic. He served as Commander-in-Chief of the Continental Army from 1775 to 1783 and as the first President of the United States from 1789 to 1797.
Early Life and Family
Washington was born into the Virginia gentry, the son of Augustine Washington and Mary Ball Washington. His father died when George was about eleven, and his elder half-brother Lawrence Washington became a paternal influence. Through Lawrence, young George was introduced to the Fairfax family of Belvoir, a refined and cultivated circle that included Lord Fairfax, a wealthy English nobleman with vast Virginia estates.
As a youth, Washington compiled his famous “Rules of Behavior in Company and Conversation” — 110 maxims covering deportment and manners. He studied geometry and surveying, and at sixteen undertook his first surveying expedition beyond the Blue Ridge into the Shenandoah Valley, keeping a detailed diary recording soil qualities, tree species, and land values.
French and Indian War Service
Washington’s military career began in 1753 when Governor Dinwiddie sent him as an emissary to the French commander on the Ohio, demanding French withdrawal. His journal of this dangerous winter mission provided the first detailed intelligence of French intentions and was widely circulated. In 1754, as a lieutenant colonel, Washington led a force toward the Ohio and was involved in the Jumonville skirmish, a controversial action that became a European cause célèbre. He built Fort Necessity at the Great Meadows but was forced to capitulate to a superior French force in July 1754.
In 1755, Washington served as an aide-de-camp to General Braddock in the disastrous expedition against Fort Duquesne. Braddock’s army was ambushed and destroyed; Washington, though ill with fever, rode through the battle and had four bullets pierce his coat without being wounded — a providential deliverance he long remembered. He later commanded Virginia’s frontier forces, defending the Shenandoah Valley against Indian raids. In 1758, he served under General Forbes in the successful campaign that finally captured Fort Duquesne (renamed Fort Pitt). Washington resigned his commission and returned to civilian life.
Planter and Legislator
Washington married Martha Dandridge Custis, a wealthy widow, in January 1759, and settled at Mount Vernon to manage his estate. He became a systematic, scientific farmer, rotating crops, experimenting with fertilizers, and keeping meticulous accounts. He served in the Virginia House of Burgesses and became increasingly active in the colonial resistance to British taxation following the Stamp Act of 1765.
Washington chaired the meeting at the Fairfax County courthouse that adopted the Fairfax Resolves (drafted largely by George Mason). He was elected a delegate to the First and Second Continental Congresses. In March 1775, at the Virginia Convention in Richmond, he heard Patrick Henry’s “Give me liberty or give me death” speech and made clear his readiness to take up arms.
Commander-in-Chief of the Continental Army
On June 15, 1775, the Continental Congress unanimously appointed Washington commander-in-chief of the Continental Army. He refused any salary, asking only that his expenses be paid. He took command at Cambridge, Massachusetts, on July 3, 1775, under the great elm tree on Cambridge Common.
Washington’s first challenge was forging a disciplined army from the heterogeneous militia regiments surrounding Boston. He organized the siege of Boston, which culminated in March 1776 when the British evacuated the city after Henry Knox brought the Ticonderoga artillery. Washington then moved to defend New York, where he suffered a series of defeats — the Battle of Long Island, the evacuation of New York City, and the retreat across New Jersey in the fall of 1776.
In a daring stroke, Washington crossed the Delaware River on Christmas night 1776 and surprised the Hessian garrison at Trenton, capturing nearly a thousand men. He followed this victory with another at Princeton in early January 1777. These victories, which Irving calls the “American Fabius” strategy, revived the revolutionary cause at its darkest moment.
The campaign of 1777 saw Benedict Arnold’s and Horatio Gates’s victory at Saratoga while Washington suffered defeats at Brandywine and Germantown and settled into winter quarters at Valley Forge. There, Friedrich Wilhelm von Steuben drilled the army into a professional force. In June 1778, Washington fought the British to a draw at Monmouth.
Washington’s strategic genius was most evident in the southern campaign. Appointing Nathanael Greene to command in the South, Washington kept the main army near New York while waiting for an opportunity to strike decisively. That opportunity came when Cornwallis moved into Virginia. Washington marched south with Comte de Rochambeau’s French army, and together they trapped Cornwallis at Yorktown. The siege culminated in Cornwallis’s surrender on October 19, 1781, effectively ending the war.
Post-War and the Presidency
After the war, Washington returned to Mount Vernon, but the weaknesses of the Articles of Confederation convinced him of the need for a stronger national government. He presided over the Constitutional Convention in Philadelphia in 1787.
In 1789, Washington was unanimously elected the first President of the United States. His administration established many precedents: the cabinet system, the inaugural address, and the use of executive departments. He appointed Alexander Hamilton as Secretary of the Treasury, Thomas Jefferson as Secretary of State, Henry Knox as Secretary of War, and Edmund Randolph as Attorney General.
Washington’s first term saw the establishment of the Treasury Department, the Bank of the United States (First Bank, 1791-1811), and the funding of the national debt — policies primarily shaped by Hamilton. Washington navigated the growing division between Hamilton’s Federalists and Jefferson’s Democratic-Republicans, striving to maintain harmony in his cabinet.
In his second term, Washington faced the Whiskey Rebellion of 1794, the Jay’s Treaty crisis, and the Citizen Genet Affair affair. He issued the American Neutrality, keeping the United States out of the European wars of the French Revolution. His Farewell Address of 1796 warned against foreign entanglements and party divisions.
Washington died at Mount Vernon on December 14, 1799, after a brief illness. Henry Lee’s famous eulogy pronounced him “first in war, first in peace, and first in the hearts of his countrymen.”
Washington’s Character
Contemporaries described Washington as dignified, reserved, and commanding. He was known for his physical strength, his imposing height (over six feet, unusual for the period), and his formidable temper, which he kept under careful control. He maintained a strict sense of honor and propriety throughout his life. His correspondence reveals a methodical mind, a commitment to duty, and a deep sense of religious Providence.
Sources

Irving, Washington. The Life of George Washington. Vols. I–V. Boston: Desmond Publishing Co., 1899.
Chernow, Ron. Alexander Hamilton. New York: Penguin Press, 2004.

entities/gouverneur-morris.title: Gouverneur Morris
entities/gouverneur-morris.content:
Gouverneur Morris
Born: January 31, 1752, Morrisania, New York
Died: November 6, 1816, Morrisania, New York
Occupation: Statesman, diplomat
Gouverneur Morris was a delegate to the Constitutional Convention of 1787 and the man who actually wrote the final text of the United States Constitution. He was a brilliant, witty Federalist who played a key role in shaping the new government.
The Constitutional Convention
Morris was one of the most active delegates at the Constitutional Convention, speaking more often than any other member. He was appointed to the Committee of Style, which was tasked with drafting the final text of the Constitution, and it was Morris who gave the document its distinctive literary form. The Preamble — “We the People of the United States” — is his formulation.
Morris argued forcefully for a strong executive, a national government with authority over individuals, and the protection of property rights. He opposed concessions to the small states but accepted the Great Compromise when it became necessary.
Later Career
After the Convention, Morris served as minister to France (1792–1794) and was an eyewitness to the French Revolution and the Reign of Terror. He was the only diplomat who remained in Paris during the Terror. He later served as a U.S. Senator from New York (1800–1803).
Morris remained a committed Federalist throughout his life. Alexander Hamilton wrote to him in the aftermath of the election of 1800, lamenting that “the Constitution is a frail and worthless fabric.”
Sources

Irving, Washington. The Life of George Washington. Vol. IV. Boston: Desmond Publishing Co., 1899.

entities/henry-knox.title: Henry Knox
entities/henry-knox.content:
Henry Knox
Born: July 25, 1750, Boston, Massachusetts Bay
Died: October 25, 1806, Thomaston, Massachusetts (now Maine)
Spouse: Lucy Flucker Knox
Occupation: Bookseller, soldier, statesman
Henry Knox was a Boston bookseller who became George Washington’s chief artillery officer and the first Secretary of War of the United States.
The Noble Train of Artillery
At the beginning of the Siege of Boston, Knox proposed a daring plan to Washington: bring the heavy artillery captured at Ticonderoga across the winter wilderness to Boston. Washington approved, and Knox undertook an epic journey in the winter of 1775–1776. His expedition hauled 59 cannon and mortars on specially built sledges across 300 miles of frozen rivers, snow-covered mountains, and primitive roads. The artillery arrived at Cambridge in January 1776 and was emplaced on Dorchester Heights, forcing the British to evacuate Boston on March 17, 1776.
Military Career
Knox served throughout the Revolution as Washington’s chief of artillery, commanding the artillery arm at the battles of Trenton, Princeton, Brandywine, Germantown, Monmouth, and Yorktown. He was promoted to major general in 1782 and was one of the founders of the Society of the Cincinnati.
Secretary of War
After the war, Knox served as Secretary of War under the Articles of Confederation and continued as the first Secretary of War under the Constitution (1789–1794). His department under Washington’s administration was much smaller than Hamilton’s Treasury — Knox had only a dozen civilians in the War Department. He oversaw the military establishment during the early Indian wars on the frontier.
Knox retired from public life in 1794 and devoted himself to his estate in Maine.
Sources

Irving, Washington. The Life of George Washington. Vols. I–V. Boston: Desmond Publishing Co., 1899.

entities/james-madison.title: James Madison
entities/james-madison.content:
James Madison
Born: March 16, 1751, Port Conway, Virginia
Died: June 28, 1836, Montpelier, Virginia
Spouse: Dolley Payne Todd Madison (m. 1794)
Occupation: Statesman, political philosopher
James Madison was the principal architect of the United States Constitution, a co-author of The Federalist Papers, and the leading figure in the First Congress. He began his career as Alexander Hamilton’s closest collaborator but later broke with Hamilton to join Thomas Jefferson in founding the Democratic-Republican Party.
Constitutional Convention
Madison arrived at the Constitutional Convention of 1787 as the best-prepared delegate. He had spent the previous year studying historical confederacies and drafting a comprehensive plan for a new national government. His Virginia Plan, presented by Governor Edmund Randolph, became the framework for the Constitution. Madison spoke more than any other delegate and kept the most complete notes of the proceedings, which remain the primary source for the Convention’s debates.
The Federalist Papers
Madison collaborated with Hamilton and John Jay on The Federalist Papers, contributing 29 essays. His most celebrated contribution is Federalist No. 10, which argues that an extended republic can control the violence of faction better than a small democracy can. He argues that in a large republic, the multiplicity of interests makes it difficult for any single faction to form a majority and oppress the minority. Federalist No. 51, also by Madison, articulates the principle of separation of powers: “Ambition must be made to counteract ambition.”
Madison also authored the essays on the legislative branch (Nos. 52–58, 62–63) and the theoretical defenses of the Constitution’s structure (Nos. 37–51).
Opposition to Hamilton
In the First Congress, Madison initially supported Hamilton’s financial program, but he broke with Hamilton over the Bank of the United States (First Bank, 1791-1811). Madison argued for “strict construction” — that the federal government could exercise only those powers specifically enumerated in the Constitution. Hamilton responded with his “broad construction” argument based on the necessary and proper clause. This debate was the opening shot in a constitutional argument that would continue for decades.
Madison joined Jefferson in organizing the Democratic-Republican Party, writing anonymous newspaper essays attacking Hamilton’s system as a “government operated by corrupt influence.” The split between the two former Federalist collaborators became irreparable.
Later Career
Madison served as Jefferson’s Secretary of State (1801–1809) and succeeded him as the fourth President (1809–1817), leading the nation through the War of 1812. After leaving the presidency, he lived in retirement at Montpelier, working on his papers and serving as rector of the University of Virginia.
Sources

Publius [Hamilton, Madison, Jay]. The Federalist Papers. 1787–1788.
Chernow, Ron. Alexander Hamilton. New York: Penguin Press, 2004.
Irving, Washington. The Life of George Washington. Vol. IV. Boston: Desmond Publishing Co., 1899.

entities/john-adams.title: John Adams
entities/john-adams.content:
John Adams
Born: October 30, 1735 (Old Style: October 19, 1735), Braintree, Massachusetts Bay
Died: July 4, 1826, Quincy, Massachusetts
Spouse: Abigail Smith Adams (m. 1764)
Occupation: Lawyer, statesman
John Adams was a leader of the American Revolution, the first Vice President of the United States, and the second President. His political career was marked by his strained relationship with Alexander Hamilton and the Federalist Party.
Revolutionary Career
Adams was a delegate to the Continental Congress and one of the earliest advocates for independence. He served on the committee to draft the Declaration of Independence and was its most forceful advocate on the floor of Congress. He nominated George Washington as commander-in-chief of the Continental Army.
During the war, Adams served as a diplomat in France and the Netherlands, helping to secure European support for the American cause. He was part of the commission that negotiated the Treaty of Paris (1783).
Vice Presidency and Presidency
Adams served two terms as the first Vice President under Washington. He described the office as “the most insignificant office that ever the invention of man contrived or his imagination conceived.” He presided over the Senate and cast 29 tie-breaking votes.
Elected President in 1796, Adams inherited the growing conflict between the Federalists and the Democratic-Republicans. His administration was dominated by the Quasi-War with France (1798–1800). Adams, distrusting Hamilton’s influence in his cabinet, split the Federalist Party by sending a peace mission to France in 1799 against the advice of Hamilton and his own cabinet. Hamilton responded with a devastating pamphlet attacking Adams as unfit for the presidency — a catastrophic error that split the Federalist Party and ensured Jefferson’s election.
Adams lost the election of 1800 to Thomas Jefferson and retired to Quincy, Massachusetts. He lived to see his son John Quincy Adams become President and died on July 4, 1826 — the 50th anniversary of the Declaration, on the same day as Jefferson. His last words were reported as “Thomas Jefferson survives.”
Sources

Irving, Washington. The Life of George Washington. Vols. IV–V. Boston: Desmond Publishing Co., 1899.
Chernow, Ron. Alexander Hamilton. New York: Penguin Press, 2004.

entities/john-jay.title: John Jay
entities/john-jay.content:
John Jay
Born: December 23, 1745, New York City
Died: May 17, 1829, Bedford, New York
Spouse: Sarah Livingston Jay (m. 1774)
Occupation: Jurist, diplomat, statesman
John Jay was the first Chief Justice of the United States Supreme Court, a diplomat of the Revolution, and one of the three authors of The Federalist Papers. He was a leading figure of the Federalist Party.
Revolutionary Career
Jay served in the Continental Congress and was its president from 1778 to 1779. He was dispatched as minister to Spain (1779–1782), where he failed to secure Spanish recognition or aid but gained valuable diplomatic experience. He was part of the peace commission that negotiated the Treaty of Paris (1783), along with Benjamin Franklin and John Adams.
After the war, Jay served as Secretary for Foreign Affairs under the Articles of Confederation (1784–1789).
The Federalist Papers
Jay contributed five essays to The Federalist Papers (Nos. 2–5, 64). His essays dealt with the dangers of foreign force and influence and the treaty-making power of the Senate. Illness prevented him from writing more, but his contributions established the framework for the arguments about national unity and foreign policy that Hamilton and Madison developed at greater length. Federalist No. 64 defends the treaty-making power as shared between the President and Senate, arguing that the supermajority requirement ensures broad agreement.
Chief Justice and Governor
President George Washington appointed Jay as the first Chief Justice of the United States in 1789. He served until 1795, establishing the early precedents of the Supreme Court.
In 1794, Washington dispatched Jay as a special envoy to London to avert war with Great Britain. The resulting Jay’s Treaty secured British evacuation of the northwest forts and established “most favored nation” trading status with Britain. The treaty was deeply controversial — Jay was burned in effigy from Georgia to Massachusetts — but it preserved peace with Britain. Hamilton defended the treaty in the “Camillus” essays.
Jay resigned as Chief Justice in 1795 and served as Governor of New York (1795–1801). He retired to his estate in Bedford, New York.
Sources

Publius [Hamilton, Madison, Jay]. The Federalist Papers. 1787–1788.
Irving, Washington. The Life of George Washington. Vols. IV–V. Boston: Desmond Publishing Co., 1899.

entities/john-marshall.title: John Marshall
entities/john-marshall.content:
John Marshall
Born: September 24, 1755, Germantown, Virginia
Died: July 6, 1835, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania
Occupation: Jurist, statesman
John Marshall was the fourth Chief Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States (1801–1835) and the principal architect of American constitutional law. His decisions established the judiciary as a co-equal branch of the federal government.
Revolutionary Service
Marshall served as an officer in the Continental Army during the Revolution, participating in the battles of Brandywine, Germantown, Monmouth, and Valley Forge. He was at Valley Forge during the terrible winter of 1777–1778, where he witnessed the army’s suffering.
Chief Justice
President John Adams appointed Marshall as Chief Justice in 1801, in the final months of Adams’s term. Marshall served for 34 years, shaping the Supreme Court into a powerful institution. His most famous decision was Marbury v. Madison (1803), which established the principle of judicial review — the power of the courts to declare laws unconstitutional.
Marshall’s constitutional jurisprudence consistently favored a strong national government, a broad interpretation of federal powers, and the protection of property rights — principles he had absorbed from the Federalist tradition of Alexander Hamilton. In McCulloch v. Maryland (1819), he cited Hamilton’s argument for “implied powers” in upholding the constitutionality of the Bank of the United States (First Bank, 1791-1811), writing that “the power to tax is the power to destroy.”
Connection to the Period
Though Marshall’s greatest decisions came in the early 19th century, his thinking was formed by his experience in the Revolution and his service in the Virginia ratifying convention (1788), where he supported the Constitution. He was one of the founding generation who translated the principles of 1787 into the living law of the republic.
Sources

Chernow, Ron. Alexander Hamilton. New York: Penguin Press, 2004.

entities/marquis-de-lafayette.title: Marquis de Lafayette
entities/marquis-de-lafayette.content:
Marquis de Lafayette
Born: September 6, 1757, Chavaniac, Auvergne, France
Died: May 20, 1834, Paris, France
Full name: Marie-Joseph Paul Yves Roch Gilbert du Motier, Marquis de Lafayette
Occupation: Soldier, statesman
Marie-Joseph Paul Yves Roch Gilbert du Motier, Marquis de Lafayette, was a French aristocrat who volunteered his service to the Continental Army and became a trusted subordinate of George Washington.
Arrival in America
Lafayette arrived in America in 1777, at age 19, offering to serve without pay as a volunteer major general. The Continental Congress initially hesitated, but Lafayette’s enthusiasm and his family connections in France — his father-in-law, the Duc d’Ayen, was a powerful courtier — made him a valuable asset for securing French support. Congress commissioned him a major general on July 31, 1777.
Lafayette quickly formed a deep bond with Washington, who treated him almost as a son. He served at the Battle of Brandywine (September 1777), where he was wounded in the leg but continued to rally the troops. He wintered at Valley Forge and was a witness to the army’s suffering and the training efforts of Friedrich Wilhelm von Steuben.
Military Service
Lafayette served with distinction at the Battle of Monmouth (June 1778) and commanded troops in Rhode Island. In 1781, he was dispatched to Virginia to contain Charles Cornwallis’s army, shadowing the British forces until Washington and Comte de Rochambeau arrived with the main army. Lafayette commanded a division at the Siege of Yorktown.
After Yorktown, Lafayette returned to France, where he became a leading figure in the early stages of the French Revolution. He visited America one last time in 1824–1825, touring the nation and receiving an emotional welcome from a grateful republic.
Sources

Irving, Washington. The Life of George Washington. Vols. I–IV. Boston: Desmond Publishing Co., 1899.

entities/martha-washington.title: Martha Washington
entities/martha-washington.content:
Martha Washington
Born: June 2, 1731 (Old Style), New Kent County, Virginia
Died: May 22, 1802, Mount Vernon, Virginia
Birth name: Martha Dandridge
Spouse: Daniel Parke Custis (m. 1750; d. 1757); George Washington (m. 1759)
Occupation: Planter’s wife, First Lady
Martha Dandridge Custis Washington was the wife of George Washington and the first First Lady of the United States. She was known for her grace, hospitality, and devotion to her husband.
Marriage to Washington
Martha was a wealthy young widow with two small children, John Parke Custis and Martha Parke Custis, when she met Washington at the estate of Mr. Chamberlayne in 1758. Their courtship was famously brief; within a few weeks, Washington proposed and was accepted. They were married on January 6, 1759, at her estate, the White House, on the Pamunkey River.
The marriage brought Washington considerable wealth and social standing. Martha’s inheritance from the Custis estate included extensive lands, slaves, and cash that enabled Washington to expand Mount Vernon.
Lady Washington in the Revolution
During the Revolution, Martha Washington joined her husband at the winter encampments, including Valley Forge (1777–1778) and Morristown. She served as a hostess, nurse, and morale-booster, earning the affection of the officers and soldiers. She traveled to Cambridge in the winter of 1775–1776 with considerable equipage — her coach-and-four and liveried servants — and established domestic affairs at the Craigie House headquarters.
First Lady
As the first President’s wife, Martha Washington presided over the social functions of the presidential household in New York and Philadelphia. She was known for her formal Friday evening receptions (called “drawing rooms”) and for her dignified, gracious manner. She set the precedents for the role of the president’s spouse.
After Washington’s death in 1799, Martha lived quietly at Mount Vernon, maintaining the estate and preserving her husband’s legacy. She died in 1802 and was buried beside Washington at Mount Vernon.
Sources

Irving, Washington. The Life of George Washington. Vols. IV–V. Boston: Desmond Publishing Co., 1899.

entities/mount-vernon.title: Mount Vernon
entities/mount-vernon.content:
Mount Vernon
Mount Vernon was the beloved plantation estate of George Washington, located on the Potomac River in Fairfax County, Virginia. It served as Washington’s home before, during, and after his public career, and was the center of his identity as a Virginia planter.
The Estate
The estate was originally owned by Washington’s half-brother Lawrence Washington, who inherited it from their father Augustine. Lawrence named it Mount Vernon after Admiral Edward Vernon, under whom he had served in the Carthagena expedition of 1741. On Lawrence’s death in 1752, George Washington eventually inherited the estate.
Washington expanded Mount Vernon substantially, eventually owning more than 8,000 acres across five farms. The mansion house was enlarged and remodeled in the Federal style, with distinctive wooden siding cut and beveled to resemble stone. The estate overlooked the Potomac River and provided a magnificent prospect.
Agricultural Management
Washington was a systematic, scientific farmer who rotated crops, experimented with fertilizers, and kept meticulous accounts. During the long period between the French and Indian War and the Revolution (1759–1775), he devoted his energies to making Mount Vernon a model plantation. He wrote detailed instructions to his agent Lund Washington when he was away commanding the army, insisting that the hospitality of the house be maintained even in his absence.
During the Revolution
Mount Vernon was at risk during the war — British cruisers on the Potomac could threaten the mansion. Washington invited his wife Martha Washington to join him at Cambridge for the winter of 1775–1776. He left Lund Washington in charge with careful instructions about the plantation, the slaves, and the accounts.
Retirement and Death
Washington returned to Mount Vernon after the war in 1783 and again after his presidency in 1797. He died at Mount Vernon on December 14, 1799, after a brief illness. He was buried in the family vault on the estate. Mount Vernon became a shrine to his memory.
Sources

Irving, Washington. The Life of George Washington. Vols. I–V. Boston: Desmond Publishing Co., 1899.

entities/nathanael-greene.title: Nathanael Greene
entities/nathanael-greene.content:
Nathanael Greene
Born: August 7, 1742, Potowomut, Rhode Island
Died: June 19, 1786, Mulberry Grove, Georgia
Spouse: Catharine Littlefield Greene
Occupation: Ironmonger, soldier
Nathanael Greene was the most trusted general of George Washington and one of the finest military commanders of the American Revolution. His command of the Southern theater from 1780 to 1783 reversed the course of the war.
Early Revolutionary Service
Greene was a Quaker-born ironmonger with no formal military education, but he educated himself in military science and became Washington’s most capable subordinate. He served as a brigadier general in the Rhode Island regiments, which Irving notes stood out for their discipline among the heterogeneous army at Boston. Greene commanded the army’s right wing at the Battle of Long Island and led the retreat across the Jerseys.
He served as Quartermaster General from 1778 to 1780, reorganizing the supply system of the Continental Army. Though the position was thankless and often criticized, Greene’s administrative abilities proved essential to the army’s survival.
The Southern Campaign
In October 1780, following the disastrous Battle of Camden (where Horatio Gates fled the field), Washington appointed Greene to command the Southern Department. Greene faced the formidable Charles Cornwallis with a shattered army and inadequate supplies.
Greene adopted a strategy of strategic retreat and attrition. He divided his already-outnumbered force, sending Daniel Morgan to the west while keeping the main army on the east side of the Catawba River. Morgan destroyed the British regiment of Banastre Tarleton at the Battle of Cowpens (January 17, 1781). Greene then conducted a masterful retreat across North Carolina, drawing Cornwallis deep into the interior while preserving his own army.
Turning to fight at Guilford Courthouse (March 15, 1781), Greene fought a tactical battle that forced Cornwallis to abandon the Carolinas and march into Virginia, where he would eventually be trapped at Yorktown. Greene then returned to the Carolinas, forcing the British back into Charleston. By the end of 1781, the British held only Charleston and Savannah in the South.
After the war, Greene returned to Rhode Island but later moved to a plantation in Georgia, where he died at the age of 43, just three years after the war’s end.
Sources

Irving, Washington. The Life of George Washington. Vols. II–V. Boston: Desmond Publishing Co., 1899.

entities/patrick-henry.title: Patrick Henry
entities/patrick-henry.content:
Patrick Henry
Born: May 29, 1736, Hanover County, Virginia
Died: June 6, 1799, Red Hill, Virginia
Occupation: Lawyer, planter, statesman, orator
Patrick Henry was the most celebrated orator of the American Revolution and a leading Anti-Federalist opponent of the Constitution. His fiery speeches rallied Virginians to the cause of independence.
The Stamp Act Speech
In May 1765, the Virginia House of Burgesses debated the Stamp Act. Henry introduced a series of resolutions asserting the colonies’ right to self-taxation and denied Parliament’s authority to tax the colonies. In the course of the debate, he delivered a speech that electrified the assembly, defying the king himself. When interrupted by cries of “Treason!”, Henry concluded: “If this be treason, make the most of it.” George Washington, sitting in the House, heard Henry’s thunder but maintained his own more measured course.
”Give Me Liberty or Give Me Death”
In March 1775, at the Virginia Convention in Richmond, Henry delivered his most famous speech, calling for the colony to arm itself against British aggression. He concluded with the words: “I know not what course others may take; but as for me, give me liberty or give me death.” Washington, rising to speak after Henry, made clear his own readiness to take up arms.
Anti-Federalism
Henry was the most prominent Anti-Federalist in the Virginia ratification convention of 1788. He argued passionately against the proposed Constitution, warning that the new national government would overshadow the states and threaten liberty. He was instrumental in securing the adoption of the Bill of Rights as a condition of Virginia’s ratification.
Henry declined office under the new federal government, preferring to remain a private citizen and a voice of skepticism about centralized power. He supported the Democratic-Republican Party in the 1790s.
Sources

Irving, Washington. The Life of George Washington. Vol. IV. Boston: Desmond Publishing Co., 1899.

entities/philadelphia.title: Philadelphia
entities/philadelphia.content:
Philadelphia
Philadelphia was the largest and most cosmopolitan city in 18th-century America. It served as the meeting place of the Continental Congress, the site of the Declaration of Independence and the Constitutional Convention, and the temporary capital of the United States from 1790 to 1800.
The Revolutionary Capital
The First and Second Continental Congresses met in Philadelphia at the Pennsylvania State House (Independence Hall). The Declaration of Independence was adopted there on July 4, 1776, and the Constitution was drafted there in 1787. During the British occupation of Philadelphia (September 1777–June 1778), Congress convened in York, Pennsylvania.
Philadelphia was also the home of Benjamin Franklin, who founded many of its enduring institutions: the Library Company of Philadelphia (America’s first subscription library), the University of Pennsylvania, and the American Philosophical Society.
The Federal Capital
When the federal government moved from New York to Philadelphia in 1790 (as an interim measure while the Federal City was being built), Philadelphia was praised by one British visitor as “one of the wonders of the world.” Alexander Hamilton moved the Treasury Department to a two-story brick building on Third Street, and he took a home at Third and Walnut.
Philadelphia was the center of America’s first securities market. Government bonds traded actively on the streets around the Merchants’ Coffee House on Second Street. The speculative fever of 1791–1792 saw the creation of the first organized securities trading in America.
The Yellow Fever Epidemic of 1793
In the late summer of 1793, Philadelphia was devastated by the worst yellow fever epidemic in American history. More than 4,000 of the city’s 50,000 residents died — roughly 8 percent of the population. Government came to a standstill; Congress adjourned, Washington retreated to Mount Vernon, and Hamilton contracted the disease but recovered. The epidemic led to the departure of many permanent residents to new settlements outside the city.
Sources

Irving, Washington. The Life of George Washington. Vols. I–V. Boston: Desmond Publishing Co., 1899.
Chernow, Ron. Alexander Hamilton. New York: Penguin Press, 2004.

entities/philip-schuyler.title: Philip Schuyler
entities/philip-schuyler.content:
Philip Schuyler
Born: November 20, 1733, Albany, New York
Died: November 18, 1804, Albany, New York
Spouse: Catherine Van Rensselaer Schuyler
Occupation: Soldier, statesman, landowner
Philip Schuyler was a New York patrician of Dutch descent, a major general in the Continental Army, and the father-in-law of Alexander Hamilton. He was a leading figure in the political and social life of New York.
Revolutionary Service
Schuyler was appointed one of the first major generals in the Continental Army in 1775, commanding the Northern Department. He organized the invasion of Canada in 1775–1776, working closely with General Richard Montgomery. Despite his organizational abilities, Schuyler suffered from chronic illness that limited his field command. He was succeeded by Horatio Gates after the fall of Ticonderoga in 1777.
Schuyler served in the Continental Congress and the New York State Senate. He supported the ratification of the Constitution in New York.
Hamilton Connection
Schuyler’s daughter, Elizabeth Schuyler Hamilton, married Alexander Hamilton in 1780. Schuyler became a strong political ally and patron of his son-in-law. In 1791, Aaron Burr defeated Schuyler for a seat in the U.S. Senate — a defeat that began the long enmity between Hamilton and Burr. Schuyler again ran for the Senate in 1797 and won, serving until his death in 1804.
Schuyler died just months after his son-in-law’s fatal duel with Burr.
Sources

Chernow, Ron. Alexander Hamilton. New York: Penguin Press, 2004.
Irving, Washington. The Life of George Washington. Vol. I. Boston: Desmond Publishing Co., 1899.

entities/robert-morris.title: Robert Morris
entities/robert-morris.content:
Robert Morris
Born: January 20, 1734, Liverpool, England
Died: May 8, 1806, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania
Spouse: Mary White Morris
Occupation: Merchant, financier, statesman
Robert Morris was the Superintendent of Finance of the United States under the Articles of Confederation and one of the most important financiers of the American Revolution. He financed the critical campaigns of the war out of his own credit when Congress’s means were exhausted.
Revolutionary Financier
Morris was a delegate to the Continental Congress and a signer of the Declaration of Independence. In 1781, Congress appointed him Superintendent of Finance, effectively making him the financial dictator of the United States. He used his personal credit and extensive commercial connections to supply George Washington’s army, enabling the Yorktown campaign. He founded the Bank of North America, the first commercial bank in the United States, to provide a stable currency and credit.
Later Career
After the war, Morris served as a delegate to the Constitutional Convention (1787) and as one of Pennsylvania’s first senators under the new Constitution (1789–1795). He strongly supported Alexander Hamilton’s financial program — the funding of the debt, the assumption of state debts, and the establishment of the Bank of the United States (First Bank, 1791-1811).
Morris engaged in extensive land speculation in the 1790s, acquiring millions of acres in western New York and Pennsylvania. The collapse of his land schemes led to his imprisonment for debt from 1798 to 1801 — an ironic end for the man who had financed the Revolution. He was released after Congress passed the first federal bankruptcy law.
Sources

Irving, Washington. The Life of George Washington. Vols. III–IV. Boston: Desmond Publishing Co., 1899.
Chernow, Ron. Alexander Hamilton. New York: Penguin Press, 2004.

entities/supreme-court-of-the-united-sta.title: Supreme Court of the United States
entities/supreme-court-of-the-united-sta.content:
Supreme Court of the United States
The Supreme Court of the United States is the highest judicial tribunal of the federal government, established by Article III of the Constitution. It began operation in 1790 under its first Chief Justice, John Jay.
Constitutional Creation
The Constitution created one Supreme Court and left Congress to establish inferior federal courts as needed. The Court has original jurisdiction in a limited class of cases (those affecting ambassadors and those in which a state is a party) and appellate jurisdiction in all others.
The Federalist Defense
Alexander Hamilton provided the most thorough contemporary defense of the federal judiciary in Federalist Nos. 78–83. In Federalist No. 78, he argued for life tenure for judges (service “during good behaviour”) as essential to judicial independence. Hamilton also articulated the doctrine of judicial review: the power of courts to declare statutes unconstitutional. He described the judiciary as “the least dangerous” branch because it has “no influence over either the sword or the purse; no direction either of the strength or of the wealth of the society; and can take no active resolution whatever.”
The First Court
The Supreme Court first met on February 1, 1790, in the Royal Exchange Building in New York City. Its first Chief Justice was John Jay, appointed by President George Washington. Associate justices included John Rutledge, William Cushing, James Wilson, John Blair, and James Iredell. The early Court had little business; it heard no cases in its first three terms and was regarded as the weakest branch of the new government.
Establishment of Authority
The Court’s authority was definitively established under Chief Justice John Marshall, appointed by President John Adams in 1801. Marshall’s decision in Marbury v. Madison (1803) established the principle of judicial review, giving the Court the power to declare acts of Congress unconstitutional. His jurisprudence consistently favored a strong national government and a broad interpretation of federal powers.
Sources

Publius [Hamilton, Madison, Jay]. The Federalist Papers. 1787–1788.
Chernow, Ron. Alexander Hamilton. New York: Penguin Press, 2004.

entities/thomas-jefferson.title: Thomas Jefferson
entities/thomas-jefferson.content:
Thomas Jefferson
Born: April 13, 1743, Shadwell, Virginia
Died: July 4, 1826, Monticello, Virginia
Spouse: Martha Wayles Skelton Jefferson (m. 1772; d. 1782)
Occupation: Planter, lawyer, philosopher, statesman
Thomas Jefferson was the first Secretary of State, the principal author of the Declaration of Independence, and the founder of the Democratic-Republican Party. His political rivalry with Alexander Hamilton defined the first party system and shaped the fundamental debates of the early republic.
Early Life and Education
Jefferson was born into the Virginia planter elite. He studied at the College of William and Mary, where he was influenced by the Enlightenment philosophy of Dr. William Small. He studied law under George Wythe and was admitted to the Virginia bar in 1767. He inherited extensive lands and slaves from his father and built Monticello, his celebrated mountaintop estate.
Revolutionary Career
Jefferson was elected to the Virginia House of Burgesses in 1769 and became an active member of the patriot faction. He was a delegate to the Continental Congress in 1775 and 1776. The Congress appointed him to the committee to draft a declaration of independence; he wrote the first draft, which was amended by John Adams and Benjamin Franklin and adopted by Congress on July 4, 1776.
