Jefferson returned to Virginia and served in the House of Delegates, where he authored the Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom (1786). He served as governor of Virginia during the war (1779–1781), a period marked by the British invasion under Benedict Arnold and Charles Cornwallis.
Minister to France and Secretary of State
After the war, Jefferson served as minister to France (1785–1789), where he witnessed the early stages of the French Revolution. He returned to America with a deepened suspicion of cities, banks, and commerce, and a vision of America as an agrarian republic of independent yeoman farmers.
As the first Secretary of State under President George Washington, Jefferson clashed repeatedly with Treasury Secretary Alexander Hamilton. Where Hamilton wanted a powerful central government, a national bank, and a modern financial system, Jefferson wanted to preserve state sovereignty, limit federal power, and maintain an agrarian economy. He believed that Hamilton’s system would create a corrupt moneyed aristocracy.
Jefferson’s differences with Hamilton were both philosophical and personal. Hamilton was combative and candid; Jefferson was courtly, guarded, and preferred indirect methods. Jefferson remembered them “daily pitted in the cabinet like two cocks.” By 1792, any pretense of civility had disappeared.
Jefferson organized the opposition through the National Gazette, edited by Philip Freneau, whom Jefferson employed as a State Department translator. He resigned as Secretary of State in December 1793 and returned to Monticello.
Later Years and Presidency
Jefferson continued to lead the Democratic-Republican opposition from retirement. In the election of 1800, he tied Aaron Burr in the Electoral College, and the election was decided in the House of Representatives when Alexander Hamilton — despite detesting Jefferson — helped secure his election. Jefferson called this “the Revolution of 1800,” marking the first peaceful transfer of power between opposing political parties.
Jefferson served as President from 1801 to 1809. His major achievements included the Louisiana Purchase (1803), which doubled the territory of the United States, and the Lewis and Clark Expedition. He died at Monticello on July 4, 1826 — the 50th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence, on the same day as John Adams.
Sources

Chernow, Ron. Alexander Hamilton. New York: Penguin Press, 2004.
Irving, Washington. The Life of George Washington. Vols. IV–V. Boston: Desmond Publishing Co., 1899.

entities/thomas-paine.title: Thomas Paine
entities/thomas-paine.content:
Thomas Paine
Born: February 9, 1737 (Old Style: January 29, 1736), Thetford, Norfolk, England
Died: June 8, 1809, New York City
Occupation: Pamphleteer, political philosopher
Thomas Paine was the most influential writer of the American Revolution. His pamphlet Common Sense (January 1776) made the case for independence in language that ordinary Americans could understand, selling hundreds of thousands of copies and transforming the political debate.
Common Sense
Paine arrived in America from England in 1774, carrying letters of introduction from Benjamin Franklin. He published Common Sense in January 1776, arguing that “the cause of America is the cause of all mankind” and that independence was not merely justified but necessary. The pamphlet electrified the colonies, shifting public opinion decisively toward independence.
The American Crisis
During the darkest days of the Revolution — the retreat across New Jersey in late 1776 — Paine wrote the first of his American Crisis essays. George Washington ordered it read to the troops before the crossing of the Delaware and the Battle of Trenton. It opens with the famous words: “These are the times that try men’s souls.” Paine continued writing Crisis papers throughout the war, serving as a propagandist for the American cause.
Later Years
After the Revolution, Paine returned to Europe and became involved in the French Revolution, writing The Rights of Man (1791–1792) in response to Edmund Randolph’s attack on the French Revolution. He was elected to the French National Convention but was imprisoned during the Terror. He also wrote The Age of Reason (1794–1795), a deist critique of organized Christianity that made him deeply unpopular in religious circles.
Paine returned to America in 1802, at Thomas Jefferson’s invitation, and died in obscurity in New York in 1809.
Sources

Irving, Washington. The Life of George Washington. Vols. I–II. Boston: Desmond Publishing Co., 1899.

entities/treasury-department.title: Treasury Department
entities/treasury-department.content:
Treasury Department
The Treasury Department was established by Congress in September 1789 as one of the first executive departments of the new federal government under the Constitution. Alexander Hamilton served as the first Secretary of the Treasury and built the department into the largest and most powerful branch of the federal government.
Hamilton’s Treasury
Hamilton organized the Treasury Department with remarkable energy and efficiency. The department quickly became a formidable bureaucracy, far larger than any other branch of the government. With the Customs Service under its control, the department’s payroll ballooned to more than 500 employees — while Henry Knox had a mere dozen civilians in the War Department and Thomas Jefferson a paltry six at State.
Hamilton’s power extended beyond his legion of employees. Seven of every eight Treasury employees worked outside the capital, supplying Hamilton with an unending stream of intelligence about economic activity across the country. He oversaw the construction of lighthouses, beacons, and buoys along the Atlantic seaboard and created the Revenue Cutter Service, the precursor to the Coast Guard.
Major Reports
Hamilton submitted a series of landmark reports from the Treasury Department that laid the foundations of American economic policy:

Report on Public Credit (January 1790) — funding the national debt and assuming state debts
Report on a National Bank (December 1790) — establishing the Bank of the United States (First Bank, 1791-1811)
Report on the Mint (1791) — creating a decimal currency
Report on Manufactures (December 1791) — promoting domestic industry

Operations
The Treasury Department managed the collection of customs duties (the principal source of federal revenue), the excise tax on distilled spirits, and the disbursement of all federal funds. When the Panic of 1792 threatened the financial system, Hamilton ordered the Treasury to purchase $150,000 in government securities to stabilize the market — the first federal intervention to prevent a financial panic.
Hamilton’s successors continued to manage the nation’s finances. His farewell report in January 1795 charted a course for extinguishing the entire national debt within thirty years.
Sources

Chernow, Ron. Alexander Hamilton. New York: Penguin Press, 2004.
Hamilton, Alexander. Report on Public Credit. 1790.
Hamilton, Alexander. Report on a National Bank. 1790.

events/battle-of-brandywine.title: Battle of Brandywine
events/battle-of-brandywine.content:
The Battle of Brandywine, fought on September 11, 1777, was a major engagement of the Philadelphia campaign. General Howe’s British army defeated George Washington’s Continental Army and opened the way for the capture of Philadelphia.
The Campaign
Howe, instead of marching overland from New York, loaded his army onto transports and sailed up the Chesapeake Bay, landing at Head of Elk, Maryland, in late August. Washington positioned his army to block the British advance on Philadelphia along Brandywine Creek, a natural defensive line.
The Battle
Washington deployed his forces along the east bank of Brandywine Creek, expecting the main British attack at Chadds Ford. Howe, however, repeated the flanking tactics that had succeeded on Long Island. He dispatched a large column under Lord Cornwallis on a long march to cross the creek at an unguarded ford, while his brother Sir William Howe staged a diversion at Chadds Ford.
Washington received conflicting intelligence about the British flanking movement. General John Sullivan, commanding the American right, was caught unprepared when Cornwallis’s column fell upon him in the afternoon. The American line collapsed. Washington rushed reinforcements from Chadds Ford, but the position could not be recovered. Lafayette, serving with the Americans, was wounded in the leg.
Aftermath
The Americans retreated in good order, but Philadelphia lay open. Congress fled the city, first to Lancaster, then to York. On September 26, Howe’s forces marched into Philadelphia, the American capital, unopposed.
Despite the defeat, the Continental Army had fought well. The army remained intact and capable of further operations. Washington, though defeated, had not been destroyed — and within weeks he would strike again at Germantown.
Sources

Irving, Washington. Life of George Washington, Vol. 2.

events/battle-of-bunker-hill.title: Battle of Bunker Hill
events/battle-of-bunker-hill.content:
The Battle of Bunker Hill, fought on June 17, 1775, was the first major battle of the American Revolutionary War. Though a tactical British victory, it proved a strategic triumph for the Americans, demonstrating that colonial militia could stand against British regulars.
The Prelude
Following the Battles of Lexington and Concord, the American army had besieged Boston, containing the British garrison. On the night of June 16-17, American forces under Colonel William Prescott and General Israel Putnam moved onto the Charlestown peninsula to fortify the heights overlooking Boston. Though ordered to fortify Bunker Hill, Prescott’s detachment instead fortified Breed’s Hill, closer to the British positions. The men worked through the night, digging redoubts and entrenchments under the silent stars.
At daybreak, the British looked out from Boston to see a formidable fortification raised overnight where there had been only an empty hill. General Howe exclaimed in astonishment: the Americans had done in one night what the best engineers in Europe would have thought possible only in a fortnight.
The Battle
The British, under General Howe, landed at Charlestown and formed for battle on the beach. The American position was held by Prescott, Putnam, Stark, and their men — farmers and mechanics who had never faced regulars in pitched battle. The British advanced in perfect order, their bright uniforms making them targets against the green hillside.
The Americans were ordered to hold their fire until they could see the whites of the enemy’s eyes. When they fired, the front ranks of the British were shattered. The troops wavered, fell back, and re-formed for a second advance. Again the deadly volleys tore through them. It was not until the third assault, when the American powder ran out, that the British carried the redoubt by bayonet. The Americans retreated, fighting as they went.
Aftermath
The British victory was a Pyrrhic one: over a thousand casualties, including a large proportion of officers. The battle proved to the colonies and the world that American militia could stand against British regulars. It also proved to Washington that he would need a disciplined army — raw courage alone would not win a war. The battle had no effect on the strategic situation; the siege of Boston continued.
Sources

Irving, Washington. Life of George Washington, Vol. 1.

events/battle-of-germantown.title: Battle of Germantown
events/battle-of-germantown.content:
The Battle of Germantown, fought on October 4, 1777, was an ambitious American attack on the main British encampment at Germantown, Pennsylvania, just outside Philadelphia. Though a tactical defeat, the battle demonstrated the growing confidence and capability of the Continental Army.
The Plan
After the defeat at Brandywine and the loss of Philadelphia, Washington sought to strike a blow before the British could consolidate their position. The British under General Howe were encamped at Germantown, a village five miles north of Philadelphia. Washington devised a complex plan involving four columns converging on the British position simultaneously at dawn.
The plan was audacious — perhaps too complex for the green American army. The various columns were to march through the night by different routes and strike at daybreak. Success depended on precise timing and coordination.
The Battle
The plan initially worked well. The American columns advanced through the predawn fog and surprised the British pickets. The British defense was thrown into confusion. For a time, it appeared the Americans might achieve a decisive victory.
But the fog grew thicker, and confusion set in. One American column became separated from the others. A critical moment came when General Greene’s column, delayed by the fog, failed to reach its objective in time. Friendly fire incidents further disordered the assault. The British, rallying under General Howe, counterattacked. The Americans, their momentum spent, retreated.
Aftermath
Washington was disappointed but not discouraged. The army had conducted a complex night march and attacked a superior force in its encampment. Though defeated, the Americans had fought with spirit and determination. The British held their position, but the attack proved that the Continental Army was growing in proficiency.
News of the battle reached Europe at the same time as news of Saratoga. Together, the two battles — one a defeat, the other a stunning victory — convinced the French court that the Americans had the capacity to wage war effectively, paving the way for the French alliance.
Sources

Irving, Washington. Life of George Washington, Vol. 2.

events/battle-of-long-island.title: Battle of Long Island
events/battle-of-long-island.content:
The Battle of Long Island, fought in August 1776, was the largest engagement of the American Revolutionary War and a disastrous defeat for the Continental Army. It forced Washington to abandon New York City and began a desperate retreat across New Jersey.
Strategic Context
After the British evacuation of Boston, Washington correctly anticipated that General Howe would strike next at New York, the strategic key to the colonies. New York’s deep-water harbor could accommodate the British fleet, and control of the Hudson River would sever New England from the other colonies. Washington moved his army to Long Island and fortified positions around Brooklyn Heights.
In July 1776, a massive British fleet under Admiral Richard Howe began arriving in New York Harbor — the largest amphibious expedition the world had seen to that time, carrying over 30,000 troops.
The Battle
On August 22, the British landed on Long Island. General Howe planned a flanking maneuver, sending Henry Clinton’s column through the lightly defended Jamaica Pass. While the British feinted against the American center, Clinton’s column fell on the American left flank, routing the divisions of Stirling and Sullivan. The American position collapsed.
Washington, watching the battle from a hilltop, was said to have exclaimed in anguish, “Good God! What brave fellows I must this day lose!” The survivors retreated to the fortified lines at Brooklyn Heights.
The Evacuation
The British, having won the field, hesitated to assault the American fortifications directly. Washington seized the opportunity. On the night of August 29-30, in one of the most brilliant operations of the war, he evacuated his entire army of 9,000 men across the East River in a fleet of small boats, using a providential fog to conceal the movement. The army escaped intact, but New York City was lost.
Sources

Irving, Washington. Life of George Washington, Vol. 2.

events/battle-of-monmouth.title: Battle of Monmouth
events/battle-of-monmouth.content:
The Battle of Monmouth, fought on June 28, 1778, was the largest single-day battle of the American Revolutionary War. The engagement demonstrated the effectiveness of Baron Friedrich Wilhelm von Steuben’s training at Valley Forge and marked the emergence of the Continental Army as a professional force.
Background
General Henry Clinton, the new British commander, had been ordered to evacuate Philadelphia and concentrate the British army in New York. In June 1778, Clinton marched his army across New Jersey toward Sandy Hook, where the Royal Navy would transport them to New York. Washington, whose army had emerged from Valley Forge reinvigorated, pursued.
The Battle
Washington ordered General Charles Lee, his second-in-command, to attack the British rear guard near Monmouth Court House. Lee had opposed the plan and conducted the attack with little conviction. When the British counterattacked, Lee ordered a retreat, throwing the American advance into confusion.
Washington arrived on the field to find his troops in disorder. He confronted Lee in a famous, furious exchange — Washington’s anger was so intense that he reportedly swore, a rare occurrence. Washington personally rallied the troops and reorganized the defense.
Steuben’s training now proved its worth. The American troops stood their ground, exchanging volleys with the British regulars. The fighting in the brutal summer heat was desperate; hundreds of men on both sides collapsed from heat exhaustion. The artillery duel was particularly intense. As night fell, the British broke off the action and continued their retreat.
Aftermath
The battle was tactically inconclusive, but strategically it was an American success. Clinton’s army had been forced to abandon its baggage and had suffered heavy casualties. More importantly, the Continental Army had fought the British to a standstill in a pitched battle — a feat it could not have accomplished six months earlier.
Lee was subsequently court-martialed for his conduct and suspended from command. Washington’s reputation was enhanced by his decisive intervention.
Sources

Irving, Washington. Life of George Washington, Vol. 2.

events/battle-of-princeton.title: Battle of Princeton
events/battle-of-princeton.content:
The Battle of Princeton, fought on January 3, 1777, was the follow-up victory to Washington’s triumph at Trenton. Together, these two engagements reversed the momentum of the war and saved the American cause after the disastrous New York campaign.
The Situation
After the victory at Trenton, Washington’s position remained precarious. General Cornwallis, assembling a large British force at Princeton, marched against Washington. On January 2, the British advance guard reached Trenton and skirmished with the Americans. Washington’s army was trapped against the Delaware River, and Cornwallis expected to finish the Americans in the morning.
Washington’s Daring Manuever
Washington left his campfires burning to deceive the British and marched his army by a back road toward Princeton. The night march was conducted in secrecy, the men moving silently through the frozen darkness. At dawn on January 3, the Americans fell upon the British rear guard at Princeton.
The battle was sharp and confused. General Hugh Mercer, commanding the American advance, was mortally wounded when his troops were thrown back by British bayonets. Washington rode to the front, rallied the fleeing men, and led a counterattack that broke the British. The British force at Princeton was routed, many fleeing toward Trenton.
Aftermath
Washington had achieved a remarkable double victory: two engagements in eight days, capturing hundreds of prisoners and inflicting heavy losses. Cornwallis, finding his supply line threatened, abandoned his pursuit and retreated toward New Brunswick. Washington led his army into winter quarters at Morristown, New Jersey, where he could observe British movements and protect the countryside.
The victories at Trenton and Princeton transformed American morale. The Continental Army had proven it could not only fight but outmaneuver the British. The French court, watching these events closely, began to take the American cause more seriously.
Sources

Irving, Washington. Life of George Washington, Vol. 2.

events/battle-of-saratoga.title: Battle of Saratoga
events/battle-of-saratoga.content:
The Battle of Saratoga, fought in September and October 1777, was the turning point of the American Revolutionary War. The American victory persuaded France to enter the war as an American ally, transforming a colonial rebellion into a global conflict.
The Campaign
General John Burgoyne, commanding a British army of approximately 8,000 men, launched an invasion from Canada in the summer of 1777, intending to drive south along Lake Champlain and the Hudson River to meet a second British force advancing from New York. The objective was to sever New England from the other colonies.
Burgoyne’s campaign was plagued by difficulties from the start. His army was slowed by the wilderness, his supply lines were overextended, and the American militia rose in his rear. A diversionary expedition under Colonel Barry St. Leger was stopped at Fort Stanwix by American forces under Benedict Arnold.
Freeman’s Farm
On September 19, Burgoyne’s army encountered the American forces under General Horatio Gates entrenched on Bemis Heights, near Saratoga. Burgoyne attacked. The resulting battle at Freeman’s Farm was a brutal engagement fought in dense woods. Benedict Arnold led the American counterattack with characteristic ferocity. The British held the field at the end of the day but at heavy cost.
Bemis Heights
Burgoyne hesitated, fortifying his position and hoping for word from General Clinton in New York. None came. On October 7, he attempted to reconnoiter the American lines. The Americans attacked in force. Arnold, though under orders not to engage, led a furious charge that broke the British line. The British position collapsed. Burgoyne retreated to Saratoga, where he was surrounded.
Surrender
On October 17, 1777, Burgoyne surrendered his army to General Gates. The captured force numbered nearly 6,000 men. The surrender was a staggering blow to British prestige. The victory at Saratoga convinced the French court that the Americans could win the war. In February 1778, France signed the Treaty of Alliance with the United States, committing French troops, money, and naval power to the American cause.
Sources

Irving, Washington. Life of George Washington, Vol. 2.

events/battle-of-trenton.title: Battle of Trenton
events/battle-of-trenton.content:
The Battle of Trenton, fought on December 26, 1776, was one of the most daring and consequential operations of the American Revolution. Washington’s surprise attack on the Hessian garrison at Trenton restored American fortunes after a series of devastating defeats.
The Crisis
By December 1776, the American cause seemed lost. Washington’s army had been driven out of New York, across New Jersey, and into Pennsylvania. The army was melting away — enlistments were expiring, desertions were rampant, and the troops were ragged, hungry, and demoralized. Thomas Paine, serving with the army, wrote: “These are the times that try men’s souls.”
General Howe had gone into winter quarters, establishing a chain of outposts across New Jersey. The Hessian garrison at Trenton was commanded by Colonel Johann Rall, a veteran of European wars who dismissed the American army as contemptible.
The Crossing
Washington conceived a bold stroke. On Christmas night, 1776, he assembled his army at McKonkey’s Ferry on the Delaware River. In the midst of a raging snowstorm, he crossed the ice-choked river with 2,400 men in Durham boats. The crossing was treacherous — the river was filled with ice floes, the wind howled, and the boats were barely manageable. The army did not reach the New Jersey shore until 3:00 a.m.
The Attack
Washington split his force into two columns. The main column advanced on Trenton from the north; the other, under General John Sullivan, approached from the west. The Hessians had celebrated Christmas the night before and were ill-prepared. At dawn, the Americans fell upon the garrison with bayonets fixed. Rall, roused from his quarters, attempted to rally his men but was mortally wounded. Within an hour and a half, the Hessians surrendered. The Americans captured nearly 1,000 prisoners, six brass cannon, and valuable supplies.
Aftermath
The victory electrified the colonies. Washington had proven that the American army could fight and win. The captured Hessian soldiers were paraded through Philadelphia, a visible demonstration of American success. More critically, the victory persuaded many soldiers to re-enlist when their terms expired at year’s end.
Sources

Irving, Washington. Life of George Washington, Vol. 2.

events/battles-of-lexington-and-concord.title: Battles of Lexington and Concord
events/battles-of-lexington-and-concord.content:
The Battles of Lexington and Concord on April 19, 1775, were the opening engagements of the American Revolutionary War. The confrontations between British regulars and Massachusetts militiamen transformed a political crisis into an armed conflict.
The British Expedition
General Thomas Gage, the British military governor of Massachusetts, received orders from London to arrest the leaders of the Provincial Congress and seize the military stores collected by the colonists at Concord. On the night of April 18-19, Gage dispatched approximately 700 elite troops under Lieutenant Colonel Francis Smith on a secret expedition. The column marched out of Boston, crossing the Charles River and advancing toward Concord.
The patriots, however, had been warned. Paul Revere and William Dawes rode through the night to alert the countryside, reaching Lexington and Concord before the British. Church bells and signal guns spread the alarm as the British advanced.
Lexington Green
At dawn on April 19, the British vanguard under Major John Pitcairn arrived at Lexington, a small town east of Concord. They found about seventy militiamen drawn up on the village green under Captain John Parker. Pitcairn ordered the colonists to disperse. In the confusion, a shot was fired — the “shot heard round the world.” The British then fired a volley and charged with bayonets. Eight Americans lay dead and ten wounded; only one British soldier was hit.
Concord and the Retreat
The British marched on to Concord, where they destroyed whatever military supplies they could find. At the North Bridge in Concord, a force of militiamen confronted a British detachment. The Americans fired, and the British returned fire. Several soldiers fell on both sides. The colonists forced the British back.
By noon, Smith ordered the retreat to Boston. The return march became a nightmare. Militiamen from every town along the route converged on the British column, firing from behind stone walls, trees, and buildings. The British, exhausted and running low on ammunition, suffered heavy casualties. Only the arrival of reinforcements under Earl Percy at Lexington saved the column from annihilation.
Aftermath
The day’s fighting left 73 British dead, 174 wounded, and 26 missing. American losses were 49 dead, 39 wounded, and 5 missing. The “cry of blood” spread through the land. The news reached Mount Vernon late in April, profoundly affecting those gathered there: Washington resolved his course to lead the Virginia forces to the defense of Boston. The war for American independence had begun.
Sources

Irving, Washington. Life of George Washington, Vol. 1.

events/boston-massacre.title: Boston Massacre
events/boston-massacre.content:
The Boston Massacre occurred on the evening of March 5, 1770, when a confrontation between a crowd of Bostonians and British soldiers escalated into bloodshed. The incident, in which five colonists were killed, electrified the colonies and became a rallying cry for the patriot cause.
Background
Tensions in Boston had been building for years. British troops had been quartered in the town since 1768 to enforce the Townshend Acts and maintain order. The non-importation agreement had proven effective in pressuring London, but the occupation itself was a source of constant friction. Bostonians resented the presence of regular soldiers, whom they saw as instruments of tyranny, while the soldiers endured the hostility and provocation of the townspeople.
The Incident
On the evening of March 5, a crowd gathered near the Custom House on King Street, where a lone British sentry stood guard. The crowd grew, hurling insults and snowballs at the sentry. Reinforcements arrived under Captain Thomas Preston. The soldiers were surrounded and pressed by the mob. In the confusion, shots were fired. When the smoke cleared, five colonists lay dead or dying, including Crispus Attucks, a man of African and Native American descent.
Aftermath
The Boston Massacre became a propaganda triumph for the patriots. Samuel Adams and others portrayed the dead as martyrs to the cause of liberty. The victims’ funeral was one of the largest public gatherings Boston had ever seen. Captain Preston and his men were tried for murder and defended by John Adams, who secured acquittals for all but two soldiers, who were convicted of manslaughter and branded on the hand.
In the wake of the Massacre, the British withdrew their troops from the town center to Castle William in the harbor. Tea became a symbol of British oppression, and colonists began a widespread disuse of the beverage.
Sources

Irving, Washington. Life of George Washington, Vol. 1.

events/boston-tea-party.title: Boston Tea Party
events/boston-tea-party.content:
The Boston Tea Party of December 16, 1773, was a direct act of colonial defiance against British authority. Disguised as Mohawk Indians, a party of colonists boarded three ships in Boston Harbor and dumped 342 chests of East India Company tea into the water, an event that precipitated the final crisis leading to the American Revolution.
Background: Lord North’s Tea Act
Lord North’s Tea Act of 1773 was designed to rescue the struggling East India Company by allowing it to ship tea directly to America, bypassing colonial merchants and underselling even smuggled Dutch tea. Though the Act actually reduced the price of tea for consumers, it retained the duty on tea — a symbolic assertion of Parliament’s right to tax the colonies. American patriots recognized the trap: by buying the cheaper tea, they would implicitly acknowledge Parliament’s taxing authority.
The Destruction of the Tea
Ships freighted with tea arrived at American ports in the autumn of 1773. At Philadelphia and New York, the tea was sent back. At Charleston, it was stored in warehouses. But at Boston, where the royal governor refused to let the ships depart without unloading, the situation reached a crisis. On the night of December 16, after a mass meeting at the Old South Meeting House failed to secure permission for the ships to leave, a group of men disguised as Mohawks marched to Griffin’s Wharf, boarded the Dartmouth, the Eleanor, and the Beaver, and methodically emptied 342 chests of tea into the harbor.
Aftermath
Parliament retaliated with the Coercive Acts (called the Intolerable Acts in America), which closed the port of Boston, altered the Massachusetts charter, allowed royal officials accused of crimes to be tried in England, and quartered troops in colonial buildings. These punitive measures united the colonies in sympathy with Massachusetts and led directly to the convening of the First Continental Congress in 1774.
Sources

Irving, Washington. Life of George Washington, Vol. 1.

events/citizen-genet-affair.title: Citizen Genet Affair
events/citizen-genet-affair.content:
The Citizen Genet Affair (1793-1794) was a diplomatic crisis triggered by the conduct of Edmond Charles Genet, the first minister of the French Republic to the United States. Genet’s violation of American neutrality inflamed political divisions and led to his recall.
Background
In 1793, revolutionary France declared war on Great Britain. President George Washington issued the American Neutrality, declaring the United States would remain impartial and warning American citizens against aiding either belligerent. The Proclamation divided the cabinet: Alexander Hamilton supported a strong declaration of neutrality; Thomas Jefferson was more sympathetic to France.
Genet’s Mission
Citizen Genet arrived in Charleston, South Carolina, in April 1793, to tremendous popular enthusiasm. Instead of proceeding directly to Philadelphia to present his credentials, Genet traveled overland, using the journey to commission American privateers to prey on British shipping, organize French consular courts to adjudicate prizes, and encourage American citizens to join French military expeditions against British and Spanish territories.
These activities directly violated American neutrality. The British government protested vigorously.
The Crisis
When Genet finally reached Philadelphia, he presented his credentials to Washington but continued his unauthorized activities. He fitted out privateers in American ports, enlisted American citizens, and even attempted to recruit American frontiersmen for an expedition against Spanish Louisiana.
Washington demanded Genet’s recall. Genet, emboldened by popular support, threatened to appeal directly to the American people over the president’s head — a threat that united even Jefferson against him. Jefferson, who had initially been sympathetic to Genet, wrote that Genet’s behavior was “indefensible.”
Resolution
The French government, in the midst of the Reign of Terror, recalled Genet in February 1794. Fearing execution if he returned to France, Genet requested and received asylum in the United States. He settled in New York, married the daughter of Governor George Clinton, and lived in America for the rest of his life.
The Genet Affair strengthened Washington’s determination to maintain American neutrality and contributed to the growing division between Federalists (pro-British and pro-neutrality) and Democratic-Republicans (pro-French and pro-French Revolution).
Sources

Irving, Washington. Life of George Washington, Vol. 5.

events/compromise-of-1790.title: Compromise of 1790
events/compromise-of-1790.content:
The Compromise of 1790 was a legendary political bargain between Alexander Hamilton, Thomas Jefferson, and James Madison that saved Hamilton’s financial program and determined the location of the permanent national capital.
The Impasse
Hamilton’s proposal that the federal government assume the state debts left over from the Revolution had provoked the most bitter congressional battle of the early republic. James Madison, who had been Hamilton’s closest ally during the Constitutional Convention and the Federalist collaboration, led the opposition in the House. Southern states, many of which had already paid their own debts, refused to shoulder the burden of northern states that had not.
The House of Representatives deadlocked. Hamilton realized his entire financial system might collapse. The deadlock was so intense that it seemed possible the union might break up over the issue.
The Dinner Bargain
Into this impasse stepped Secretary of State Thomas Jefferson. According to Jefferson’s account, he invited Hamilton and Madison to dinner at his Maiden Lane residence in New York City in June 1790. Over that dinner, the famous bargain was struck:
Hamilton agreed to secure northern votes for locating the permanent national capital on the Potomac River, with a ten-year interim in Philadelphia. In exchange, Jefferson and Madison would deliver southern votes for assumption of state debts.
The Residence Act, establishing the Potomac site for the capital, passed Congress on July 16, 1790. The Assumption Act followed on August 4. The bargain infuriated Pennsylvanians, who had hoped Philadelphia would remain the permanent capital, and disappointed New Yorkers, who saw their city lose its chance at political preeminence.
Aftermath
The Compromise of 1790 probably saved the union. Hamilton, the quintessential New Yorker, bargained away his city’s chance to become the political capital, testifying to the transcendent value he placed on assumption. Jefferson later repudiated his role, telling Washington he had been “duped” by Hamilton.
The compromise was the last time Hamilton, Jefferson, and Madison ever cooperated to advance a common agenda. The battle lines of the first party system began to take shape.
Sources

Chernow, Ron. Alexander Hamilton.
Irving, Washington. Life of George Washington, Vol. 4.

events/constitutional-convention.title: Constitutional Convention
events/constitutional-convention.content:
The Constitutional Convention met in Philadelphia from May to September 1787, charged with revising the Articles of Confederation. Instead, the delegates — including George Washington, James Madison, Alexander Hamilton, and Benjamin Franklin — produced an entirely new frame of government: the United States Constitution.
Convening
The convention was the culmination of years of agitation for a stronger national government. Alexander Hamilton had called for a convention in his 1780 letter to James Duane, and the Annapolis Convention of 1786 had issued a call for a general convention. Shays’ Rebellion in Massachusetts provided the final impetus. Congress authorized the convention “for the sole and express purpose of revising the Articles of Confederation.”
Twelve states (Rhode Island alone absent) sent fifty-five delegates to Philadelphia. The delegates met at the Pennsylvania State House (Independence Hall), elected George Washington as president of the convention, and immediately resolved to keep their proceedings secret.
The Virginia Plan
The convention opened with the Virginia Plan, drafted by James Madison and presented by Governor Edmund Randolph. It proposed a national government of three branches — legislative, executive, and judicial — with a bicameral legislature whose representation in both houses was based on population. Large states supported this plan.
The New Jersey Plan
The small states, fearing domination by Virginia, Pennsylvania, and Massachusetts, countered with the New Jersey Plan, which proposed merely amending the Articles to give Congress limited additional powers while preserving equal state representation.
The Great Compromise
The convention deadlocked for weeks. The solution — the Connecticut Compromise, which Benjamin Franklin helped to broker — gave the House of Representatives proportional representation and the Senate equal representation for each state. The compromise saved the convention.
Hamilton’s Speech
On June 18, Hamilton delivered a six-hour speech outlining his vision for the new government, which included a president and Senate serving “on good behavior.” Though his plan was supported by nobody, Hamilton subordinated his ego and campaigned vigorously for ratification of the Constitution that emerged from the convention’s compromises. He was the lone New York delegate to sign the charter.
Franklin’s Appeal
As the convention drew to a close, Franklin — at eighty-one the oldest delegate — urged his fellow delegates to support the imperfect document. His speech, delivered by James Wilson because Franklin was too weak to stand, asked delegates to “doubt a little of their own infallibility” and accept the Constitution as the best they could achieve.
Signing
On September 17, 1787, thirty-nine delegates signed the Constitution. The convention transmitted the document to Congress, which submitted it to the states for ratification by special conventions.
Sources

Irving, Washington. Life of George Washington, Vol. 4.
Chernow, Ron. Alexander Hamilton.
The Federalist Papers (Publius, 1787-1788).

events/conway-cabal.title: Conway Cabal
events/conway-cabal.content:
The Conway Cabal (1777-1778) was a shadowy political intrigue by a group of officers and congressmen who sought to replace General George Washington as commander-in-chief of the Continental Army with General Horatio Gates, the victor of Saratoga.
Background
After the victories at Saratoga, Gates had emerged as a potential rival to Washington. Some in Congress and the army believed that Washington had failed by losing Philadelphia and that a more aggressive commander was needed. The winter encampment at Valley Forge, with its terrible suffering, amplified criticism of Washington’s leadership.
The Conspiracy
The cabal took its name from General Thomas Conway, an Irish-born French officer serving in the Continental Army. Conway wrote a letter to Gates criticizing Washington’s leadership. The letter’s contents were leaked to Washington, who famously wrote to Conway: “I shall … in no shape treat the matter with that caution which your extreme wariness may have made necessary.”
Other figures implicated included General Mifflin, General James Wilkinson, and several members of Congress. The conspirators proposed appointing Gates as quartermaster general and promoting Conway to major general — steps that would diminish Washington’s authority.
Collapse
Washington handled the crisis with characteristic skill. He confronted his critics directly, maintained the confidence of Congress, and let the intrigue collapse under its own weight. Gates’s reputation suffered from his association with the cabal. Conway, after quarreling with nearly everyone, was wounded in a duel and resigned from the army. The affair never posed a serious threat to Washington’s command, but it revealed the political divisions within the revolutionary movement.
Sources

Irving, Washington. Life of George Washington, Vol. 2.

events/declaration-of-independence.title: Declaration of Independence
events/declaration-of-independence.content:
The Declaration of Independence, adopted by the Second Continental Congress on July 4, 1776, proclaimed the thirteen American colonies’ formal separation from Great Britain. It remains the founding document of the United States and one of the most influential political statements in human history.
Background
By the spring of 1776, the movement for independence had gained irresistible momentum. Thomas Paine’s Common Sense, published in January 1776, had sold tens of thousands of copies and shifted public opinion decisively toward independence. On June 7, Richard Henry Lee of Virginia introduced a resolution in Congress: “That these United Colonies are, and of right ought to be, free and independent States.”
Congress appointed a Committee of Five — Thomas Jefferson, John Adams, Benjamin Franklin, Roger Sherman, and Robert R. Livingston — to draft a declaration. Jefferson, the youngest member, was chosen to write the draft. He produced the document in seventeen days, drawing on the Virginia Declaration of Rights and the natural rights philosophy of John Locke.
The Drafting and Revision
Jefferson wrote the document and submitted it to Adams and Franklin for revision. Benjamin Franklin’s editorial hand improved several passages, notably substituting “We hold these truths to be sacred and undeniable” with “We hold these truths to be self-evident.” Franklin also contributed the famous story of the hatter’s sign — a joke about a man who kept simplifying his shop sign until nothing was left — as a warning against excessive revision.
Congress debated the draft for three days, making numerous changes. The most significant was the deletion of Jefferson’s lengthy passage condemning the slave trade, removed to satisfy delegates from Georgia and South Carolina.
Adoption
On July 4, 1776, Congress adopted the Declaration. John Hancock, the president of Congress, affixed his bold signature, famously remarking that King George could read it without spectacles. At age seventy, Benjamin Franklin signed with the others, reputedly quipping: “Indeed we must all hang together, or most assuredly we shall all hang separately.” The bell in the Pennsylvania State House steeple — later known as the Liberty Bell — was rung to mark the occasion.
The Declaration’s preamble articulates the fundamental principles of American government: that all men are created equal, that they are endowed by their Creator with certain unalienable rights, that governments derive their just powers from the consent of the governed, and that the people have the right to alter or abolish a government that becomes destructive of these ends.
Sources

Irving, Washington. Life of George Washington, Vol. 1.
Chernow, Ron. Alexander Hamilton.
Isaacson, Walter. Benjamin Franklin: An American Life.

events/first-continental-congress.title: First Continental Congress
events/first-continental-congress.content:
The First Continental Congress met in Philadelphia in September and October 1774, gathering delegates from twelve of the thirteen British colonies (Georgia alone was absent). It was the first unified political assembly of the American colonies and marked a decisive step toward united resistance against British policy.
Composition and Character
The delegates assembled at Carpenter’s Hall and included the most distinguished figures in America: George Washington and Patrick Henry from Virginia, John Adams and Samuel Adams from Massachusetts, John Jay from New York, and many others. Irving describes the opening ceremonies with their solemnity and gravity. Patrick Henry and Henry (“Light-Horse Harry”) Lee delivered speeches long remembered for their eloquence and fire.
Proceedings and Resolutions
The Congress adopted a Declaratory Resolution asserting the rights of the colonies and enumerating their grievances against the Crown and Parliament. It endorsed the Suffolk Resolves, which declared the Coercive Acts unconstitutional and called for a boycott of British goods. The Congress also drafted state papers — addresses to the King, to the people of British America, and to the inhabitants of the Province of Quebec.
Most significantly, the Congress established the Continental Association, a comprehensive agreement to cease all trade with Great Britain until the Coercive Acts were repealed. Local committees were empowered to enforce the boycott, creating an infrastructure of resistance that would later underpin the revolutionary movement.
Aftermath
In England, Lord Chatham (William Pitt) spoke in favor of the Congress and urged conciliation, but the government was unmoved. Washington corresponded with his former military acquaintance Captain Mackenzie, revealing his mind at this critical juncture: he was not yet for independence, but convinced that the colonies must resist arbitrary power or submit to slavery.
The Congress adjourned in late October having agreed to reconvene in May 1775 if their grievances were not addressed. By the time the Second Continental Congress met, the Battles of Lexington and Concord had already been fought.
Sources

Irving, Washington. Life of George Washington, Vol. 1.

events/first-presidential-election.title: First Presidential Election
events/first-presidential-election.content:
The first presidential election of the United States was conducted from December 1788 to January 1789. George Washington was unanimously elected the first President, and John Adams became Vice President.
The Electoral Process
The Constitution, recently ratified, provided for an Electoral College: each state would choose electors equal to its total representation in Congress, and the electors would vote for two candidates. The candidate with the most votes would become President; the runner-up, Vice President.
Unlike modern elections, there was no popular vote in the modern sense. In several states, legislatures chose the electors directly. In others, electors were chosen by popular vote in districts or statewide. All knew the result was predetermined: Washington was the unanimous choice to be the first President.
The Unanimous Choice
Washington had retired to Mount Vernon after the war, hoping to spend his remaining years as a private citizen. But the nation’s calls would not be denied. He accepted the presidency with profound reluctance, writing to a friend: “My movement to the chair of Government will be accompanied with feelings not unlike those of a culprit who is going to the place of his execution.”
Every elector cast one of his two votes for Washington. The remaining electoral votes were divided among several candidates, with John Adams receiving the second-largest number, thereby becoming Vice President. Washington’s unanimous election was a unique distinction; no subsequent president has been elected unanimously.
Aftermath
Washington traveled from Mount Vernon to New York City, the temporary capital, for his inauguration. He was greeted along the route by crowds, celebrations, and ceremonial arches. On April 30, 1789, he took the oath of office on the balcony of Federal Hall, becoming the first President of the United States.
Sources

Irving, Washington. Life of George Washington, Vol. 4.

events/french-and-indian-war.title: French and Indian War
events/french-and-indian-war.content:
The French and Indian War (1754-1763) was the North American theater of the Seven Years’ War, pitting Great Britain against France for control of the continent. It proved to be the formative military schooling of George Washington and set the stage for the imperial crisis that would lead to the American Revolution.
Washington’s Early Military Service
In 1753, Governor Robert Dinwiddie of Virginia dispatched Major Washington, then only twenty-one, on a mission to deliver an ultimatum to the French commandant at Fort Le Boeuf, demanding the French withdraw from the Ohio Valley. Washington made the arduous journey through the winter wilderness, delivered the message, and returned with a French refusal — a mission that made his name known in Virginia and London.
In 1754, Washington was promoted to lieutenant colonel and led a small force into the Ohio country. At a place called the Great Meadows, his troops clashed with a French scouting party under Ensign Jumonville, who was killed in the engagement. This skirmish ignited the war. Washington constructed Fort Necessity but was soon surrounded by a superior French force and compelled to surrender on July 4, 1754.
Braddock’s Defeat
In 1755, Major General Edward Braddock arrived with British regulars to lead an expedition against Fort Duquesne. Washington served as a volunteer aide-de-camp. Braddock, contemptuous of American provincial troops and Indian methods of warfare, marched his army directly toward the fort. On July 9, 1755, the British column was ambushed near the Monongahela River by French and their Indian allies. The regulars, unable to adapt to forest fighting, were cut down in dreadful numbers. Braddock was mortally wounded. Washington, the only mounted officer unharmed, distinguished himself by rallying the survivors; he later wrote that he had four bullets through his coat and two horses shot from under him.
Later Campaigns and Outcome
Washington commanded the Virginia Regiment, defending the frontier through years of grueling service. In 1758, General John Forbes mounted a successful expedition against Fort Duquesne; the French abandoned and destroyed the fort before the British arrived. The war in North America ended decisively with the British capture of Quebec in 1759 and Montreal in 1760.
The Treaty of Paris (1763) formally ended the war, stripping France of her North American empire. Great Britain emerged as the dominant power on the continent but also accumulated a massive war debt — a debt that would lead Parliament to seek new revenues from the American colonies, setting the stage for the revolutionary crisis.
Sources

Irving, Washington. Life of George Washington, Vol. 1.

events/hamiltons-financial-program.title: Hamilton's Financial Program
events/hamiltons-financial-program.content:
Alexander Hamilton’s financial program as the first Secretary of the Treasury was the most ambitious and consequential set of economic policies ever proposed in American history. Through four great state papers, Hamilton laid the foundations of the American financial system.
Report on Public Credit (January 1790)
Hamilton’s first and most consequential report called for the federal government to “fund” the entire national debt — approximately $54 million — by pledging specific revenues to guarantee interest payments. He argued that a funded debt would be “a national blessing,” providing the capital that a commercial economy required.
The most controversial element was the proposal that the federal government “assume” the approximately $25 million in state debts left over from the Revolutionary War. Hamilton argued that assumption would unify the interests of all creditors behind the national government, create economies of scale, and bind the states more closely to the Union.
Report on a National Bank (December 1790)
Hamilton proposed a Bank of the United States with a capital of $10 million, one-fourth in specie and three-fourths in government securities. The bank would serve as the fiscal agent of the federal government, provide a uniform national currency through its bank notes, and increase the active capital of the country.
The bank sparked a fierce constitutional debate. Thomas Jefferson argued that the Constitution did not authorize Congress to create a corporation. Hamilton’s masterful defense — the doctrine of implied powers based on the necessary and proper clause — convinced President Washington to sign the bill.
Report on the Establishment of a Mint (January 1791)
Hamilton proposed a decimal coinage system with the dollar as the money unit, containing 371.25 grains of fine silver. He recommended a bimetallic standard at a ratio of approximately 15:1 between gold and silver. The report laid the foundation for the Coinage Act of 1792 and the establishment of the U.S. Mint.
Report on Manufactures (December 1791)
Hamilton’s most comprehensive state paper called for government encouragement of domestic manufacturing through protective duties, bounties, and internal improvements. He argued that a nation that combined agriculture and manufacturing would be more prosperous, more independent, and more secure than one that relied solely on agriculture.
Legacy
Hamilton’s program established the financial infrastructure of the United States — a funded national debt, a central bank, a national coinage, and the foundations of industrial policy. It also created the political divisions that evolved into the first party system, with Hamilton’s Federalists supporting the program and Jefferson’s Democratic-Republicans opposing the concentration of financial power.
Sources

Chernow, Ron. Alexander Hamilton.
Irving, Washington. Life of George Washington, Vol. 4.
Hamilton, Alexander. Report on Public Credit (1790).
Hamilton, Alexander. Report on a National Bank (1790).
Hamilton, Alexander. Report on the Establishment of a Mint (1791).
Hamilton, Alexander. Report on Manufactures (1791).

events/jays-treaty.title: Jay's Treaty
events/jays-treaty.content:
Jay’s Treaty (1794-1795) was a treaty between the United States and Great Britain negotiated by Chief Justice John Jay. Though deeply controversial and attacked as a betrayal of American interests, it averted a war with Britain and established a framework for Anglo-American relations.
Background
By 1794, relations with Great Britain had deteriorated dangerously. The British had not evacuated the northwestern frontier posts as required by the Treaty of Paris (1783). British naval vessels were seizing American ships trading with France and impressing American sailors into the Royal Navy. The British also stirred up Native American resistance in the Northwest Territory.
War sentiment ran high. Hamilton, however, argued that war with Britain would be disastrous for the American economy, which depended heavily on British trade and British credit.
The Negotiations
Washington dispatched Chief Justice John Jay to London as a special envoy. Jay arrived in June 1794 to find the British in a difficult position: France’s revolutionary armies had conquered Belgium, and Britain was isolated in Europe. The British were willing to negotiate.
Jay’s instructions were to secure British evacuation of the frontier posts, compensation for seized American ships, and a commercial treaty. He secured the first two objectives but failed to achieve the third in a satisfactory manner.
The Treaty
The treaty provided for:

British evacuation of the northwestern posts by June 1796
A commission to settle the boundary between the United States and Canada
A commission to adjudicate American claims for British seizures
Limited commercial privileges, including the right of Americans to trade with the British West Indies in small vessels (subject to restrictions that the Senate rejected)
Agreement on arbitration of pre-Revolutionary debts
No mention of impressment or the rights of neutral shipping

The Controversy
When the treaty’s terms became known, it provoked a firestorm of criticism. The Democratic-Republicans, led by Jefferson and Madison, attacked it as a surrender to British interests, a betrayal of France, and a humiliation of American honor. Ratification was possible only because Washington, after agonizing deliberation, threw his prestige behind the treaty.
The Senate ratified the treaty on a strict party-line vote of 20-10. Washington signed it in August 1795. The controversy over the treaty deepened the division between Federalists and Democratic-Republicans and gave birth to organized political opposition.
Sources

Irving, Washington. Life of George Washington, Vol. 5.

events/newburgh-conspiracy.title: Newburgh Conspiracy
events/newburgh-conspiracy.content:
The Newburgh Conspiracy (March 1783) was a shadowy episode in which a group of Continental Army officers, frustrated by Congress’s failure to pay their wages, threatened to take matters into their own hands. The conspiracy was defused by George Washington’s dramatic personal intervention at Newburgh, New York.
Background
By 1783, the war was effectively over, but the Continental Army remained unpaid. Congress had promised the officers five years of full pay in lieu of lifetime half-pay pensions (commutation), but the treasury was empty. The army had not been paid in months, and the officers feared that once the army disbanded, Congress would simply abandon its obligations.
The Conspiracy
An anonymous letter circulated among the officers encamped at Newburgh, calling for a meeting to consider a threat to Congress: if the army’s demands were not met, the officers would refuse to disband. The letter expressed the bitterness of men who had sacrificed everything for a country that seemed ready to forget them.
Alexander Hamilton, then a delegate to Congress, was aware of the officers’ grievances. Chernow suggests he may have had some role in encouraging the officers’ demands as a way of pressuring Congress to adopt the commutation and, more broadly, to strengthen the central government.
Washington’s Intervention
Washington, learning of the planned meeting, called his own meeting for March 15. When he arrived, he delivered a moving address urging the officers to trust the patience and good faith of Congress. He then read a letter from a congressman supporting the army’s cause — and paused, fumbling for his spectacles, saying: “Gentlemen, you will permit me to put on my spectacles, for I have not only grown gray but almost blind in the service of my country.”
The gesture — whether calculated or spontaneous — had a profound effect. Many officers wept. The conspiracy dissolved. Congress subsequently voted the commutation, and the army eventually disbanded peacefully. The Newburgh crisis confirmed Washington’s moral authority over the army and his commitment to civilian control of the military.
Sources

Irving, Washington. Life of George Washington, Vol. 3.
Chernow, Ron. Alexander Hamilton.

events/quasi-war-with-france.title: Quasi-War with France
events/quasi-war-with-france.content:
The Quasi-War (1798-1800) was an undeclared naval war between the United States and revolutionary France. The conflict arose from French depredations on American shipping and the deterioration of Franco-American relations following Jay’s Treaty with Great Britain.
Background
The French revolutionary government viewed Jay’s Treaty (1794) as a violation of the Franco-American alliance of 1778 and evidence that the United States had aligned itself with Great Britain. In retaliation, French privateers began seizing American merchant ships trading with Britain. By 1797, French cruisers and privateers had captured over 300 American vessels.
President John Adams, who succeeded Washington in 1797, sought a diplomatic solution. He dispatched a commission of three envoys — Charles Cotesworth Pinckney, John Marshall, and Elbridge Gerry — to Paris to negotiate a settlement.
The XYZ Affair
The French Foreign Minister, Charles Maurice de Talleyrand, refused to receive the American envoys directly. Instead, three French agents — designated X, Y, and Z in the dispatches — demanded a bribe of 250,000 and a loan of 12 million before negotiations could begin. Pinckney’s reported reply — “No! No! Not a sixpence!” — became a rallying cry.
When the dispatches were published in 1798, the nation erupted in outrage. The cry “Millions for defense, but not one cent for tribute!” swept the country. Congress abrogated the treaties of 1778 with France and authorized military preparations.
The Naval War
Congress authorized the construction of warships, commissioned privateers, and established a separate Navy Department. The United States Navy, barely a decade old, was rapidly expanded. American frigates — including the Constellation, the United States, and the Constitution — were deployed to protect American commerce.
The naval war produced several notable engagements. The USS Constellation captured the French frigate L’Insurgente in February 1799 and fought a bloody draw with La Vengeance in February 1800. American privateers preyed on French commerce. French losses exceeded 100 vessels captured.
Resolution
Despite the popular war fever, President Adams carefully avoided a formal declaration of war. In 1799, he took the politically risky step of sending a new peace mission to France. The Convention of 1800 (Treaty of Mortefontaine) ended the Quasi-War, restored normal diplomatic relations, and released the United States from the 1778 alliance — which had become an embarrassment rather than an asset.
Adams’s decision to pursue peace cost him the support of the Hamiltonian wing of the Federalist Party and contributed to his defeat in the election of 1800.
Sources

Irving, Washington. Life of George Washington, Vol. 5.

events/ratification-of-the-constitution.title: Ratification of the Constitution
events/ratification-of-the-constitution.content:
The ratification of the United States Constitution (1787-1788) was the process by which the thirteen states debated and approved the new frame of government. The struggle between Federalists and Anti-Federalists produced the most searching public debate on political principles in American history.
The Framework
Article VII of the proposed Constitution provided that it would take effect when ratified by conventions in nine of the thirteen states. This provision bypassed the state legislatures, which were likely to resist the diminution of their powers, and appealed directly to the people.
The Federalist Campaign
The Federalists, led by Alexander Hamilton, James Madison, and John Jay, mounted a coordinated campaign to secure ratification. Hamilton conceived a comprehensive explication of the Constitution: The Federalist Papers. Published under the pseudonym “Publius,” the eighty-five essays explained and defended every provision of the proposed Constitution.
Hamilton wrote fifty-one of the essays, Madison twenty-nine, and Jay five. The essays appeared in New York newspapers four times per week. Federalist No. 10, written by Madison, dissected the dangers of faction and argued that an extended republic could control their effects better than a small democracy. Federalist No. 78, written by Hamilton, articulated the doctrine of judicial review.
The Anti-Federalists
The Anti-Federalists, a diverse coalition that included Patrick Henry, George Mason, and Samuel Adams, argued that the Constitution created a government too powerful and too distant from the people. They demanded a Bill of Rights to protect individual liberties from the new federal government.
The Ratification Contests
The struggle was fiercest in the largest states. Delaware was the first to ratify (December 7, 1787). Pennsylvania followed quickly. Massachusetts ratified after a close contest in February 1788, with the Federalists promising to add amendments.
In Virginia, the battle was led by Madison for ratification and Patrick Henry against. Virginia ratified in June 1788. The most dramatic contest was in New York, where Hamilton led the Federalist delegation against Governor Clinton’s powerful Anti-Federalist majority. Hamilton spoke twenty-six times during the convention, carrying the debate for six exhausting weeks. The final vote was thirty to twenty-seven — the narrowest margin of any state.
Completion
New Hampshire, the ninth state, ratified on June 21, 1788, making the Constitution legally operative. By 1790, all thirteen states had ratified. The new government began operations in 1789, with Washington’s Inauguration on April 30.
Sources

The Federalist Papers (Publius, 1787-1788).
Chernow, Ron. Alexander Hamilton.
Irving, Washington. Life of George Washington, Vol. 4.

events/second-continental-congress.title: Second Continental Congress
events/second-continental-congress.content:
The Second Continental Congress convened in Philadelphia on May 10, 1775, shortly after the Battles of Lexington and Concord. It served as the de facto national government of the American colonies throughout the Revolutionary War, assuming the powers of a federal union, authorizing the raising of armies, issuing currency, and conducting foreign relations.
Early Sessions
John Hancock was chosen as president of the Congress. The body adopted the Olive Branch Petition, affirming American loyalty to the Crown and seeking redress of grievances — a last attempt at reconciliation that was rejected by King George III. At the same time, Congress began preparing for war. It authorized the raising of armies, appointed generals, and issued paper currency to finance military operations.
Appointment of Washington
The critical question before Congress was who should command the Continental Army. John Adams rose and, in a carefully prepared speech, nominated George Washington of Virginia — a choice calculated to bind the southern colonies to a struggle then centered on New England. Washington was appointed commander-in-chief on June 15, 1775. He accepted the command but refused any salary, asking only that his expenses be paid.
Declaration of Independence
By the spring of 1776, sentiment in Congress had shifted decisively toward independence. On June 7, Richard Henry Lee introduced a resolution declaring independence. Congress appointed a Committee of Five — Thomas Jefferson, John Adams, Benjamin Franklin, Roger Sherman, and Robert R. Livingston — to draft a declaration. Jefferson wrote the document; Franklin and Adams made revisions. On July 4, 1776, Congress adopted the Declaration of Independence.
Wartime Government
Congress governed the war effort throughout the conflict, managing finances, raising troops, negotiating treaties, and directing military strategy. It struggled constantly with financial difficulties, the limitations of the Articles of Confederation, and the need to coordinate the efforts of thirteen sovereign states. The Congress fled Philadelphia in 1777 when the British occupied the city, reconvening briefly at York, Pennsylvania.
Later Sessions
Congress remained the central governing body until 1781, when the Articles of Confederation were finally ratified, creating a formal confederation. Even then, the Congress continued to function under the Articles until the new government under the Constitution was established in 1789.
Sources

Irving, Washington. Life of George Washington, Vol. 1.

events/shays-rebellion.title: Shays' Rebellion
events/shays-rebellion.content:
Shays’ Rebellion (1786-1787) was an armed uprising in western Massachusetts led by Revolutionary War veteran Daniel Shays. The rebellion exposed the weakness of the Articles of Confederation and galvanized support for a stronger national government, culminating in the Constitutional Convention of 1787.
Causes
After the Revolutionary War, the American economy entered a severe depression. The states, particularly Massachusetts, had imposed heavy taxes to pay their war debts. Farmers, many of whom had served in the war, found themselves unable to pay their debts and taxes. Courts began seizing farms and jailing debtors.
The farmers petitioned the state legislature for relief — paper money to ease the currency shortage, laws to delay debt collection, and lower court fees. When their petitions were ignored, they resorted to direct action. In August 1786, armed mobs began preventing the courts from sitting.
The Rebellion
Shays, a former captain in the Continental Army, emerged as the leader of the insurgents. The rebels, calling themselves “Regulators,” marched on the federal arsenal at Springfield in January 1787. The state government, under Governor James Bowdoin, raised a force of 4,400 militia under General Benjamin Lincoln to suppress the uprising.
Lincoln’s forces routed the rebels at the Springfield arsenal and pursued them through the winter countryside. By February, the rebellion was effectively crushed. Several leaders were captured, and Shays escaped to Vermont. Four rebels were sentenced to death but later pardoned.
Impact
The rebellion terrified the American political elite. Washington wrote: “We are fast verging to anarchy and confusion!” The impotence of the national government — which could neither raise troops nor funds to suppress the rebellion — demonstrated the fatal weakness of the Articles of Confederation.
The rebellion directly contributed to the drive for a new constitution. The Annapolis Convention of 1786 had already called for a general convention; Shays’ Rebellion provided the urgency needed to follow through. When the Constitutional Convention met in Philadelphia in May 1787, the memory of armed farmers closing courts was fresh in every delegate’s mind.
Sources

Irving, Washington. Life of George Washington, Vol. 4.

events/siege-of-boston.title: Siege of Boston
events/siege-of-boston.content:
The Siege of Boston (April 1775 – March 1776) was the opening military campaign of the American Revolutionary War. Following the Battles of Lexington and Concord, the American militia surrounded the British garrison in Boston, trapping General Gage and his forces within the town.
Washington Takes Command
When George Washington arrived in Cambridge on July 2, 1775, he found a motley collection of militia regiments — poorly armed, badly supplied, and lacking any common organization. The British, under General Howe, occupied fortified Boston with a well-supplied regular army and naval support. Washington’s strategic object was to distress the British — to cut off supplies, harass foraging parties, and make the occupation so costly that Howe would be forced to evacuate.
The Powder Crisis
A startling discovery was made in the American camp: the army had barely thirty-six rounds of powder per man, and the total supply amounted to only about ninety-three barrels — enough for a few hours of fighting. Washington took desperate measures, enforcing strict economy of ammunition. If the British had known of this weakness, they could have marched out and destroyed the American army.
Knox’s Noble Train of Artillery
The critical deficiency in artillery was addressed by Henry Knox, a Boston bookseller turned artillerist. Knox proposed bringing the cannon captured at Fort Ticonderoga across the winter wilderness to Boston. Washington approved, and Knox departed on his epic mission. During the winter of 1775-76, Knox transported fifty-nine cannons and mortars by boat, ox-drawn sled, and sheer human effort over 300 miles of snow-covered terrain — a feat that became legendary in American military history.
Evacuation
When the Ticonderoga artillery was emplaced on Dorchester Heights in March 1776, the British position became untenable. Howe recognized that the American guns commanded the town and harbor. On March 17, 1776, the British evacuated Boston by sea, sailing for Halifax, Nova Scotia. Washington entered the town in triumph.
Sources

Irving, Washington. Life of George Washington, Vol. 1.

events/siege-of-yorktown.title: Siege of Yorktown
events/siege-of-yorktown.content:
The Siege of Yorktown (September-October 1781) was the final major engagement of the American Revolutionary War. The surrender of General Charles Cornwallis’s army to the combined American and French forces effectively ended the war and secured American independence.
The Strategic Situation
By 1781, the war had become a global conflict. The French alliance had brought French troops, money, and — critically — the French navy into the war. Washington’s army, with the Comte de Rochambeau’s French expeditionary force, sought a decisive blow against the British. The opportunity came when Cornwallis marched his army into Virginia and established a fortified base at Yorktown on the York River peninsula.
The Campaign
Washington and Rochambeau marched their combined army from the Hudson Highlands to Virginia, a movement of over 400 miles conducted with remarkable secrecy and speed. Simultaneously, the French fleet under Admiral de Grasse sailed from the West Indies to the Chesapeake Bay, arriving on August 30, 1781. De Grasse defeated the British fleet under Admiral Graves at the Battle of the Chesapeake, securing control of the bay and cutting Cornwallis’s seaward escape route.
The Siege
The allied army arrived at Yorktown on September 28, 1781, and immediately began siege operations. Over the next three weeks, the Americans and French constructed trenches, parallels, and artillery emplacements, systematically tightening the noose around the British position. The artillery pounding was relentless.
On the night of October 14, the allies stormed two critical British redoubts — Redoubt No. 9 by the French and Redoubt No. 10 by the Americans. The American assault on Redoubt No. 10 was led by Alexander Hamilton, who commanded a light infantry battalion in Lafayette’s division. Hamilton’s men stormed the redoubt with unloaded muskets and fixed bayonets, taking it in less than ten minutes. The victory at Yorktown effectively ended the war, and Hamilton earned the battlefield glory he had craved.
Surrender
On October 17, Cornwallis requested a ceasefire. On October 19, 1781, the British army marched out between the lines of the victorious Americans and French and laid down their arms. The British band played “The World Turned Upside Down.” Cornwallis, feigning illness, sent his second-in-command to surrender his sword.
Aftermath
When news of Yorktown reached London, Lord North’s government fell. Peace negotiations began in Paris, culminating in the Treaty of Paris (1783), which recognized American independence.
Sources

Irving, Washington. Life of George Washington, Vol. 3.

events/stamp-act-crisis.title: Stamp Act Crisis
events/stamp-act-crisis.content:
The Stamp Act Crisis of 1765 marked a watershed in the imperial relationship between Great Britain and her American colonies. The Act, passed by Parliament under Prime Minister George Grenville, required that all legal documents, newspapers, pamphlets, and playing cards in the colonies bear stamps purchased from British authorities — the first direct tax ever levied on the colonists by Parliament.
The Act and Colonial Reaction
The Stamp Act ignited a firestorm of opposition throughout the colonies. In Virginia, the House of Burgesses erupted in debate. Patrick Henry delivered his incendiary speech, defying the king himself, crying “Caesar had his Brutus, Charles I his Cromwell, and George III —” before being interrupted by cries of “Treason!” Henry finished: “may profit by their example.” The assembly adopted Henry’s resolutions asserting the colonists’ rights as Englishmen.
George Washington, sitting in the Virginia House, heard Henry’s thunder but maintained his own measured course. In correspondence, Washington deplored the Act as unconstitutional, arguing that the colonists could only be taxed by their own representatives. However, he opposed the violent demonstrations that erupted in Boston and New York, where effigies were burned and customs officials were attacked.
Non-Importation and Repeal
Merchants in the major ports agreed on a non-importation agreement to pressure British merchants. In London, the Grenville ministry fell and was replaced by the Rockingham Whigs. Benjamin Franklin appeared before the House of Commons in February 1766, delivering a masterful examination of 174 questions that exposed the practical impossibility of enforcing the Stamp Act. Asked how the colonies would react to military enforcement, he replied: “Suppose a military force were sent to America. It will find no man in arms. What will it do then? It cannot force a man to buy a stamp if he chooses to do without it.”
Parliament repealed the Act in 1766. Washington wrote of his joy, expressing hope for restored harmony. But Parliament immediately passed the Declaratory Act, asserting its right to legislate for the colonies “in all cases whatsoever” — a harbinger of future conflict.
Sources

Irving, Washington. Life of George Washington, Vol. 1.
Isaacson, Walter. Benjamin Franklin: An American Life.

events/treaty-of-paris-1783.title: Treaty of Paris (1783)
events/treaty-of-paris-1783.content:
The Treaty of Paris of 1783 formally ended the American Revolutionary War and recognized the independence of the United States. The American negotiating team — Benjamin Franklin, John Adams, and John Jay — secured extraordinarily favorable terms that gave the new nation vast territory and resources.
The Negotiations
Peace negotiations began in Paris in 1782, following the British defeat at Yorktown. Franklin, the sole American minister plenipotentiary to France since 1779, led the American commission. The negotiations tested Franklin’s diplomatic skills to their limit.
Franklin’s strategy was masterfully patient. He knew time was on America’s side as British war fatigue grew, and he refused to be rushed into a settlement that would betray the French alliance — the bedrock of his policy. Lord Shelburne’s government sent secret envoys to sound out terms; Franklin received them but kept the French informed of every contact.
Adams and Jay, suspicious of French motives, pushed for direct negotiations with Britain, violating the spirit of the alliance. Franklin, the master of compromise, navigated between them all, ultimately securing an extraordinarily favorable treaty. During the negotiations, Franklin kept a detailed journal of every meeting, noting each diplomat’s temperament, arguments, and possible weaknesses.
Terms
The treaty granted the United States:

Full and complete independence
Vast western territories extending to the Mississippi River
Fishing rights off the coast of Newfoundland and the Gulf of St. Lawrence
The right to navigate the Mississippi River
The withdrawal of all British troops from American soil
The recommendation that Congress restore confiscated property to Loyalists (though this provision was largely ignored)
