On the Constitutionality of a National Bank
Submitted to President George Washington, February 23, 1791
Alexander Hamilton, Secretary of the Treasury
Source
Hamilton, Alexander. On the Constitutionality of a National Bank. DigiCat, 2022. EAN 8596547315391. Modern republication of Hamilton’s original 1791 opinion.
Digital source: DigiCat EPUB.
Text
raw/hamilton-constitutionality-bank.txt — ~12,800 words, 75K characters. Clean, modern-format text extracted from the DigiCat EPUB.
Context
In February 1791, Congress passed a bill chartering the First Bank of the United States for twenty years. President Washington, uncertain of the bill’s constitutionality, requested written opinions from his cabinet. Secretary of State Thomas Jefferson and Attorney General Edmund Randolph both submitted opinions arguing the bank was unconstitutional. Hamilton, as Secretary of the Treasury and the bill’s original proponent, submitted this opinion in defence of the bank’s constitutionality. Washington ultimately accepted Hamilton’s reasoning and signed the bill into law.
Hamilton opens by acknowledging his personal stake as the measure’s originator and his “firm persuasion, that principles of construction, like those espoused by the Secretary of State and Attorney-General, would be fatal to the just and indispensable authority of the United States.” The opinion proceeds as a single sustained legal argument, systematically dismantling Jefferson’s and Randolph’s objections.
Contents
I. The Nature of Sovereignty and the Doctrine of Implied Powers
Hamilton states his fundamental axiom: every power vested in a government is in its nature SOVEREIGN, and includes by force of the term a right to employ all means requisite and fairly applicable to the attainment of the ends of such power, provided those means are not precluded by constitutional restrictions, are not immoral, and are not contrary to the essential ends of political society. This principle, he argues, would be admitted as an axiom in its application to government in general; the burden falls on those who would deny it to prove a distinction showing that a rule essential to the preservation of social order is inapplicable to the United States.
The division of sovereignty does not alter the principle. The fact that powers of sovereignty are divided between national and state governments does not mean that each portion of power is not sovereign with regard to its proper objects. Each has sovereign power as to certain things, and not as to other things. To deny that the federal government has sovereign power as to its declared purposes because its power does not extend to all laws would be equally to deny that state governments have sovereign power in any case, because their power does not extend to every case. The Supremacy Clause (Article VI) is decisive: the Constitution, laws made in pursuance thereof, and treaties made under their authority are the supreme law of the land. “The power which can create the supreme law of the land, in any case, is doubtless sovereign as to such case.”
Incorporation is incident to sovereign power. This general and indisputable principle puts at once an end to the abstract question of whether the United States have power to erect a corporation: it is unquestionably incident to sovereign power to erect corporations, and consequently to that of the United States in relation to the objects entrusted to the management of the government. The difference is this: where the authority of the government is general, it can create corporations in all cases; where it is confined to certain branches of legislation, it can create corporations only in those cases. Hamilton notes with particular force that the fundamental principle he advances “has been untouched by either” Jefferson or Randolph.
The doctrine of implied and resulting powers. Hamilton concedes that the Constitution is founded on the principle that all powers not delegated are reserved. This is a mere consequence of the republican maxim that all government is a delegation of power. But how much is delegated in each case is a question of fact to be made out by fair reasoning and construction upon the particular provisions of the Constitution, taking as guides the general principles and general ends of government. He makes a crucial tripartite distinction: there are express powers, implied powers (as effectually delegated as the former), and resulting powers — a distinct class exemplified by the sovereign jurisdiction the United States would acquire over conquered territory, which would result from the whole mass of the government’s powers and from the nature of political society rather than from any enumerated power.
The only question in any case is whether the means to be employed has a natural relation to any of the acknowledged objects or lawful ends of the government. Thus Congress may not erect a corporation for superintending the police of Philadelphia, because they are not authorized to regulate that city’s police. But one may be erected in relation to the collection of taxes, trade with foreign countries, trade between the states, or trade with Indian tribes, because it is the province of the federal government to regulate those objects, and it is incident to a general sovereign or legislative power to regulate a thing to employ all the means which relate to its regulation to the best and greatest advantage.
Hamilton attacks what he calls “a strange fallacy” in the reasoning of his opponents: the treatment of incorporation as “some great independent substantive thing, as a political engine of peculiar magnitude and moment,” when in truth it is merely “a quality, capacity, or mean to an end.” He traces the power of incorporation to Roman law, under which a voluntary association of individuals at any time or for any purpose was capable of producing it, and notes that in English law it is part of the executive authority often delegated. The importance of the power has been exaggerated, leading to erroneous conclusions.
II. The General Denial of Corporate Power — Rebuttal of Jefferson and Randolph
Jefferson and Randolph argued that since the Constitution does not explicitly grant Congress the power to charter corporations, the bank is unconstitutional. Hamilton counters this with multiple independent arguments.
The express grant of exclusive legislation in certain places refutes the general denial. Congress has express power to exercise exclusive legislation in all cases whatsoever over the District (not exceeding ten miles square) and over all places purchased for forts, arsenals, dock-yards, and other needful buildings. Language does not afford a more complete designation of sovereign power than “exclusive legislation in all cases whatsoever.” This necessarily includes the power to erect corporations. “Surely, it can never be believed, that Congress, with exclusive power of legislation, in all cases whatsoever, cannot erect a corporation within the district which shall become the seat of government, for the better regulation of its police.” Yet Jefferson had declared the power to erect corporations “a right remaining exclusively with the states.”
The convention’s rejection of a corporate power clause is unreliable evidence. Jefferson argued that the Constitutional Convention rejected a proposition to empower Congress to make corporations. Hamilton responds: “What was the precise nature or extent of this proposition, or what the reasons for refusing it, is not ascertained by any authentic document, or even by accurate recollection.” As far as any document exists, it specifies only canals. Some affirm it was confined to canals; others that it embraced banks; others that it extended to incorporating generally. Some say it was rejected as improper, others as unnecessary and inexpedient to furnish an additional topic of objection. “In this state of the matter, no inference whatever can be drawn from it.” Moreover, even if the proposition had been exactly as Jefferson claimed, the intention of the framers is to be sought in the instrument itself according to the usual rules of construction — extrinsic circumstances regarding the convention’s intention must be rejected if a power is deducible by fair inference from the Constitution’s actual provisions.
The argument that incorporation is too important to be implied is circular. The claim that if the Constitution intended to confer so important a power it would have been expressly mentioned rests on “an exaggerated and erroneous conception of the nature of the power.” Hamilton reiterates that it is a mean, not an end, and ought to have been left to implication rather than expressly granted.
III. The Doctrine of Necessary and Proper Means — Liberal Construction
The meaning of “necessary.” Jefferson had argued that no means are necessary but those without which the grant of the power would be nugatory — and further, that the necessity which warrants constitutional exercise of the power depends on “casual and temporary circumstances.” Hamilton demolishes this: “an idea which alone refutes the construction.” The expediency of exercising a particular power at a particular time may depend on circumstances, but the constitutional right of exercising it must be uniform and invariable, the same today as tomorrow.
“According to both [the grammatical and popular sense], necessary often means no more than needful, requisite, incidental, useful, or conducive to.” It is common to say “it is necessary for a government or a person to do this or that thing” when nothing more is intended than that the interest of the government or person requires or will be promoted by it. The whole turn of the necessary and proper clause indicates “that it was the intent of the convention, by that clause, to give a liberal latitude to the exercise of the specified powers.” To understand the word as Jefferson does would be to depart from its obvious and popular sense and give it a restrictive operation “never before entertained” — as if “absolutely or indispensably” had been prefixed.
The consequences of Jefferson’s construction. Such a construction would beget endless uncertainty and embarrassment. There are few measures of any government which would stand so severe a test. To insist upon it would make the criterion of any implied power “a case of extreme necessity, which is rather a rule to justify the overleaping of the bounds of constitutional authority, than to govern the ordinary exercise of it.” By the same reasoning, one could prove that no state government has a right to incorporate a bank, since the state’s public business could be performed without one — and indeed that there was no power to incorporate a town for police purposes, since an incorporation may be dispensed with even if it is better to have one.
The correct test: relation to end, not degree of necessity. “The degree in which a measure is necessary, can never be a test of the legal right to adopt it. That must be a matter of opinion, and can only be a test of expediency. The relation between the measure and the end; between the nature of the mean employed towards the execution of a power, and the object of that power; must be the criterion of constitutionality; not the more or less of necessity or utility.”
The lighthouse precedent. The act concerning light-houses, beacons, buoys, and public piers — passed under the power to regulate trade — is a decisive example of the government’s own practice contradicting Jefferson’s restrictive rule. It cannot be affirmed that the exercise of that power was strictly necessary, or that the power to regulate trade would be nugatory without that of regulating such establishments.
The rule of liberal construction. Powers contained in a constitution of government, especially those concerning the general administration of the affairs of a country — its finances, trade, defence — ought to be construed liberally in advancement of the public good. This rule does not depend on the particular form of government or the demarcation of its boundaries, “but on the nature and objects of government itself.” The means by which national exigencies are to be provided for, national inconveniences obviated, and national prosperity promoted are of such infinite variety and complexity that there must be great latitude of discretion.
Randolph’s distinction refuted. The Attorney-General admitted the rule but argued it should be stricter for the federal constitution because there is more danger of error in defining partial than general powers. Hamilton responds: the reason for the rule — the variety and extent of public exigencies, a far greater proportion of which are objects of national administration — forbids such a distinction. Greater danger of error may be a prudential reason for caution in practice, but it cannot be a rule of restrictive interpretation. Randolph himself defined “necessary” as “incidental” and “the natural means of executing a power,” yet failed to apply this definition consistently.
The necessary and proper clause gives explicit sanction to implied powers. While the clause gives no new or independent power, it provides “an explicit sanction to the doctrine of implied powers” and is equivalent to an admission that the government as to its specified powers and objects has plenary and sovereign authority — in some cases paramount to the states, in others coordinate with it.
The doctrine is not unlimited. Hamilton clarifies that his doctrine does not affirm that the national government is sovereign in all respects, but only to the extent of the objects of its specified powers. The criterion of constitutionality is: (1) is the end clearly comprehended within any specified power? (2) does the measure have an obvious relation to that end? (3) is it forbidden by any particular provision? An additional useful criterion: does the proposed measure abridge a preexisting right of any state or individual? If not, there is a strong presumption in favour of constitutionality.
IV. Application to the Bank — Specific Powers
Hamilton applies his doctrine by tracing “a natural and obvious relation between the institution of a bank, and the objects of several of the enumerated powers of the government.”
A. The power to collect taxes. A bank relates to tax collection in two ways: indirectly, by increasing the quantity of circulating medium and quickening circulation, which facilitates the means of paying; directly, by creating a convenient species of medium in which taxes are to be paid. To designate or appoint the money or thing in which taxes are to be paid is a proper and necessary exercise of the power of collection. Congress could have required payment in kind, in state paper money, in bills of existing banks, or in bills issued under federal authority. The appointment of the medium is an incident to the power of collection.
Hamilton constructs an elegant hypothetical: the government could itself issue bills payable on demand, set apart a fund for answering them, and appoint officers to direct the fund — all of which would be constitutional and would amount to the institution of a bank. “The simplest and most precise idea of a bank, is, a deposit of coin or other property, as a fund for circulating a credit upon it, which is to answer the purpose of money.” If the fund were vested in the officers and their successors as private property incapable of being resumed without violating the sanction protecting property rights, this would amount to the erection of a corporation — for the true definition of a corporation is “a legal person, or a person created by act of law; consisting of one or more natural persons, authorized to hold property or a franchise in succession, in a legal, as contradistinguished from a natural, capacity.”
B. The power to borrow money. A bank has a direct relation to borrowing because it is “an usual, and in sudden emergencies, an essential instrument, in the obtaining of loans to government.” A nation threatened with war needs large sums quickly; taxes require time to collect; anticipation is indispensable. With a bank the supply can at once be had; without one, loans from individuals must be sought — often too slow, sometimes not practicable at all.
Hamilton uses a concrete example from the very moment of writing: “An Indian expedition is to be prosecuted. The only fund out of which the money can arise consistently with the public engagements, is a tax, which only begins to be collected in July next. The preparations, however, are instantly to be made. The money must therefore be borrowed; and of whom could it be borrowed, if there were no public banks?” He posits that if no banks existed, it would be necessary to create one, and if individuals offered to lend on condition that they be incorporated as a bank, “Can it be believed that a compliance with this proposition would be unconstitutional?”
C. The power to regulate trade between the states. A bank is conducive to creating a convenient medium of exchange between states and maintaining full circulation by preventing the frequent displacement of metals in reciprocal remittances. Money is “the very hinge on which commerce turns” — and this includes paper as well as gold and silver. Hamilton rejects Randolph’s contention that the medium of circulation is confined to coin: it is even supposable that the whole or greatest part of the coin might be carried out of the country.
D. The power of common defence and the property clause. The aid of such an institution is essential to measures for protecting the frontiers, as demonstrated by the Indian expedition. Moreover, the bank is within the clause authorizing Congress to make all needful rules and regulations concerning the property of the United States. The government becomes a joint proprietor of the bank’s stock. Hamilton argues by analogy: it is admitted that under this clause Congress can erect a government (a corporation of the highest nature) over the Western Territory. “By what rule of construction can it be maintained, that the same words, in a constitution of government, will not have the same effect when applied to one species of property as to another, as far as the subject is capable of it?”
V. Response to Jefferson’s and Randolph’s Specific Objections
Against the laws of alienage, descent, escheat, forfeiture, distribution, and monopoly. Jefferson argued that the proposed incorporation creates capacities and attributes against these foundation laws of the states and “prostrates” state jurisprudence. Hamilton responds: if these are truly the foundation laws of the several states, then most of them have subverted their own foundations, since scarcely one has not made material alterations in its law of descents. Moreover, the erection of a corporation does not violate these laws — it creates a kind of person to which they are inapplicable. An artificial person can have no country (alienage inapplicable), no heirs (descent inapplicable), cannot commit a crime (forfeiture inapplicable), and cannot die (distribution inapplicable). “To do a thing which is against the law, is to do something which it forbids, and which is a violation of it.”
Even if incorporation did alter state laws, Hamilton argues this proves nothing against constitutionality: almost every new law alters an old one in some way. Congress’s power to establish uniform bankruptcy laws or regulate foreign coin necessarily alters state laws. The power to prohibit exportation alters the common law right of every citizen to export property. “It can, therefore, never be good reasoning, to say, this or that act is unconstitutional, because it alters this or that law of a state.”
Monopoly rebuttal. Jefferson characterized the bank as a monopoly. Hamilton responds: the bill neither prohibits any state from erecting as many banks as it pleases, nor any number of individuals from associating to carry on the business. “Monopoly implies a legal impediment to the carrying on the trade by others than those to whom it is granted.” No such impediment exists here.
Paramount laws rebuttal. Jefferson charged that the bank’s by-laws would be paramount to state laws. Hamilton: the by-laws of a bank can operate only upon its own members and concern only the disposition of its own property, essentially resembling the rules of a private mercantile partnership. They are expressly not to be contrary to law — meaning state law as well as federal law. If a corporate by-law is contrary to state law, it must be overruled as void unless the state law is contrary to federal law, in which case the question is between state and federal law, not between state and corporate law.
Randolph’s enumeration critique. Randolph attempted to enumerate what powers are included under each head of federal authority and concluded that incorporation was not among them. Hamilton demolishes this approach by showing the enumerations are radically incomplete. Under the power to regulate commerce, Randolph omitted: the power to prohibit exportation; to prescribe rules for American shipping (how vessels shall be navigated, by citizens or foreigners); to regulate the manner of contracting with seamen and ship policies; to grant bounties to certain vessels and merchandise; to prescribe inspection rules for exports; to regulate pilots; to regulate bills of exchange between states. Under the borrowing power, Randolph omitted pledging or mortgaging a fund, collateral conditions, and lotteries as borrowing expedients. The enumerations are “so imperfect as to authorize no conclusion whatever.”
“The practice of mankind.” Hamilton invokes a powerful argument from usage: all principal commercial nations have made use of trading corporations or companies for external commerce, proving that their establishment is incident to the regulation of commerce. Banks are “an usual engine in the administration of national finances, and an ordinary, and the most effectual, instrument of loans.” It pleads strongly against the supposition that a government clothed with most of the important prerogatives of sovereignty — in relation to its revenues, debt, credit, defence, trade, and intercourse with foreign nations — is forbidden to make use of that instrument. “To all questions of this nature, the practice of mankind ought to have great weight against the theories of individuals.”
The aggregate view of the Constitution. The combined powers of laying and collecting taxes, borrowing money indefinitely, coining money and regulating foreign coins, and making needful rules concerning property — together with the reason and nature of the thing — speak strongly that “it is the manifest design and scope of the constitution, to vest in Congress all the powers requisite to the effectual administration of the finances of the United States.” To suppose the government precluded from so usual and important an instrument as a bank is to suppose what does not coincide with the general tenor and complexion of the Constitution. “Little less than a prohibiting clause can destroy the strong presumptions which result from the general aspect of the government. Nothing but demonstration should exclude the idea that the power exists.”
VI. Summary of Hamilton’s Position
Hamilton concludes by restating the propositions he has demonstrated:

The power of the government as to the objects entrusted to its management is in its nature sovereign.
The right of erecting corporations is one inherent in, and inseparable from, the idea of sovereign power.
The position that the government can exercise no power but such as is delegated does not militate against this principle.
The word “necessary” in the general clause can have no restrictive operation derogating from this principle — the degree to which a measure is necessary is a test of expediency only, not of constitutional right.
The power to erect corporations is not an independent and substantive power, but an incidental and auxiliary one, more properly left to implication than expressly granted.
The principle does not extend the power of government beyond prescribed limits, because it only affirms a power to incorporate for purposes within the sphere of the specified powers.
The right to exercise such a power in certain cases is unequivocally granted in the most positive and comprehensive terms (as in the exclusive legislation clause).
Such a power has actually been exercised in two eminent instances: the erection of governments northwest and southwest of the Ohio River — the last independent of any antecedent compact.

Hence results “a full and complete demonstration, that the Secretary of State and Attorney-General are mistaken, when they deny generally the power of the national government to erect corporations.”
VII. Conclusion
Having shown the bank’s natural relation to the power of collecting taxes, regulating trade, providing for the common defence, and the property clause, Hamilton rests his case. He notes that the proposed measure stands even the most severe test on the question of whether it abridges any preexisting right of any state or individual — each state may still erect as many banks as it pleases, and every individual may still carry on banking to any extent. He corrects Jefferson’s misstatement that the bill contemplates a repayment rather than a loan to the government, explaining that the government remains a proprietor of the stock and will share in profit or loss — hence the sum is manifestly and in the strictest sense a loan.

sources/hamilton-establishment-mint.content:
Report on the Establishment of a Mint
Hamilton’s comprehensive plan for a national coinage system, responding to six specific questions posed by the House of Representatives and detailing the organization of the mint itself.

Submitted to the House of Representatives, January 28, 1791
Alexander Hamilton, Secretary of the Treasury
Source
Hamilton, Alexander. “Report on the Establishment of a Mint.” In Report on the Establishment of a National Bank and a Mint, by Alexander Hamilton, 272–325. Philadelphia: William M’Lean, 1791. Reprinted in The Works of Alexander Hamilton (Vol. I).
Digital source: FRASER (Federal Reserve Archival System for Economic Research), Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis. OCR text from the digitized 1791 edition.
Text
raw/hamilton-establishment-mint.txt — 2,833 lines, ~103K characters. OCR text from the FRASER digitization of the 1791 Philadelphia edition. OCR quality is moderate with some garbled characters, but substantively readable.
Contents
Hamilton’s report on the mint addresses six specific questions posed by the House of Representatives, plus the organization of the mint itself. The report opens with a framing of the immense stakes involved: “The general state of debtor and creditor; all the relations and consequences of price; the essential interests of trade and industry; the value of all property; the whole income, both of the state and of individuals, are liable to be sensibly influenced, beneficially, or otherwise, by the judicious, or injudicious regulation of this interesting object.” He acknowledges the difficulty of the subject — one that “has frequently occupied the reflections and researches of politicians, without having harmonized their opinions on some of the most important of the principles.”
Hamilton then answers why reform is necessary at all: “The immense disorder which actually reigns in so delicate and important a concern, and the still greater disorder which is every moment possible, call loudly for a reform.” He notes that the dollar, originally contemplated in the money transactions of the country, had “by successive diminutions of its weight and fineness, sustained a depreciation of five per cent.” Furthermore, “a nation ought not to suffer the value of the property of its citizens to fluctuate with the fluctuations of a foreign mint, and to change with the changes in the regulations of a foreign sovereign.” The unequal values allowed in different parts of the union for coins of the same intrinsic worth, the defective species embarrassing circulation, and the dissimilarity in the several state monies of account are all cited as inconveniences that a national coinage would remedy.
I. What Ought to Be the Money Unit?
Hamilton examines the existing monetary situation in depth. The pound is the unit of account in all states but with varying values — the Pennsylvania pound equals 2.6666 Spanish dollars, while the Virginia pound equals 2.5 dollars. However, there being no formal regulation on the point (the resolutions of Congress of July 6, 1785, and August 8, 1786, never having been carried into operation), the actual unit can only be inferred from usage. The manner of adjusting foreign exchanges indicates the dollar as best entitled to that character: “the old piastre of Spain, or old Seville piece of eight rials, of the value of four shillings and six pence sterling, is evidently contemplated.” For instance, one hundred pounds sterling equals one hundred and sixty-six and two-thirds pounds Pennsylvania currency, corresponding with the proportion between four shillings six pence sterling and seven shillings six pence, the current value of the dollar in that state.
But Hamilton notes that this circumstance “loses much of its weight” from two considerations: the Spanish dollar “has never had any settled or standard value, according to weight or fineness; but has been permitted to circulate by tale without regard to either; very much as a mere money of convenience,” while gold has had a fixed price by weight with an eye to its fineness. This “greater stability of value of the gold coins is an argument of force for regarding the money unit as having been hitherto virtually attached to gold, rather than to silver.”
The old Seville piece weighed 17 dwt. 12 grains and contained 386 grains 15 mites of fine silver, but this piece “has been long since out of circulation.” The dollars now in common circulation are of recent date and much inferior both in weight and fineness — average weight 17 dwt. 8 grains. The most reliable experiment makes the new dollar contain 370 grains and 933 thousandth parts of a grain of pure silver. The Spanish standard for silver coin in 1761 was 261 parts fine and 27 parts alloy; but this standard has since been altered considerably for the worse. From market computations in Amsterdam and London, the new dollar appears to contain about 368 grains of fine silver, and its immediate predecessor about 374 grains.
Hamilton ultimately argues for preserving the identity of the dollar for public confidence, and recommends the dollar as the money unit of the United States. He defines the dollar as containing 371.25 grains of fine silver (or the equivalent value in gold, 24.75 grains of fine gold). This figure is “within a small fraction of the mean of the two last emissions of dollars; the only ones which are now found in common circulation, and of which the newest is in the greatest abundance.” The alloy in each case to be one-twelfth of the total weight, making the unit 27 grains of standard gold and 405 grains of standard silver.
II. The Proportion Between Gold and Silver
Hamilton addresses the bimetallic ratio at great length, presenting one of the most sophisticated early American analyses of bimetallism. He surveys ratios adopted by European nations — England at 15.2:1, France at 15.5:1, Holland varying — and examines the dynamics of bimetallic flow in detail. His reasoning on the bimetallic question proceeds through several stages.
The case against exclusive attachment to either metal. Hamilton notes that a preference “ought to be given to neither of the metals for the money unit.” He directly challenges the prevailing Congressional resolutions (July 6, 1785 and August 8, 1786) which had attached the unit to silver, arguing that “if either were to be preferred, it ought to be gold rather than silver.” His reasons: gold “may, perhaps, in certain senses, be said to have greater stability than silver. As being of superior value, less liberties have been taken with it in the regulations of different countries. Its standard has remained more uniform. As being not so much an article of merchandize, owing to the use made of silver in the trade with the East-Indies and China, it is less liable to be influenced by circumstances of commercial demand.”
However, Hamilton ultimately concludes that attaching the unit exclusively to either metal “cannot be done effectually, without destroying the office and character of one of them as money; and reducing it to the situation of a mere merchandize.” He argues that “to annul the use of either of the metals as money, is to abridge the quantity of circulating medium, and is liable to all the objections which arise from a comparison of the benefits of a full, with the evils of a scanty circulation.” He dismisses the counterargument that only the favored metal would find its way into the country: “The practicability of this would in some measure depend on the abundance or scarcity of it in the country paying.” Furthermore, “it is often in the course of trade as desirable to possess the kind of money, as the kind of commodities, best adapted to a foreign market.”
The dynamics of bimetallic flow. Hamilton provides a rigorous explanation: “If two countries are supposed, in one of which the proportion of gold to silver is as 1 to 16, in the other as 1 to 15, gold being worth more, silver less, in one than in the other; it is manifest, that in their reciprocal payments, each will select that species which it values least, to pay to the other where it is valued most.” He then cites empirical evidence: “In Spain and England, where gold is rated higher than in other parts of Europe, there is a scarcity of silver; while it is found to abound in France and Holland, where it is rated higher in proportion to gold, than in the neighbouring nations.” He also notes the global flow “from Europe to China and the East-Indies, owing to the comparative cheapness of it in the former, and dearness of it in the latter.”
The danger of specie reduction. Hamilton warns that a more serious consequence than the mere banishment of one metal is “the diminution of the total quantity of specie which a country would naturally possess.” As often as a country over-rating either metal receives payment in that metal, it gets a less actual quantity than it ought. “There will be a continual effort to make payment to it in that species to which it has annexed an exaggerated estimation, wherever it is current at a less proportional value.” He qualifies this with caution, noting that “in such matters, there are always some local, and, many other particular circumstances, which qualify and vary the operation of general principles.”
A third ill consequence is “a greater and more frequent disturbance of the state of the money unit, by a greater and more frequent diversity between the legal and market proportions of the metals.” Though not yet experienced in the United States, Hamilton warns this would follow when commerce attained maturity.
The recommended ratio. Hamilton surveys the historical and contemporary evidence. He cites Sir Isaac Newton’s 1717 representation to the British Treasury: “By the course of trade and exchange between nation and nation in all Europe, fine gold is to fine silver as 14⅘ or 15 to 1.” Hamilton acknowledges that more than seventy years have passed since Newton’s calculation, but believes “the state of the matter, as represented by Sir Isaac Newton, is not very remote from its actual state.” In Holland, in December 1789, gold was to silver as 1 to 14.88; in London it approached 1 to 15. The existing proportion in the United States is about 1 to 15. Hamilton notes that “the innovations of the Spanish mint have imperceptibly introduced a proportion so analogous as this is, to that which prevails among the principal commercial nations.” The proportion of 1 to 15 is further recommended “by the particular situation of our trade, as being very nearly that which obtains in the market of Great-Britain, to which nation our specie is principally exported.” He recommends approximately 15:1, noting that “there can hardly be a better rule, in any country, for the legal, than the market proportion; if this can be supposed to have been produced by the free and steady course of commercial principles.”
III. The Proportion and Composition of Alloy
Pure gold and silver are too soft for practical coinage. Hamilton reviews English standards (11 parts fine gold to 1 part alloy — i.e., 22 carats fine), noting this coincides with the proportion in the coins of Portugal, England, France, and Spain. In the two former it is real; in the two latter there is a deduction for “remedy of weight and alloy.” The principal gold coins in Germany, Holland, Sweden, Denmark, Poland, and Italy are finer, ranging from 1¼ to 1⅞ carats above the English standard. Silver standards vary widely: Great Britain’s is 222 parts fine to 18 alloy, while other European nations range from 17 parts better to 75 worse.
The principal reasons for alloy are “the saving of expense in the refining of the metals” and “the rendering of them harder, as a security against too great waste by friction or wearing.” Hamilton notes that the reality of the hardening effect has been denied — “experience has been appealed to, as proving that the more alloyed coins wear faster than the purer” — but he considers the saving of trouble and expense sufficient inducement to follow existing examples. He recommends following the nations with whom the US has most intercourse: Spain, Portugal, England, and France.
For silver, copper is “the only proper one” for alloy. For gold, a mixture of silver and copper is used — in English coins equal parts, in other countries varying from one-third to two-thirds silver. The silver counteracts copper’s tendency to injure the coin’s color, while copper prevents the too great whiteness that silver alone would confer. Hamilton recommends establishing by law that the proportion of silver to copper in gold coins shall not be more than one-half nor less than one-third, vesting discretion in some proper place to regulate within those limits as experience recommends.
IV. Whether the Expense of Coinage Shall Be Defrayed by the Government
Hamilton presents an extended argument on gratuitous vs. duty-based coinage, calling it “perhaps, one of the nicest questions in the doctrine of money.” The practice of different nations is dissimilar: in England coinage is entirely free (the mint price of bullion equals the value in coin); in France there is a duty of eight percent; in Holland a difference of .96 percent on gold and 1.48 percent on silver. The resolution of August 8, 1786, had proceeded on the idea of a deduction of half percent from gold and two percent from silver.
Hamilton identifies two methods of defraying coinage expense out of the metals: (1) reducing the quantity of fine gold and silver in the coins, or (2) establishing a difference between the value of metals in coin and the mint price in bullion. He declares the first method “inadmissible,” unable to distinguish it from “raising the denomination of the coin; a measure which has been disapproved by the wisest men of the nations in which it has been practised, and condemned by the rest of the world.” To declare that less weight of gold or silver shall pass for the same sum “obliging creditors to receive less than their just dues, and depreciating property of every kind.” He warns that “there is scarcely any point, in the economy of national affairs, of greater moment than the uniform preservation of the intrinsic value of the money unit. On this the security and steady value of property essentially depend.”
The second method — letting the same sum of money represent the same quantity of metal, but allowing a mint price below coin value — is “greatly to be preferred.” But Hamilton exposes the complexity of the issue at length, analyzing the French experience and the English practice of mint delays. He ultimately argues that if the government charges significant seigniorage, bullion owners will send their metal abroad to be coined cheaper. Drawing on English precedent of free coinage and the experience of France (where “the government has found it necessary, on some occasions, to employ very violent methods to compel the bringing of bullion to the mint”), Hamilton argues for government bearing the cost. He recommends an experiment of one-half percent difference on each of the metals — “the least exceptionable expedient for restraining the melting down, or exportation of the former” — with immediate payment at the mint.
He also considers and rejects the alternative of increasing alloy content as a means of preventing exportation, citing objections of augmented expense, actual and perceived depreciation of the coin, and greater danger of counterfeiting: “the perfection of the coins is a great safe-guard against counterfeits.”
V. The Number, Denominations, Sizes, and Devices of the Coins
Hamilton proposes a decimal system following the resolution of August 8, 1786, which he says “has been approved abroad, as well as at home,” and “nothing can be more simple or convenient, than the decimal subdivisions.” The unit in the money of account continues as a dollar; its multiples are dimes, cents, and milles (tenths, hundredths, and thousandths).
The proposed coins are:

Gold coins: An “eagle” equal in weight and value to ten units or dollars (the largest gold piece). A second gold piece equal to a tenth part of the former, which shall also be a unit or dollar — this smaller piece is intended not to be numerous but to “have a sensible object in that metal, as well as in silver, to express the unit.” Fifty thousand at a time in circulation may suffice for this purpose.
Silver coins: The dollar (a unit). The disme or dime (a tenth part of the dollar) — “less than the least of the silver coins now in general currency in England.”
Copper coins: The cent (a hundredth part of a dollar). The half-cent (half the value of the former).

Hamilton discusses appropriate sizes and weights. He recommends the cent weigh 11 pennyweight, which “will about correspond with the value of the copper and the expense of coinage.” He notes that pieces of very small value are “a great accommodation, and the means of a beneficial economy to the poor; by enabling them to purchase in small portions, and at a more reasonable rate, the necessaries of which they stand in need.” The half-cent enables the poor to procure necessaries cheap, allowing them “with more comfort to themselves, to labour for less.”
On coin size, Hamilton is attentive to wear: “the more superficies or surface, the more the piece will be liable to be injured by friction; or, in other words, the faster it will wear.” Hence the form of the double guinea or double louis d’or is preferable to that of the half johannes for the large gold piece. To fortify the idea of the dollar’s identity, the new silver dollar’s form and size should agree with the present Spanish dollar as far as the quantity of matter permits.
For devices, Hamilton recommends simple emblematic designs: “The devices of the coins are far from being matters of indifference, as they may be made the vehicles of useful impressions. They ought, therefore, to be emblematical, but without losing sight of simplicity. The fewer sharp points and angles there are, the less will be the loss by wearing.” The eagle is acknowledged as “not a very expressive or apt appellation for the largest gold piece, but nothing better occurs.”
VI. Whether Foreign Coins Shall Be Permitted to Remain Current
A gradual phase-out, carefully designed to prevent a sudden stagnation of circulation:

Year 1 (after mint commences): Foreign coins continue at their present rates. The moneys paid into the treasury during this year, being recoined before re-issue, will afford a partial substitute before any interruption to pre-existing circulation.
Year 2: Privilege continued only to gold coins of Portugal, England, and France, plus Spanish silver coins. Treasury revenues and newly minted coins will materially extend the substitute.
Year 3: The remaining foreign coins at mint rates only. The extension of national coinage will be “so far increased during the third year, by the facility of procuring the remaining species to be recoined, which will arise from the diminution of their current values, as probably to enable the dispensing wholly with the circulation of the foreign coins, after that period.”
After: All foreign coin ceases to be legal tender. The progress of bank bill currency during the same time will also afford a substitute.

Hamilton recommends the President be given discretionary authority over the Spanish dollar — “It is possible that an exception in favour of this particular species of coin may be found expedient: and it may tend to obviate inconveniences, if there be a power to make the exception in a capacity to be exerted when the period shall arrive.”
Regarding the proposal of Secretary of State Jefferson to align the dollar’s weight with the unit of weight, Hamilton notes that the five-grain addition this would require is “so considerable a change in the money unit” that it would “abandon the advantage of preserving the identity of the dollar.” He suggests the end might be obtained by increasing the proportion of alloy in silver coins, but “this would destroy the uniformity, in that respect, between the gold and silver coins.”
VII. Organization of the Mint
Hamilton proposes a lean administrative structure:

Director of the Mint — general superintendence of the business
Assay-Master or Assayer — to receive metals brought to the mint, ascertain their fineness, and deliver them to be coined
Master Coiner — to conduct the making of the coins
Cashier — to receive and pay out coins
Auditor — to keep and adjust the accounts of the mint
Clerks — as many as the Director deems necessary, to assist the different officers
Workmen — as many as found requisite; the number is left indefinite because at certain times more are needed than at others, though they “will never be numerous”
Porter

Hamilton notes that European mints have various other officers, but those listed “appear to be indispensable.” Persons in the capacity of clerks will suffice instead of additional specialized officers, “with the advantage of greater economy.” The estimated ordinary annual expense of the establishment is 15,000–20,000.
VIII. Remedy for Errors in Weight and Alloy
Hamilton describes the English “pix” practice in detail:
“A certain number of pieces are taken promiscuously out of every fifteen pounds of gold coined at the mint, which are deposited for safe keeping in a strong box called the pix. This box, from time to time, is opened in the presence of the lord chancellor, the officers of the treasury, and others; and portions are selected from the pieces of each coinage, which are melted together, and the mass assayed by a jury of the company of goldsmiths. If the imperfection and deficiency, both in fineness and weight, fall short of a sixth of a carat or 40 grains of pure gold upon a pound of standard, the master of the mint is held excusable; because it is supposed that no workman can reasonably be answerable for greater exactness.”
Hamilton recommends similar regulation for the United States, noting that “the expediency of some similar regulation seems to be manifest.”

sources/hamilton-report-manufactures.title: [source] Report on Manufactures (Hamilton, 1791)
sources/hamilton-report-manufactures.content:
Report on Manufactures
Communicated to the House of Representatives, December 5, 1791
Alexander Hamilton, Secretary of the Treasury
Source
Hamilton, Alexander. Report on Manufactures, Communicated to the House of Representatives, December 5, 1791. Good Press, 2022. EAN 4064066063658. Modern republication of Hamilton’s original 1791 report.
Digital source: Good Press EPUB.
Text
raw/hamilton-manufactures.txt — ~32,700 words, 196K characters. Clean, modern-format text extracted from the Good Press EPUB. The longest of Hamilton’s Treasury reports.
Contents
This is Hamilton’s most comprehensive state paper, often considered the founding document of American economic nationalism. It is a single continuous treatise without chapter divisions, but contains the following major arguments and subjects:
I. The Question Stated: Should Manufactures Be Encouraged?
Hamilton opens by noting that the House resolution of January 15, 1790, directs him to report on means of promoting manufactures — particularly those that would render the United States independent of foreign nations for military and other essential supplies. He observes that the expediency of encouraging manufactures, once deemed very questionable, is now “pretty generally admitted.” The embarrassments obstructing external trade have led to reflections on enlarging domestic commerce; foreign restrictions on agricultural exports create a desire for more extensive domestic demand; and the success of existing manufacturing enterprises justifies hope that obstacles are less formidable than previously apprehended.
Nevertheless, Hamilton acknowledges “respectable patrons of opinions unfriendly to the encouragement of manufactures” and summarizes their full case:

Agriculture is the most beneficial object of human industry, especially for the United States with its immense tracts of fertile, uninhabited territory. Nothing can afford so advantageous an employment of capital and labor as converting wilderness into cultivated farms.
Industry left to itself infallibly finds the most profitable employment. To accelerate manufactures by government patronage is to transfer industry from a more to a less beneficial channel by “force and art.”
Scarcity of hands — the small population relative to territory, the allurements of emigration to unsettled lands, and the ease with which artisans become independent farmers produce “a scarcity of hands for manufacturing occupation and dearness of labor generally.”
Deficiency of pecuniary capital makes successful competition with European manufactures appear “little less than desperate.” Extensive manufactures, the argument runs, can only be the offspring of a full or redundant population.
Monopoly and enhanced prices — if government does force manufactures prematurely through duties, prohibitions, or bounties, it only sacrifices the community to particular classes, creating virtual monopolies with inflated prices defrayed at public expense.

Hamilton concedes this mode of reasoning “has certainly respectable pretensions” and that if it had governed nations more generally they might have attained greater prosperity. But he immediately cautions that “most general theories admit of numerous exceptions, and there are few, if any, of the political kind which do not blend a considerable portion of error with the truths they inculcate.”
II. The Superior Productiveness of Agriculture — Examined and Refuted
Hamilton devotes his most sophisticated economic reasoning to dismantling the physiocratic claim that agriculture is not only the most productive but the only productive species of industry. He notes that this thesis “has not been verified by any accurate detail of facts and calculations” and that the general arguments for it “are rather subtle and paradoxical than solid or convincing.”
The physiocratic argument stated. The claim runs as follows: labor on land produces enough not only to replace expenses and maintain workers, but to yield a net surplus — rent — for the landlord. Manufacturing labor, by contrast, does nothing more than replace the stock employed (materials, tools, wages) and yield the ordinary profit on that stock. It produces nothing equivalent to rent; the additional value it gives to raw materials is counterbalanced by the value of agricultural produce consumed by manufacturers. Manufacturing, therefore, can augment society’s revenue only through parsimony, not through positive productiveness.
Hamilton’s three-part rebuttal. First, he argues that manufacturing labor does reproduce a value equal to what it consumes and continues the original capital in existence — this alone should exempt it from being considered “wholly unproductive.” Even if the consumption of agricultural produce by manufacturers exactly equals the value added to materials, the total amount of consumption and production in a given period would be double the agricultural produce consumed. There would “at every moment, in consequence of their labor, a greater value of goods in the market.”
Second, the claim that artificers can augment revenue only by parsimony is “true in no other sense than in one which is equally applicable to husbandmen or cultivators.” All classes can increase wealth only through savings; manufacturing enjoys no special disability here.
Third, the annual produce of a country can only be increased in two ways — by improvements in the productive powers of existing labor, or by increases in the quantity of labor. Manufacturing labor, being more susceptible to subdivision and simplification of operations, is capable of greater improvement in productive powers than agricultural labor.
The nature-cooperates-with-man fallacy. One physiocratic argument holds that in agriculture nature cooperates with man, so their joint labor must be greater than man’s alone. Hamilton calls this “both quaint and superficial.” It is quite conceivable that skilled human labor alone, applied to complex manufacturing, may be more productive in value than the combined labor of nature and man directed at simpler agricultural operations. Moreover, the mechanical powers — fire and water — are made “auxiliary to the prosecution of manufactures” to a far greater extent than in agriculture. Hamilton also notes that agricultural labor is “periodical and occasional, depending on seasons, and liable to various and long intermissions,” while manufacturing labor is “constant and regular, extending through the year, embracing in some instances night as well as day.”
The rent fallacy exposed. The central physiocratic argument — that manufacturing yields nothing equivalent to the rent of land — Hamilton dismisses as “rather verbal than substantial.” What appears as rent in agriculture is simply the ordinary profit of a separate capital: the land itself, advanced by its owner to a tenant. The farmer’s profit and the landlord’s rent are nothing more than “the ordinary profits of two capitals belonging to two different persons and united in the cultivation of a farm.” In manufacturing, the same division occurs: one person may lend capital (receiving interest, which corresponds to rent) while another carries on the enterprise (receiving profit, corresponding to the farmer’s return). Both together constitute the ordinary profit on the total capital employed. Hamilton concludes that “the rent, therefore, accruing to the proprietor of the land, far from being a criterion of exclusive productiveness, is no criterion even of superior productiveness.”
The hypothetical examples. Hamilton constructs a series of economic models demonstrating that manufacturing augments total societal revenue. If there is only a farmer, he must divide his labor between cultivation and making clothing and tools — producing less of both. If there is a farmer and an artificer, the farmer specializes in cultivation, producing provisions and raw materials; the artificer produces manufactured goods. The result: two quantities of value exist instead of one, and total revenue and consumption are double. If there are two farmers and no artificer, each dividing his time, the total product equals only what one farmer and one artificer would produce. The artificer’s labor, therefore, is “as positively productive as that of the farmer, and as positively augments the revenue of the society.”
Hamilton decomposes the artificer’s production into three parts: (1) the portion purchasing subsistence and materials from the farmer; (2) the portion supplying his own manufactured necessaries; and (3) the profit on stock employed — which “is, in every sense, as effective an addition to the income of the society as the rent of land.”
III. The Seven Circumstances by Which Manufactures Augment National Wealth
Rather than claim manufacturing is more productive than agriculture, Hamilton argues that the establishment of manufactures renders “the total mass of useful and productive labor, in a community, greater than it would otherwise be.” He enumerates seven circumstances:
1. Division of Labor. Hamilton enumerates three advantages: greater skill and dexterity from constant application to a single object; economy of time by avoiding transitions between operations; and extension of the use of machinery, since “a man occupied on a single object will have it more in his power and will be more naturally led to exert his imagination in devising methods to facilitate and abridge labor.” The mere separation of the cultivator from the artificer has the effect of augmenting the productive powers of labor.
2. Extension of Machinery. Machinery is “an artificial force brought in aid of the natural force of man; and, to all purposes of labor, is an increase of hands, an accession of strength, unencumbered, too, by the expense of maintaining the laborer.” Manufacturing pursuits are susceptible to the application of machinery in far greater degree than agriculture. When a nation procures its fabrics from abroad instead of making them at home, it “transfers to foreign nations the advantages accruing from the employment of machinery.” Hamilton cites the cotton mill invented in England within the last 20 years — where all spinning processes are performed by machines put in motion by water and attended chiefly by women and children — as a signal illustration.
3. Employment of Classes Otherwise Non-Productive. Manufacturing establishments provide “occasional and extra employment to industrious individuals and families” during the intermissions of ordinary pursuits. The husbandman experiences a new source of profit from the industry of his wife and daughters, “invited and stimulated by the demands of the neighboring manufactories.” Women and children are rendered more useful, and children more early useful. Of persons employed in the cotton manufactories of Great Britain, nearly four-sevenths are women and children, many of tender age.
4. Promotion of Immigration. Artisans will emigrate from Europe for better prices, cheaper provisions, exemption from taxes, greater personal independence, and “a perfect equality of religious privileges.” But they will not readily become farmers. Manufacturing draws skilled European workmen to America: “we shall, in a great measure, trade upon a foreign stock, reserving our own for the cultivation of our lands and the manning of our ships.”
5. Diversity of Talents and Dispositions. Minds of the strongest powers “fall below mediocrity and labor without effect if confined to uncongenial pursuits.” When all kinds of industry obtain in a community, each individual can find his proper element and “call into activity the whole vigor of his nature.” Hamilton adds that if there is truth to the observation of “a peculiar aptitude for mechanic improvements” in the American genius, it is a forcible reason for propagating manufactures.
6. A More Ample Field for Enterprise. The spirit of enterprise “must necessarily be contracted or expanded in proportion to the simplicity or variety of the occupations” in a society. It is less in a nation of mere cultivators than in one of cultivators and merchants, and less in a nation of cultivators and merchants than in one of cultivators, artificers, and merchants.
7. A Steady Domestic Market for Agricultural Surplus. This is “among the most important of the circumstances” and has “an immediate and direct relation to the prosperity of agriculture.” A domestic market is greatly preferable to a foreign one because it is far more reliable. Foreign demand is precarious — subject to artificial policy restrictions (European nations striving to supply themselves), seasonal fluctuations, and glut from coincident harvests. “Manufacturers, who constitute the most numerous class after the cultivators of the land, are for that reason the principal consumers of the surplus of their labor.” Hamilton emphasizes that the multiplication of manufactures “not only furnishes a market for those articles which have been accustomed to be produced in abundance in a country; but it likewise creates a demand for such as were either unknown, or produced in inconsiderable quantities. The bowels, as well as the surface of the earth, are ransacked for articles which were before neglected.”
IV. Response to Practical Objections
Scarcity of hands. Hamilton qualifies this objection significantly. Large districts are “pretty fully peopled” with flourishing towns. Moreover, the employment of women and children, the use of machinery (substituting “the agency of fire and water”), the engagement of persons ordinarily in other occupations during their leisure hours, and the attraction of foreign emigrants all “materially diminish everywhere the effect of a scarcity of hands.”
Dearness of labor. Hamilton provides a precise numerical example: suppose the labor cost difference between two countries for fabricating a given article is 10, and a machine performs half the necessary labor. The labor cost difference is reduced from 10 to 5. The “extra charges” on foreign manufactured goods — shipping, insurance, commissions, duties, fees — cannot be estimated at less than 15 to 30 per cent on the cost at the manufactory. This sum “may confidently be regarded as more than a counterpoise for the real difference in the price of labor.”
Want of capital. Hamilton calls this “the most indefinite of the objections.” He identifies three compensating resources: (1) banks, which “have a powerful tendency to extend the active capital of a country”; (2) foreign capital, which has already been experienced in external commerce and internal improvements; and (3) most originally and extensively, the funded debt.
Hamilton’s funded debt argument is a landmark of fiscal theory. Public funds answer the purpose of capital because of the ease and dispatch with which they can be turned into money. Against the objection that they destroy other capital to an equal amount, Hamilton constructs a numerical demonstration: if the annual revenue applied to service a 6% stock is in the ratio of 8 per 100 (6 interest, 2 principal), then the capital destroyed bears a proportion of only 8 to 100 compared to the capital created of 100. An augmentation of 92 exists in the first year. Though the excess diminishes annually, "there will constantly be more capital in capacity to be employed than capital taken from employment" until the principal is reduced to the level of the redeeming annuity (8). Hamilton further argues that the payment of interest involves “at most, a temporary transfer of some other capital… which he again restores to the circulation to resume the offices of a capital.” However, he carefully distinguishes between an absolute increase of real wealth and “an artificial increase of capital as an engine of business,” conceding that a funded debt has no pretensions in the first sense — but in the latter, its pretensions “are not easy to be controverted.” He warns against the conclusion that more debt is always better, noting “there may be a plethora in the political as in the natural body.”
V. Specific American Manufacturing Industries Already Established
Hamilton provides the most comprehensive inventory of American manufacturing ever compiled to that date, organized by material and trade:
1. Skins. Tanned and tawed leather, dressed skins, shoes, boots, slippers, harness and saddlery, portmanteaux and trunks, leather breeches, gloves, muffs and tippets, parchment, and glue.
2. Iron. Bar and sheet iron, steel, nail rods and nails, implements of husbandry, stoves, pots and other household utensils, steel and iron work for carriages and shipbuilding, anchors, scale beams and weights, tools of artificers, and arms of different kinds (though the last had diminished for want of demand).
3. Wood. Ships (built “nowhere in greater perfection”), cabinet wares and turnery, wool and cotton cards, machinery for manufactures and husbandry, mathematical instruments, coopers’ wares.
4. Flax and Hemp. Cables, sailcloth, cordage, twine, and pack thread.
5. Bricks and coarse tiles, and potters’ wares.
6. Ardent spirits and malt liquors.
7. Paper. Writing, printing, sheathing and wrapping paper, pasteboards, fullers or press papers, paper hangings.
8. Hats of fur, wool, and mixtures; women’s stuff and silk shoes.
9. Refined sugars.
10. Oils of animals and seeds, soap, spermaceti and tallow candles.
11. Copper and brass wires, particularly utensils for distillers, sugar refiners, and brewers; andirons and other household articles; philosophical apparatus.
12. Tin wares for most purposes of ordinary use.
13. Carriages of all kinds.
14. Snuff, chewing and smoking tobacco.
15. Starch and hair powder.
16. Lampblack and other painters’ colors.
17. Gunpowder.
Household manufacturing. Beyond regular trades, Hamilton describes a “vast scene of household manufacturing” which contributes more largely to supply than could be imagined. Great quantities of coarse cloths, coatings, serges, flannels, linsey-woolseys, hosiery, fustians, jeans, muslins, checked and striped cotton and linen goods, bedticks, coverlets, tow linens, and table linens are made in families — often for sale and even for exportation. Hamilton reports that in many districts two-thirds, three-fourths, and even four-fifths of all clothing is made by the inhabitants themselves.
VI. The Superiority of Manufacturing-and-Agricultural Nations in Trade
Hamilton argues there is “a moral certainty that the trade of a country which is both manufacturing and agricultural will be more lucrative and prosperous than that of a country which is merely agricultural.” He provides three reasons:
First, demand for agricultural products is irregular (affected by weather, seasons, and foreign harvests), while demand for manufactured goods is constant and regular. This uniformity on one side and unsteadiness on the other necessarily causes the exchange to turn to the disadvantage of purely agricultural states.
Second, a more diversified market attracts more foreign customers. “The greatest resort will ever be to those marts where commodities, while equally abundant, are most various.” The field of enterprise is enlarged for merchants in proportion to the variety as well as the abundance of commodities they find at home for export.
Third, diversification insulates against trade stagnations. A nation with few articles is “more quickly and sensibly affected” by stagnations than one with great variety. The latter “commonly finds itself indemnified by the high prices of some articles for the low prices of others.”
From these circumstances, Hamilton draws two inferences: (1) there is always a higher probability of a favorable balance of trade in manufacturing-agricultural countries; (2) such countries are likely to possess more pecuniary wealth. He cites the West India Islands, whose fertile soils “exchange to a loss with almost every other country,” as corroboration. Pre-Revolutionary America’s debt to Great Britain was progressive; post-Revolution, states with more manufactures “recovered fastest from the injuries of the late war and abound most in pecuniary resources.”
VII. Independence, Security, and the Burden of Distance
Hamilton elevates the argument to national security: “Every nation, with a view to those great objects, ought to endeavor to possess within itself all the essentials of national supply. These comprise the means of subsistence, habitation, clothing, and defense.” The extreme embarrassments of the Revolutionary War from an incapacity to supply themselves are “still matter of keen recollection.” The want of a navy renders external commerce a peculiarly precarious reliance.
Distance from Europe adds extra charges of 15 to 30 per cent on imports — a deadweight loss deducted from the value of American exports. These charges “principally fall upon us” and “are an additional cause of extraordinary deduction from the primitive value of our own products.” In time of war, these burdens would become catastrophic. Hamilton also notes that the fisheries of the United States suffer from the want of an adequate market, and that manufacturing would create demand for fish oils, bones, and skins.
VIII. The Proposed Means of Encouraging Manufactures
Hamilton enumerates eleven principal means, drawing on the practices of European nations:
1. Protective duties on rival foreign articles — amounting to a virtual bounty on domestic fabrics by enhancing charges on competitors. Hamilton notes this is “sanctioned by the laws of the United States in a variety of instances” and has “the additional recommendation of being a resource of revenue.”
2. Prohibitions or equivalent duties — fit only when a manufacture has progressed enough to insure due competition and adequate supply. Hamilton argues that considering “a monopoly of the domestic market to its own manufacturers as the reigning policy of manufacturing nations,” a similar policy is dictated “by the principles of distributive justice.”
3. Prohibitions of exportation of materials — to be adopted “with great circumspection, and only in very plain cases.”
4. Pecuniary bounties — “one of the most efficacious means” and “in some views the best.” Bounties have four advantages: they are more positive and direct than other modes; they avoid the temporary augmentation of price incident to duties; they do not tend to produce scarcity; and they are the only proper expedient for uniting the encouragement of agriculture with that of manufactures. Hamilton acknowledges “a degree of prejudice against bounties” but argues that “there is no purpose to which public money can be more beneficially applied than to the acquisition of a new and useful branch of industry.”
5. Premiums — distinguished from bounties in that they reward “some particular excellence or superiority” rather than the whole quantity produced. “Contrived so as to be both honorary and lucrative, they address themselves to different passions — touching the chords as well of emulation as of interest.”
6. Exemption of raw materials from duty — “It can hardly ever be advisable to add the obstructions of fiscal burdens to the difficulties which naturally embarrass a new manufacture.”
7. Drawbacks — refunds of duties on materials re-exported as finished goods, citing the examples of salt and molasses.
8. Encouragement of inventions and introduction of foreign improvements — “among the most useful and unexceptionable of the aids which can be given to manufacturers.” Hamilton recommends extending benefits to introducers as well as inventors.
9. Inspection systems — to prevent frauds, improve quality, and preserve the character of national manufactures. He notes the reputation of flour, lumber, and potash established by inspection.
10. Facilitating pecuniary remittances — a general circulation of bank paper and improvements in inland bills of exchange would promote commerce between states.
11. Internal improvements — roads and canals, which “put the remote parts of a country more nearly upon a level with those in the neighborhood of the town.” Hamilton cites the example of Great Britain’s improvements, noting that good roads and canals “encourage the cultivation of the remote, which must always be the most extensive circle of the country.”
IX. Constitutional Authority
Hamilton addresses potential constitutional objections to the manufacturing program. The National Legislature has express authority “to lay and collect taxes, duties, imposts, and excises, to pay the debts, and provide for the common defense and general welfare” — with only three qualifications (uniformity, apportionment of direct taxes, and no export duties). The phrase “general welfare,” he argues, “was doubtless intended to signify more than was expressed or imported in those which preceded.” It is “as comprehensive as any that could have been used.” The only admissible qualification is that the object must be “general and not local; its operation extending, in fact or by possibility, throughout the Union.”
On bounties specifically, Hamilton dismisses constitutional doubts as having “certainly no good foundation.” The power to raise money is “plenary and indefinite,” and “whatever concerns the general interests of learning, of agriculture, of manufactures, and of commerce is within the sphere of the national councils, as far as regards an application of money.”
X. Conclusion
Hamilton submits his report with the conviction that the encouragement of manufactures is essential to national independence and prosperity. He proposes establishing a Board for Promoting Arts, Agriculture, Manufactures, and Commerce — a commission of at least three members, funded by the surplus of additional duties, empowered to defray emigration expenses of skilled workmen, reward useful discoveries and inventions, and dispense premiums. He warns that “the progress of particular manufactures has been much retarded by the want of skillful workmen” and that “the capitals employed are not equal to the purposes of bringing from abroad workmen of a superior kind.” The board would administer rewards under “proper discretionary direction,” since it is “impracticable to apportion by general rules specific compensations for discoveries of unknown and disproportionate utility.”
The report closes with a call for Congress to act: “In what can it be so useful as in prompting and improving the efforts of industry? All which is humbly submitted.”
