Report on a National Bank
Hamilton’s great report on the establishment of a national bank, one of the four pillars of his financial program alongside the Reports on Public Credit, the Mint, and Manufactures.

Submitted to the House of Representatives, December 13, 1790
Alexander Hamilton, Secretary of the Treasury
Source
Hamilton, Alexander. The Report of the Secretary of the Treasury (Alexander Hamilton) on the Subject of a National Bank. New-York: S. Whiting & Co., No. 118, Pearl-street, 1811. J. Seymour, print.
Digital source: Ann’s Archive scan of the University of California Library copy (UCAL 31175011221879). OCR text extracted from 52 page images.
Text
raw/hamilton-national-bank.txt — 1,721 lines, ~86K characters. OCR text from the 1811 S. Whiting reprint. OCR quality is good; the text is fully readable. The scan includes the original 1811 title page and library markings.
Contents
Hamilton’s report on the establishment of a national bank opens with an extended theoretical justification of banking institutions before presenting the detailed plan. The structure is as follows:
Preliminary Observations: The Utility of Banks
Hamilton first establishes the principles and benefits of banks in general, arguing from the experience of the principal and most enlightened commercial nations, which have universally found admission and patronage for public banks. He identifies three principal advantages:
Firstly — Banks increase the active capital of a country. Hamilton explains the mechanism with precision: a bank can lend and circulate a greater sum than the amount of its coin capital through three converging circumstances. First, a bank lends not only its own stock but the money deposited with it, which depositors are unlikely to all withdraw simultaneously — experience proves that money “much oftener changes proprietors than place,” and what is drawn out is generally speedily replaced, making deposits an effective fund. Second, a bank lends its credit through bank notes, which circulate as money, “performing in every stage the office of money” until extinguished by a discount with someone who has a payment to make to the bank. Third, there is always a large quantity of gold and silver in the bank’s repositories beyond its own stock, placed there partly for safe-keeping and partly for accommodation. Through these mechanisms, “large sums are lent and paid, frequently through a variety of hands, without the intervention of a single piece of coin.”
The ability to circulate a greater sum than actual capital is acquired gradually and must be preceded by a firm establishment of confidence — confidence that may be “bestowed on the most rational grounds, since the excess in question will always be bottomed on good security of one kind or another.” Every well-conducted bank carefully requires such security before advancing money or credit.
The consequence for national wealth is profound: money that would otherwise lie idle while awaiting employment is instead deposited or invested in bank stock, where it “administers to the wants of others” while remaining accessible to its owner. This yields extra profit from what others pay for the use of it, and “keeps the money itself in a state of incessant activity.” In the “almost infinite vicissitudes and competitions of mercantile enterprise,” there is never danger of the money remaining idle in the vaults. This additional employment given to money, and the bank’s faculty to lend and circulate a greater sum than its stock in coin, constitute “to all the purposes of trade and industry, an absolute increase of capital.” Bank paper or credit effects purchases as effectually as an equal sum of gold and silver. Thus banks “become nurseries of national wealth” — a consequence “as satisfactorily verified by experience, as it is clearly deducible in theory.”
Secondly — Banks give greater facility to government in obtaining pecuniary aids, especially in sudden emergencies. The capitals of a great number of individuals are collected to a point and placed under one direction. The mass formed by this union is “magnified by the credit attached to it.” While this mass is always ready and can be put in motion at once in aid of the government, the bank’s own interest in preserving its relationship with the government constitutes “a sure pledge for its disposition to go as far in its compliances, as can in prudence be desired.” There is, Hamilton notes, “an intimate connection of interest between the government and the bank of a nation.”
Thirdly — Banks facilitate the payment of taxes. This advantage is produced in two ways. First, those who have access to the bank can borrow to meet tax obligations punctually — an accommodation “sensibly felt in the payment of the duties heretofore laid, by those who reside where establishments of this nature exist.” Second, banks increase the quantity of circulating medium and quicken circulation. Hamilton illustrates: when payments must be made between different places, if no private bills or bank notes with currency in both places exist, coin must be remitted — “attended with trouble, delay, expense, and risk.” But if bank notes are current in both places, transmission by post or other convenient conveyance answers the purpose, and these notes are frequently returned, obviating the transportation and re-transportation of metals. The metals themselves continue in activity, administering to ordinary circulation. Whatever enhances the quantity of circulating money “adds to the ease with which every industrious member of the community may acquire that portion of it, of which he stands in need.”
Reply to Objections Against Banks
Hamilton addresses six principal charges against banks, arguing that on close and candid survey they are either without foundation, proceed from other or partial causes, or are more than counterbalanced by opposite advantages:
1. That banks serve to increase usury. Hamilton acknowledges the kernel of truth: the punctuality in payments that banks necessarily exact has sometimes obliged those who have adventured beyond both capital and credit to resort to usurers for aid at any price. But experience and practice gradually bring a cure. A general habit of punctuality among traders is the natural consequence of the necessity of observing it with the bank — a circumstance that “more than compensates for any occasional ill.” Traders can calculate their expectations with greater certainty and are in proportionably less danger of disappointments that might compel borrowing at usury. The directors of a bank, though initially tempted to extend accommodation beyond strict prudence to build business, grow more circumspect as affairs become established and the evils of too great facility are experimentally demonstrated. They observe more narrowly the operations and pursuits of those with whom they deal; they “economize the credit they give to those of suspicious solidity; they refuse it to those whose career is more manifestly hazardous.” In the course of practice, “the interest will make it the policy of a bank, to succour the wary and industrious; to discredit the rash and unthrifty; to discountenance both usurious lenders and usurious borrowers.” Most fundamentally, banks’ property of increasing the quantity and quickening the circulation of money tends to abridge usury: if usury prevails according to the proportion of demand for borrowing to the quantity of money at market, whatever renders supply more equal to demand must counteract the progress of usury.
2. That banks tend to prevent other kinds of lending. The objection holds that because bank stock yields profits exceeding the legal rate of interest, money-lenders prefer investing in it rather than lending at interest, with additional motives of prompt command of capital and frequent returns. Hamilton gives this charge only qualified admission, particularly in reference to the American situation. First, the great bulk of bank stock will consist of the funds of men in trade (who cannot spare capitals for long-term mortgages) and monied foreigners (who would not be subjected to the casualties and delays of lending in a distant country). Second, there will always be a considerable proportion of cautious money-lenders who prefer mortgages on real estate, which they consider more secure than bank stock. Moreover, the supposed effect is temporary: a bank’s capital is restricted within a defined limit; once subscriptions are completed, no additional capital can be invested. Stock may change hands, but the money the buyer takes from the common mass, the seller receives and restores to it. Future surpluses must take their natural course, and lending at interest goes on as if there were no bank — indeed, “it must flow in a more copious stream,” since the bank furnishes extraordinary supply for borrowers within its sphere, leaving larger supply for borrowers elsewhere.
3. That banks furnish temptations to over-trading. Hamilton concedes that by affording additional aid to mercantile enterprise, banks may induce merchants to adventure beyond the prudent point. But “the very statement of the thing shows that the subject of the charge is an occasional ill, incident to a general good.” Credit of every kind is chargeable with the same inconvenience; it even applies to gold and silver when abundant. “Would it be wise on this account to decry the precious metals; to root out credit; or to prescribe the means of that enterprise, which is the main spring of trade, and a principal source of national wealth, because it now and then runs into excesses?” The evil is to be compared with the good, and the new energies derived to commercial enterprise from banks are “a source of general profit and advantage, which greatly outweigh the partial ills.”
4 & 5. That banks aid ignorant adventurers and give fraudulent traders fictitious credit. These charges, considered together, have some foundation but far less than pretended. The practice of giving fictitious credit is “one of those evils which experience, guided by interest, speedily corrects.” The bank itself is in jeopardy of suffering, giving it the strongest inducement to be on guard. The directors, selected from the class of traders, are expected to possess accurate knowledge of the characters and situations of those with whom they deal, supplemented by the course of dealing itself — “in most cases a good index of the state in which those persons are.” The artifices and shifts employed by those in desperate circumstances are “so many prognostics, not difficult to be interpreted.” Hence banks are often the first to discover unsoundness and, by withholding credit, announce to the public that such characters are not entitled to it. And even when banks are betrayed into error, “they more frequently enable honest and industrious men, of small or perhaps of no capital, to undertake and prosecute business, with advantage to themselves and to the community” and assist merchants of capital and credit who meet unforeseen shocks to make head against misfortunes — “circumstances which form no inconsiderable encomium on the utility of banks.”
6. That banks tend to banish gold and silver from the country. This is the most serious charge and the most extensively examined. The force of the objection rests on banks being an engine of paper credit that furnishes a substitute for the metals. Hamilton notes it is an objection that lies not peculiarly against banks but against every species of paper credit. The common answer — that it is immaterial what serves as money, and that national wealth is measured by productions of labour and industry rather than precious metals — is not destitute of solidity but not entirely satisfactory. Hamilton offers a more conclusive answer: a nation without mines must derive precious metals from others in exchange for the products of its labour and industry. The quantity it possesses is regulated by the favourable or unfavourable balance of trade. Well-constituted banks favour the increase of precious metals because they augment the active capital of a country — generating employment, animating and expanding labour and industry, creating more products for exportation, and thus conducing to a favourable balance of trade.
Hamilton addresses counter-objections: that bank paper, by substituting for specie, counteracts the necessity for metals that might restrain exportation in case of a wrong balance, and that it retards economizing reforms. He acknowledges some truth but argues these are exceptions rather than overthrows. The support of industry is “probably in every case, of more consequence towards correcting a wrong balance of trade, than any practicable retrenchments in the expenses of families or individuals.” Moreover, bank circulation is always in a compound ratio to the fund upon which it depends and the demand for it; as that fund is itself affected by the exportation of metals, there is no danger of overstocking as with government paper emissions. Comparisons between different countries to illustrate the objection are fallible, depending on “an infinite variety of facts and combinations” — the mass and value of productions, the nature of foreign establishments, the kind of wars, trade privileges — rendering the investigation “too complex to justify any reliance on the vague and general surmises” hazarded on the point.
Temporary exportation for particular purposes is indeed facilitated by banks, but “their utility is in nothing more conspicuous, than in these very cases.” Banks enable the government to pay foreign debts and meet external exigencies; they enable the merchant to support credit when special circumstances prevent remittances; they enable enterprises that ultimately tend to augment the species of wealth in question. Gold and silver may often be employed in procuring commodities abroad which, in a circuitous commerce, “replace the original fund, with considerable addition.”
Historical Context: The Post-War Situation
Hamilton argues that many observed evils attributed to banks were actually caused by the general devastation of personal property occasioned by the late war. The war naturally produced on one hand a great demand for money, and on the other a great deficiency of it to answer the demand. Injudicious laws that grew out of the public distresses, impairing confidence and causing part of the inadequate sum to be locked up, aggravated the evil. The dissipated habits contracted by many during the war, plunging them into expenses beyond their incomes; the number of adventurers without capital who rushed into trade; the employment of considerable sums in speculations upon the public debt, which from its unsettled state was incapable of becoming a substitute — all these circumstances concurring necessarily led to usurious borrowing. Those who erroneously blamed banks might have avoided their mistake “by turning their eyes towards places where there were none; and where, nevertheless, the same evils would have been perceived to exist, even in a greater degree.”
These evils have either ceased or been greatly mitigated. Hamilton looks for their more complete extinction from “that additional security to property, which the Constitution of the United States happily gives” — a circumstance of “prodigious moment in the scale both of public and private prosperity”; from the attraction of foreign capital under that security; from the consistency and stability the public debt is fast acquiring; and from the more copious circulation to be created by a well-constituted national bank.
The establishment of banks is recommended by reasons of a peculiar nature. Previously to the Revolution, circulation was carried on largely by paper emitted by local governments — in Pennsylvania alone the quantity was near a million and a half of dollars. This auxiliary is now at an end, and there has been a deficiency of circulating medium. Evidence includes the vast tracts of waste land and the little advanced state of manufactures. Progressive settlement draws off circulating money, diverts labour from furnishing materials for foreign trade, and consumes rather than produces surplus for exportation. Manifestations include greater prevalence of direct barter in interior districts and difficulty in advantageous alienation of improved real estate.
Hamilton notes the constitutional prohibition on state paper emissions and warns against federal paper money: though emissions under general authority “might have some advantages not applicable, and be free from some disadvantages” of state emissions, they are “of a nature so liable to abuse — and it may even be affirmed, so certain of being abused — that the wisdom of the government will be shown in never trusting itself with the use of so seducing and dangerous an expedient.” In times of tranquillity it might have no ill consequence, “but in great and trying emergencies, there is almost a moral certainty of its becoming mischievous.” The stamping of paper is so much easier than laying taxes that a government would rarely fail to indulge too far. A crucial difference between government paper and bank paper is that in the first case there is no standard for the quantity that will satisfy or surcharge circulation; in the latter, “that standard results from the demand.” If more is issued than necessary, it returns upon the bank — a limitation in the nature of things, whereas government discretion is the only measure.
Deficiencies of the Existing Bank of North America
Hamilton surveys the three existing banks — North America (Philadelphia), New York, and Massachusetts — and finds only the first has had a direct relation to the federal government. The Bank of North America originated in a resolution of Congress of May 26, 1781, founded on a proposition of the Superintendent of Finance, carried into execution by an ordinance of December 31, 1781. Its aid during the remaining period of the war “was of essential consequence.” However, the directors have since accepted a new charter from Pennsylvania materially variant from the original one, “which so narrows the foundation of the institution, as to render it an incompetent basis for the extensive purposes of a national bank.”
Hamilton identifies several critical deficiencies:


Capital too small. The Pennsylvania charter limits capital to 2 million, whereas the original congressional ordinance contemplated 10 million. So small a capital “promises neither the requisite aid to government, nor the requisite security to the community.” It may answer local accommodation but is “an inadequate foundation for a circulation co-extensive with the United States; embracing the whole of their revenues, and affecting every individual into whose hands the paper may come.”


Discretionary capital increases. The charter leaves capital increases to stockholder discretion. It is “naturally to be expected that the allurements of an advanced price of stock and of large dividends may disincline those who are interested to an extension of capital.” Public utility is thus made subordinate to private profit. Hamilton insists: “Public utility is more truly the object of public banks, than private profit. And it is the business of government, to constitute them on such principles, that while the latter will result, in a sufficient degree, to afford competent motives to engage in them, the former be not made subservient to it.”


No principle of rotation in directors. Hamilton argues that the reasons against rotation in political constitutions do not apply to banks. The administration of a bank “is regulated by a few simple fixed maxims, the application of which is not difficult to any man of judgment.” Rotation lessens “the danger of combinations among the directors, to make the institution subservient to party views” and renders “public confidence more firm, stable, and unqualified.” The necessary secrecy of directors’ transactions “gives unlimited scope to imagination to infer that something is, or may be, wrong,” making periodical changes a needed check. The head of the direction should be excepted, and periodical exclusion ought not to reach the whole board at once.


Improper voting rule. The original one-vote-per-share rule allows a few major stockholders to monopolize power; the new charter’s silence on the point might imply equal votes, which would be “a rule in a different extreme, not less erroneous.” A prudent mean is needed. The Bank of North America’s by-law attempts such a mean, but “a like majority with that which enacted this law, may at any moment repeal it.”


No safeguards against foreign influence. It is “scarcely reconcilable with a due caution, to permit that any but citizens should be eligible as directors of a national bank, or that non-resident foreigners should be able to influence the appointment of directors by the votes of their proxies.” However, existing foreign stockholders’ rights must be preserved.


Hamilton emphasizes: “Such a bank is not a mere matter of private property, but a political machine of the greatest importance to the state.”
Principles of Organization for a New National Bank
Branch banking. Hamilton acknowledges that the situation of the United States naturally inspires a wish for a plurality of branches. Besides more general accommodation, it would lessen the danger of a run upon the bank. However, various considerations discourage this idea: the complexity would inspire doubts deterring adventurers, and the practicability of safe administration “cannot be made so manifest in perspective, as to promise the removal of those doubts.” The most advisable course is to insert a provision that may lead to branches hereafter, if experience demonstrates utility. The argument against immediate branches is that each must be under a distinct, though subordinate, direction with considerable discretion; as the whole institution’s property would be liable for every part’s engagements, “the mismanagement of either branch might hazard serious disorder in the whole.”
Land as bank fund. Another wish — that the bank could lend to proprietors of land — yields to the difficulty of accomplishment. Land is “alone an unfit fund for a bank circulation.” If notes issued upon it were not payable in coin on demand, “this would amount to nothing more than a repetition of the paper emissions, which are now exploded by the general voice.” If notes are payable in coin, the land must first be converted into it by sale or mortgage — the difficulty of effecting this is “the very thing which begets the desire of finding another resource.” Neither is a mixed fund of coin and land free from impediments: these two species of property do not generally unite in the same hands. “Will the monied man consent to enter into a partnership with the landholder, by which the latter will share in the profits which will be made by the money of the former? The money, it is evident, will be the agent or efficient cause of the profits — the land can only be regarded as an additional security.”
Public vs. private direction. Hamilton firmly rejects the idea of the bank’s profits redounding to the immediate benefit of the state, however desirable it appears. “To attach full confidence to an institution of this nature, it appears to be an essential ingredient in its structure, that it shall be under a private, not a public direction; under the guidance of individual interest, not of public policy.” A government-directed bank would be “liable to being too much influenced by public necessity.” The suspicion of this “would most probably be a canker that would continually corode the vitals of the credit of the bank.” It would be “little less than a miracle, should the credit of the bank be at the disposal of the government, if in a long series of time, there was not experienced a calamitous abuse of it.” The keen, steady sense of their own interest in the directors — “pointing invariable to its true pole, the prosperity of the institution” — is the only security that can always be relied upon.
Hamilton distinguishes the European precedents: the Bank of Amsterdam is under municipal rather than governmental direction, and is a bank of deposit rather than of loan or circulation — “less liable to abuse, as well as less useful.” The state may be a holder of part of the stock and a sharer in profits, but “ought not to desire any participation in the direction.” However, the government owes itself and the community the right of ascertaining the state of the bank as often as necessary, excluding all pretension to control. This right “stands upon the clearest reasons,” for if bank paper is to be permitted in all the revenues and transactions of the country, “it becomes, in either view, a national concern of the first magnitude.”
The Plan
Hamilton presents the specific plan of 24 articles:


Capital stock: 10 million, divided into 25,000 shares of 400 each. Subscriptions open on the first Monday of April next. Bodies politic as well as individuals may subscribe.


Payment structure: Each share payable one-fourth in gold and silver coin, three-fourths in that part of the public debt bearing an accruing interest of 6% per annum. Payments made in four equal parts at six-month intervals. Failure in any subsequent payment forfeits dividends accrued prior to the delay.


Incorporation: Subscribers incorporated until final redemption of the part of stock consisting of public debt.


Property limit: Corporation capacity limited to $15 million including original capital. Lands and tenements permitted only for immediate accommodation of the institution, bona fide mortgages, or satisfaction of debts previously contracted.


Debt restriction: Total debts (except deposits) shall never exceed capital stock. Directors under whose administration excess occurs are personally liable. Dissenting directors may excuse themselves by giving notice to the President and stockholders.


Trading restrictions: The company may sell or demise lands and public debt, but “shall trade in nothing, except bills of exchange, gold and silver bullion, or in the sale of goods pledged for money lent.” Interest rate limited to 6% on loans or discounts.


Governmental loans: No loan for the use of the federal government or any state exceeding $50,000, or of any foreign power, unless authorized by a law of the United States — serving as “a barrier to executive encroachments and to combinations inauspicious to the safety, or contrary to the policy of the Union.”


Management: Twenty-five directors, one of whom shall be president. Annual election on the first Monday of January by plurality of stockholders’ suffrages. Directors choose president from among their number.


Voting rights: A graduated scale: for one to two shares, one vote; for every two shares above two up to ten, one vote; for every four shares above ten up to thirty; for every six shares above thirty up to sixty; for every eight shares above sixty up to one hundred; for every ten shares above one hundred. Maximum thirty votes for any person, co-partnership, or body politic. Shares must be held three months to confer suffrage. Only resident stockholders may vote by proxy.


Rotation: Not more than three-fourths of directors (exclusive of president) eligible for the next succeeding year. The president may always be re-elected. Only citizen stockholders eligible as directors.


Stockholder rights: Any sixty or more stockholders holding two hundred shares or upwards may call a general meeting with six weeks’ notice.


Dividends: Half-yearly dividends of such profits as directors deem advisable. Every three years directors must lay before stockholders a detailed statement of debts remaining unpaid after treble the original credit term and surplus profits after losses and dividends.


Receivability: Bills and notes payable on demand in coin receivable in all payments to the United States.


Government oversight: The Treasury head shall be furnished, not exceeding once a week, with statements of capital stock, debts due, monies deposited, notes in circulation, and cash in hand, with right to inspect general accounts — “provided that this shall not be construed to imply a right of inspecting the account of any private individual.”


Exclusive privilege: No similar institution shall be established during the bank’s continuance.


Offices (branches): Directors may establish offices for discount and deposit within the United States.


Government subscription: The President authorized to subscribe up to $2 million on behalf of the United States, to be paid out of borrowed monies, borrowing an equal sum from the bank, reimbursable in ten years.


Explanation of Key Provisions
Public debt as capital. The combination of public debt in the capital is the principal provision requiring explanation. The chief object is to enable creation of a capital sufficiently large for extensive circulation. To collect $10 million in gold and silver in this country “may, without hesitation, be pronounced impracticable” — hence the necessity of an auxiliary, which the public debt presents. This part of the fund will be always ready to come in aid of specie, commanding a ready sale and expeditiously convertible into coin if exigency requires. This quality of prompt convertibility distinguishes it from land. The quarter-yearly receipts of interest will be an actual addition to the specie fund during intervals between dividends. The debt will produce a direct annual revenue of 6% from the government, entering into the half-yearly dividends. Hamilton notes the important precedent: the Bank of England “in its first erection, rested wholly on that foundation” — subscribers to a loan of £1,200,000 sterling were incorporated as a bank, with the debt created by the loan and its interest as the sole fund.
Interest rate limitation. Hamilton notes that different rates prevail in different parts of the Union, and as bank operations may extend throughout, some rule is necessary. He questions whether the limitation ought to be five rather than six per cent, as the former “would yield an ample dividend; perhaps as much as the latter, by the extension which it would give to business.” The natural effect of low interest is to increase trade and industry. “The difference of one per cent. in the rate at which money may be had, is often capable of making an essential change for the better, in the situation of any country or place.” However, Hamilton defers to practical considerations: the persons whose funds must constitute the stock might be diffident of profits below the accustomed rate, and “the hazard of contrary reasoning among the mass of monied men is a powerful argument against the experiment.”
Government subscription. The main design of authorizing a $2 million government subscription is to enlarge the specie fund and enable earlier extension of operations. Though borrowing with one hand what is lent with the other, the disbursement will be progressive, and bank notes may be thrown into circulation instead of gold and silver. Annual reimbursement of part of the sum borrowed will finally operate as an actual investment of specie. Moreover, as far as the dividend on stock exceeds interest paid on the loan, “there is a positive profit.”
Conclusion and Submission
Hamilton concludes by recommending that if the Bank of North America shall come forward with propositions for grafting onto that institution the characteristics necessary for a national bank, “there are, in his judgment, weighty inducements to giving every reasonable facility to the measure.” The pretensions of that institution from its original relation to the government and the services it has rendered “are such as to claim a disposition favourable to it, if those who are interested in it are willing, on their part, to place it on a footing satisfactory to the government.” Its co-operation would materially accelerate the accomplishment of the great object, and the collision that might otherwise arise “might, in a variety of ways, prove equally disagreeable and injurious.”
The report concludes: “All which is humbly submitted. ALEXANDER HAMILTON, Sec’ry of the Treasury.”

Report on Public Credit
Submitted to the House of Representatives, January 9, 1790
Alexander Hamilton, Secretary of the Treasury
Source
Hamilton, Alexander. Report of the Secretary of the Treasury on Public Credit, Under Date of January 9, 1790. 60th Congress, 1st Session, Senate Document No. 224. Washington: Government Printing Office, 1908. Reprint of the original 1790 report.
Digital source: Ohio State University library scan, available via the HathiTrust / Internet Archive.
Text
raw/hamilton-public-credit.txt — 1,677 lines, ~97K characters. OCR text from the 1908 Government Printing Office reprint. Clean, legible scan-to-text conversion.
Contents
Hamilton’s first and most consequential report as Secretary of the Treasury, laying out the financial foundation of the new federal government. The report is a single continuous document without chapter divisions, but proceeds through the following major subjects:
I. The Necessity of Public Credit
Hamilton opens by recounting the House resolution of September 21, 1789, which directed him to prepare “a proper plan for the support of the Public Credit.” He describes his anxieties about the task — “difficulty of the task, from a well-founded diffidence of his own qualifications” — and his conviction that adequate provision for public credit is “a matter of high importance to the honour and prosperity of the United States.”
He sets out three “plain and undeniable truths”: (1) that exigencies requiring borrowing will inevitably occur in national affairs; (2) that loans in times of public danger, especially foreign war, are an indispensable resource even for the wealthiest nations; and (3) that in a country “possessed of little active wealth, or in other words little monied capital,” the necessity for that resource is proportionately urgent. When a nation’s credit is questionable, it must pay “an extravagant premium, in one shape or another, upon all the loans it has occasion to make” — and the same disadvantage extends to everything bought on terms of future payment. From this constant borrowing and buying dear, the expenses of a nation over time are vastly augmented by an unsound state of public credit.
Hamilton argues that on the “due observance at the present critical juncture, materially depends, in his judgment, the individual and aggregate prosperity of the citizens of the United States: their relief from the embarrassments they now experience; their character as a people; the cause of good government.”
II. The Principle of Good Faith
The means of maintaining public credit is “by good faith, by a punctual performance of contracts. States, like individuals, who observe their engagements, are respected and trusted.” Every breach of the public engagements, whether from choice or necessity, is hurtful to public credit in different degrees. Where necessity truly exists, the evils can only be palliated “by a scrupulous attention on the part of the government, to carry the violation no further than the necessity absolutely requires.”
Hamilton warns that governments should examine necessity carefully before yielding to it — “there is great reason to believe, that they exist far less frequently than precedents indicate; and are oftenest either pretended through levity, or want of firmness, or supposed through want of knowledge.” He notes that creditors of a nation are “generally speaking, enlightened men” who “will understand their true interest too well to refuse their concurrence in such modifications of their claims, as any real necessity may demand.”
Beyond political expediency, he invokes “considerations of still greater authority”: the “immutable principles of moral obligation” and the “intimate connexion between public virtue and public happiness.” The debt of the United States has a special character — “It was the price of liberty. The faith of America has been repeatedly pledged for it, and with solemnities, that give peculiar force to the obligation.” He acknowledges regret that the debt has not been kept — the necessities of war, “conspiring with inexperience in the subjects of finance,” produced direct infractions, and the subsequent period was “a continued scene of negative violation, or non-compliance.” But he notes that the last seven years had exhibited earnest efforts to retrieve national credit, and the “embarrassments of a defective constitution” that defeated those efforts “have ceased.”
He points to evidence of restored confidence: from January to November 1789, public securities rose thirty-three and a third per cent, and from that period rose fifty per cent more. Intelligence from abroad announced proportionately favourable effects. Hamilton lists the ends to be secured: “To justify and preserve their confidence; to promote the increasing respectability of the American name; to answer the calls of justice; to restore landed property to its due value; to furnish new resources both to agriculture and commerce; to cement more closely the union of the states; to add to their security against foreign attack; to establish public order on the basis of an upright and liberal policy.”
III. The Nature and Extent of the Public Debt
Hamilton surveys the existing debt, distinguishing between foreign, domestic, and state debts.
Foreign debt: Owed to France (approximately 10,070,307 in principal, with 1,640,071 in arrears of interest), Spain (about 300,000), and Holland (2.5 million principal with 300,000 in arrears). Total foreign debt: approximately 11,710,378 — principal and interest combined. This debt bears interest at four and five per cent.
Domestic debt: Subdivided into liquidated and unliquidated portions. The liquidated part includes loan office certificates (27,383,917 in principal, bearing six per cent interest), army certificates (3.2 million including depreciation adjustments), continental certificates (5.6 million), and liquidated state debts shipped to Congress (3.9 million). Arrears of interest to the end of 1790 amount to 13,030,168. The unliquidated portion, consisting chiefly of continental bills of credit not yet settled, is estimated at approximately 2 million. Total domestic debt: approximately 42,414,085 including arrears. Total debt of the United States: 54,124,464.
State debts: Not equally well ascertained, but Hamilton presumes the total may be safely stated at 25 million in principal and interest. The interest rate on state debts is generally the same as the domestic debt of the union — six per cent. On the supposition that arrears of interest should be provided for on the same terms as principal, the total annual interest payable on the entire mass of public debt would be approximately 4,587,444 — 542,599 on foreign debt and 4,044,845 on domestic and state debt.
Hamilton observes that the present depreciated state of landed property is a serious calamity — cultivated land values have fallen since the Revolution from 25 to 50 per cent, with even steeper declines in the southern states. This decrease “ought, in a great measure, to be attributed to the scarcity of money.” A funded debt, he argues, would augment the monied capital of the country and have a proportional effect in raising land values, as demonstrated by the “most decisive experience in Great-Britain.”
IV. The Plan for Funding
The Discrimination Debate
Hamilton devotes extensive attention to the question “whether a discrimination ought not to be made between original holders of the public securities, and present possessors, by purchase.” Those advocating discrimination argue for paying full nominal value to original holders but only the purchase price plus interest to those who bought at depreciated prices. The argument is that “it would be unreasonable to pay twenty shillings in the pound, to one who had not given more for it than three or four,” and that it would “aggravate the misfortune of the first owner, who, probably through necessity, parted with his property at so great a loss, by obliging him to contribute to the profit of the person who had speculated on his distresses.”
Hamilton rejects this doctrine as “equally unjust and impolitic; as highly injurious, even to the original holders of public securities; — as ruinous to public credit.” His reasoning proceeds on several grounds:
First, breach of contract. The nature of the contract from its origin is that the public will pay the sum expressed in the security “to the first holder, or his assignee.” The intent in making securities assignable is that the proprietor may sell for what it is worth in the market and the buyer may be safe in the purchase. “Every buyer, therefore, stands exactly in the place of the seller — has the same right with him to the identical sum expressed in the security.”
Second, the purchaser is a fair purchaser. “Whatever necessity the seller may have been under, was occasioned by the government, in not making a proper provision for its debts. The buyer had no agency in it, and therefore ought not to suffer.” The buyer paid what the commodity was worth in the market, took the risk of reimbursement — “a hazard which was far from inconsiderable, and which, perhaps, turned on little less than a revolution in government” — and gave a fair equivalent.
Third, original holders’ claims are against the government alone. Those who sold from necessity “have not only nothing to object to the persons who relieved their necessities by giving them the current price of their property, but they are even under an implied condition to contribute to the reimbursement of those persons.”
Fourth, practical impossibility. Not all original holders sold from necessity — some sold from “want of confidence” or for “allurements of some profitable speculation.” How can these classes be discriminated? “How shall it be known, whether, if the purchaser had employed his money in some other way, he would not be in a better situation?” Questions “multiply themselves without end, and demonstrate the injustice of a discrimination, even on the most subtile calculations of equity.”
Fifth, constitutional prohibition. Article VI of the Constitution provides that “all debts contracted, and engagements entered into, before the adoption of that Constitution, shall be as valid against the United States under it, as under the confederation” — which Hamilton interprets as a “constitutional ratification of the contracts respecting the debt, in the state in which they existed under the confederation.” Under that standard, “the rights of assignees and original holders must be considered as equal.”
Hamilton cites the circular address of Congress of April 26, 1783, which declared that “To discriminate the merits of these several descriptions of creditors, would be a task equally unnecessary and invidious. If the voice of humanity plead more loudly in favour of some than of others, the voice of policy, no less than of justice, pleads in favour of all. A WISE NATION will never permit those who relieve the wants of their country, or who rely most on its faith, its firmness, and its resources, when either of them is distrusted, to suffer by the event.”
Arrears of Interest
Hamilton argues that arrears of interest “have pretensions at least equal to the principal.” The liquidated debt originated from two sources: loans (which were payable at fixed periods that have long since elapsed, with creditors preferring to continue their money at interest rather than receive it in depreciated currency) and services performed / articles supplied (which ought to have been paid at the time but were converted by government acts into capital bearing six per cent interest). Regarding arrears, “these are now due, and those to whom they are due, have a right to claim immediate payment.” The equivalent for their detention “ought to be a real and fair one. And what other fair equivalent can be imagined for the detention of money, but a reasonable interest?”
The Six Loan Proposals
Hamilton proposes a loan to the full amount of the debt (both union and state) upon the following terms, allowing creditors to choose:
First plan: For every $100 subscribed, the subscriber receives two-thirds funded at six per cent interest, redeemable at the pleasure of the government by payment of principal, and the other third in lands in the Western Territory at twenty cents per acre. Hamilton defends the land valuation — the general price of western lands had been a dollar per acre in public securities, but those securities were then worth less than three shillings in the pound. Twenty cents per acre is an equitable proportion between the value at the time and likelihood of increase. The public retains the advantage of any fall in market interest rates.
Second plan: The whole sum funded at four per cent, irredeemable by any payment exceeding five dollars per annum on account of both principal and interest, with 15.80 in land as compensation for the reduction of interest. This plan is grounded on the supposition that interest will fall to five per cent in five years and to four per cent in twenty years. The present value of the compensation is calculated at 15.792 — a fraction less than the sum proposed. Should interest fall faster than anticipated, the creditor stands to gain.
Third plan: 66.67 funded immediately at six per cent, irredeemable by any payment exceeding 4.67 per annum, with $26.88 funded at the same rate at the end of ten years. This plan proceeds on the same supposition of a successive fall in the rate of interest. Hamilton is sincere in affirming that this plan “will be likely to prove, to the full, as beneficial to the creditors, as a provision for his debt upon its present terms.”
Fourth and fifth plans: Life annuities at four per cent, with payment deferred — on a single life contingency of living to a given age not less than ten years distant, or on the survivorship of the youngest of two persons. A hundred dollars advanced on the life of a person of eleven years would produce an annuity of 10 commencing at twenty-one, 18 at thirty-one, 37 at forty-one, or 78 at fifty-one. These deferred annuities afford “a comfortable provision for the evening of life, or for wives who survive their husbands.”
Sixth plan: Five per cent interest on subscriptions payable half in specie and half in debt, irredeemable by any payment exceeding six dollars per annum. This plan is “highly advantageous to the creditors, who may be able to make that payment; while the specie itself could be applied in purchases of the debt, upon terms, which would fully indemnify the public for the increased interest.” Foreign holders of domestic debt may particularly embrace this arrangement.
The Tontine Proposal
As an auxiliary experiment, Hamilton proposes a tontine consisting of six classes by age: 20-and-under (8.40 annuity per share), 21–30 (8.65), 31–40 (9.00), 41–50 (9.65), 51–60 (10.70), and above 60 (12.80). Each share is $200, with an indefinite number of shares per class. The annuities of those who die are equally divided among survivors until four-fifths are dead, at which point the principle of survivorship ceases and each annuitant enjoys their dividend as a several annuity during life.
Guiding Principle
Hamilton emphasizes that offering various propositions is vital: “Different tempers will be governed by different views of the subject.” He insists that creditors’ consent must be voluntary in fact as well as in name — “every proposal of a change ought to be in the shape of an appeal to their reason and to their interest; not to their necessities.” Any surplus revenue after satisfying interest on new loans and current service should be divided among non-subscribing creditors, though limited to four per cent. Quarter-yearly interest payments are proposed to facilitate circulation and give creditors effectively a higher rate — six per cent paid quarterly is truly worth 6.135 per 100.
V. Assumption of State Debts
Hamilton presents a forceful argument for federal assumption of state debts. His reasoning proceeds on multiple grounds:
Unity of purpose: State debts were incurred for the same object — the Revolution. “The defence of each part, is that of the whole; and unless all the expenditures are brought into a common mass, the tendency must be, to add to the calamities suffered by being the most exposed to the ravages of war, an increase of burthens.”
Economy and efficiency: Whether provision is made wholly by the United States or partly by the states, no greater total revenue is required. But a single general plan “issuing from one authority” avoids the competition for resources inevitable with separate plans. Separate provisions would produce “interfering regulations, and thence collision and confusion.” The most productive objects of revenue are not numerous — either one side engrosses them or both resort to the same objects in different modes, causing over-accumulation.
Constitutional constraints: The Constitution requires that “all duties, imposts, and excises, shall be uniform throughout the United States.” If a single state has already imposed a duty on an article, the general government would be constrained either to refrain from further imposition or confine itself to the difference. Thus “the preoccupancy of an article by a single state, would tend to arrest or abridge the impositions of the union on that article.”
Unity of creditor interest: If all public creditors receive their dues from one source “distributed with an equal hand,” their interest will be the same and they will unite in support of fiscal arrangements. Distinct provisions would create “distinct interests, drawing different ways” and produce “mutual jealousy and opposition.”
State creditors’ vulnerability: State creditors would likely fare worse than union creditors without assumption — a principal branch of revenue is exclusively vested in the union, and a state is always checked in imposing taxes on consumption goods from the “want of power to extend the same regulation to the other states.” Their dissatisfaction would “operate injuriously, both for the creditors and the credit of the United States.” Hence it is even in the interest of union creditors that state debts be assumed.
Objection and response: The principal objection is that assumption would increase the difficulty of an equitable settlement between states and the United States. Hamilton thinks such discussion premature. He proposes, as a framework, that each state be charged with advances from the US treasury (with six per cent interest) and the amount of its assumed securities, and credited for monies paid and articles furnished to the United States during the war. The whole to be liquidated to specie value with six per cent interest. Commissioners with equitable discretion would superintend the arrangement. He expresses little doubt that balances would appear in favour of all states against the United States.
VI. Means of Providing for the Debt
Hamilton estimates the total annual sum needed at 2,239,163 for interest (on the foreign debt at existing rates and the domestic debt at four per cent on the new capital formed), plus 600,000 for current service — total $2,839,163. He proposes to raise this through:
Import duties on wines (Madeira, Sherry, and other wines at rates from 20 to 35 cents per gallon), distilled spirits (graded by proof, from 20 to 30 cents per gallon), teas (Hyson at 40 cents/lb, other green at 24 cents, Souchong at 20 cents, Bohea at 12 cents), and coffee (5 cents/lb).
Excise taxes on domestic distilled spirits — on spirits distilled from foreign materials (molasses, sugar) at 11 to 20 cents per gallon by proof; on spirits from domestic materials in cities, towns, or villages at 9 to 17 cents per gallon; and on stills used in rural areas for domestic materials at 60 cents per gallon of still capacity per year.
Hamilton argues for carrying these duties “as high as will be consistent with the practicability of a safe collection,” noting that these articles are “in reality, luxuries — the greatest part of them foreign luxuries; some of them, in the excess in which they are used, pernicious luxuries.” The consumption of ardent spirits “is carried to an extreme, which is truly to be regretted, as well in regard to the health and the morals, as to the economy of the community.” Should higher duties decrease consumption, “the effect would be, in every respect desirable.”
Collection mechanism: Hamilton proposes an interior inspection system — pursuing each article from importation “into the hands of the dealers in it” — as the only way to reconcile high duties with secure collection. Under the existing system, “the evasion of the duties depends, as it were, on a single risk” — landing goods in defiance of customs officers — and “where the inducement is equivalent to the risk, there will be found too many who are willing to run it.” An interior scrutiny so greatly enhances the risk of detection that “few, in comparison, will venture to incur it. Indeed every dealer, who is not himself the fraudulent importer, then becomes, in some sort, a centinel upon him.”
He includes strong protections against official misconduct — officers are made criminally punishable and answerable in damages, and even where seizures are made with probable cause, if the article is acquitted, compensation for injury and detention is made from the public treasury.
The estimated net product of the proposed duties is about $1,703,400, which, together with existing duties on imports and tonnage, should complete the sum required. Hamilton acknowledges the uncertainty of data in “so unexplored a field” and recommends an auxiliary resource for the first year.
VII. A Sinking Fund
The report concludes with a plan for a sinking fund — a designated fund to purchase and retire public debt securities in the open market. Hamilton proposes that the net product of the post-office (which the postmaster-general estimates at not less than $100,000 annually, and which must be a growing fund from its nature) be vested in commissioners — comprising the Vice-President (or President of the Senate), the Speaker of the House, the Chief Justice, the Secretary of the Treasury, and the Attorney-General — to be applied to discharging the public debt, either by market purchases or principal payments, until the whole debt is discharged.
Hamilton explicitly addresses the maxim that “public debts are public benefits”: “Persuaded as the Secretary is, that the proper funding of the present debt will render it a national blessing; yet he is so far from acceding to the position, in the latitude in which it is sometimes laid down … a position inviting to prodigality, and liable to dangerous abuse, that he ardently wishes to see it incorporated, as a fundamental maxim, in the system of public credit of the United States, that the creation of debt should always be accompanied with the means of extinguishment. This he regards as the true secret for rendering public credit immortal.”
He further proposes that the commissioners be authorized (with the President’s approval) to borrow up to 12 million, to be applied to: (1) paying interest and instalments of the foreign debt (3,491,923); (2) covering any deficiency in funds for domestic debt interest; (3) refinancing the five per cent portion of the foreign debt at a lower rate; and (4) purchasing public debt in the market while it remains below true value. This last measure would become “altogether unexceptionable” after funding is in place — it would raise stock value in favour of creditors, and the difference between true value and purchase price would be “clear gain to the public.” Hamilton argues that if the government does not undertake this operation, foreigners will reap the profit: “By the government’s entering into competition with them, it will not only reap a part of the profit itself, but will contract the extent, and lessen the extra profit of foreign purchases.”
He concludes by urging no further delay — delay would “sink the price of stock” and tempt foreign speculation, and “millions would probably be lost to the United States.” The report is submitted with the hope “that an effectual plan for that purpose may, during the present session, be the result of the united wisdom of the legislature.”
Structure
The report follows a formal structure:

Opening — the House resolution and Hamilton’s commission
General principles of public credit
Detailed examination of the existing debt
The funding plan with supporting arguments
The assumption proposal
Revenue measures to service the debt
The sinking fund mechanism
Hamilton’s concluding submission

Overview
Volume I opens Hildreth’s continuous narrative of British America with discovery, Spanish and French rivals, and the planting of the English colonies through the late Stuart age. The Advertisement rejects “centennial sermons and Fourth-of-July orations” and promises founders “unbedaubed with patriotic rouge,” drawn from laws, state papers, documents, and manuscript collections. The revised three volumes, Hildreth states, give “a pretty correct outline” of British America nearly three centuries down to the organization of the United States under the Federal Constitution.
Chapters I–XV cover voyages and territorial claims; the aspect and aboriginal inhabitants of North America; early Spanish, French, and Dutch lodgments; Virginia; New Netherland; Plymouth and Laconia; Massachusetts Bay, New Hampshire, Ligonia, and Pemaquid; Maryland and Virginia; the growth of Connecticut, Providence, Rhode Island, New Haven, and Maine; New England under the Long Parliament; Virginia and Maryland in the English civil wars and Commonwealth; New England under the Commonwealth; New Sweden, New Netherland, and the English conquest; New England under Charles II; and Virginia and Maryland under Charles II and James II. Body narrative begins near PAGE 33 after title, advertisement, and contents.
Full Chapter-by-Chapter Breakdown
Chapter I — Voyages of Discovery. Territorial Claims
Columbus sails while the Cape route to India is still unknown; Marco Polo’s East fires his design (1492). The chapter surveys Spanish, Portuguese, English, French, and later Dutch claims from first Atlantic crossings through Cabot, Verrazzano, Cartier, Raleigh’s patents, and competing papal and royal titles that frame later colonial charters.
Chapter II — Aspect and Aboriginal Inhabitants of North America
Within half a century of discovery the Spaniards occupy large tropical tracts; island colonies suffer native depopulation. Hildreth turns to the physical face of the temperate continent and to languages, war, hunting, fishing, and social customs of the aboriginal nations of the regions later colonized by the English—material he treats as background to settlement rather than romance.
Chapter III — Carolina. Colony of Saint Augustine. New Mexico. Virginia. Acadie. New France. New Netherland
Religious revolution divides Western Europe into Protestant and Catholic parties with “very important influences on the colonization of North America.” First lodgments: Spanish St. Augustine and New Mexico; French Acadie and New France; Dutch on the Hudson; abortive or early English attempts on the Carolina and Virginia coasts before the successful Jamestown enterprise.
Chapter IV — Settlement of Virginia
London Company charter names Gates, Somers, Hakluyt, and Wingfield (1606); Sir Thomas Smith and other merchants join. Voyage, arrival, Jamestown, Starving Time, Dale and Argall, tobacco, the House of Burgesses, and the shift from company rule toward royal province—the first durable English plantation on the Chesapeake.
Chapter V — Settlement of New Netherland
Two years after the first English colony in Virginia, and in the year of Hudson’s river discovery (1609), the Dutch obtain a Spanish truce amounting to independence. Dutch East India Company origins, West India Company, Fort Orange and Manhattan, trade with the Iroquois, and early friction with English neighbors.
Chapter VI — New England. Colony of New Plymouth. Laconia
Virginia’s first charter contemplated a second, northern colony (Hanham, Raleigh Gilbert, Parker, Popham, 1606). Failed Popham / Sagadahoc venture; Separatist flight to Holland; Mayflower compact and Plymouth; fishing and trading posts; Gorges and the Council for New England; Laconia and northern grants.
Chapter VII — Colony of Massachusetts Bay. New Hampshire. Ligonia. Pemaquid
Dorchester and other Puritan (non-separatist) projects seed Massachusetts Bay. Charter transfer, Winthrop fleet, freemen and General Court, New Hampshire settlements, Ligonia and Pemaquid on the eastern coast, and the uneasy border with French claims in Nova Scotia / Acadie.
Chapter VIII — Settlement of Maryland. Progress of Virginia
English Catholics face severer penalties than Puritan nonconformists. Calvert’s Avalon and Maryland charter; Ark and Dove; religious toleration experiments; boundary and trade friction with Virginia; Virginia’s tobacco economy and political consolidation in the same decades.
Chapter IX — Progress of Massachusetts. Connecticut. Providence. Rhode Island. New Haven. New Somerset. Maine
After freemen reclaim legislative rights (1634), deputies sit with magistrates. Connecticut River towns, Hooker’s migration, Pequot War, Williams at Providence, Portsmouth and Newport, Davenport’s New Haven, and Maine / New Somerset under Gorges and Massachusetts claims—proliferation of New England polities.
Chapter X — New England during the Long Parliament
Emigrant coin drains for imports; while migration continues, new arrivals restock money and demand. Currency, wampum, fishery, shipbuilding, manufactures; relations with the English Long Parliament; Antinomian aftermath; confederation impulses among the Puritan colonies amid civil war at home.
Chapter XI — Virginia and Maryland during the English Civil Wars and the Commonwealth
Long Parliament news rejoices Virginia as well as Massachusetts (1641). Burgesses seek liberties under the “happy Parliament”; Maryland’s proprietary crises; Claiborne and Ingle; submission and restoration of local authority under the Commonwealth—southern colonies navigating English revolution without New England’s theocratic frame.
Chapter XII — New England during the Commonwealth
Massachusetts freemen press for a complete code and fixed penalties; magistrates defend judicial discretion. Revised codes; persecution of Quakers; relations among the United Colonies; Rhode Island’s divergent charter path; and the posture of Puritan New England toward Cromwell’s England.
Chapter XIII — New Sweden. Progress of New Netherland. Its Conquest by the English
Usselinx, dissatisfied with the Dutch West India Company, finds a patron in Gustavus Adolphus; New Sweden on the Delaware. Stuyvesant’s rule; English pressure from Connecticut and Long Island; Nicolls and the 1664 conquest that renames New Netherland as New York under the Duke of York.
Chapter XIV — New England under Charles II
Puritan colonists watch the Restoration with anxiety (1660). The same ship that brings news of Charles II brings regicides Whalley and Goffe. Royal commissioners; Connecticut and Rhode Island charters; Massachusetts resistance and partial submission; King Philip’s War and its devastation; and the approach of charter crisis.
Chapter XV — Virginia and Maryland under Charles II and James II
Under the Commonwealth Virginia had enjoyed a popular government—taxpayers voting for burgesses, Assembly electing officers. Restoration reverses that course: royal governors, Navigation Acts enforcement, Bacon’s Rebellion, Culpeper and Howard, and Maryland’s proprietary and religious struggles under the later Stuarts, closing the volume on the eve of the Glorious Revolution (continued in Vol. II).

sources/hildreth-history-united-states-v.title: [source] The History of the United States of America, Vol. II (Hildreth)
sources/hildreth-history-united-states-v.content:
The History of the United States of America — Vol. II (Hildreth)
Author: Richard Hildreth (1807–1865)
Working imprint: The History of the United States of America. Revised Edition. In Six Volumes. Vol. II. The Bradley Company, Publishers, New York. (Continuous narrative pair to Harper three-volume Vol. I colonial and Vol. III revolutionary; six-volume binding labels this middle colonial book Vol. II.)
Series placement: Continuous Chapters XVI–XXIX of the 1497–1789 half. Follows Vol. I (Ch. I–XV, colonial to 1688); precedes Vol. III (Ch. XXX–XLVIII, Revolutionary 1773–1789).
Working text: Page-OCR ZIP hash 8a6678168ee96c71afa6eaf513074c90
Raw extract: wiki/raw/hildreth-history-united-states-vol2.txt (page-sorted OCR)
Extract stats: 604 leaf pages · 23,636 lines · ~181,045 words · 1,082,896 bytes
Overview
Volume II is the late colonial and imperial-crisis volume of Hildreth most tightly aligned with this wiki’s chronological frame. It carries the story from the settlement of Carolina and the middle colonies under the later Stuarts through the Glorious Revolution in America, French expansion on the lakes and Mississippi, Louisiana, Georgia, four intercolonial wars culminating in English mastery east of the Mississippi, and the first parliamentary taxation schemes—Grenville’s Stamp Act and Townshend’s duties—down to the eve of the tea crisis treated in Vol. III.
Chapters XVI–XXIX form a continuous political and military narrative of British America from roughly the 1660s/1680s proprietary foundations through 1770. Body chapter heads begin near PAGE 35 after front matter and contents.
Full Chapter-by-Chapter Breakdown
Chapter XVI — Settlement of Carolina
Early in Charles I’s reign, about the time Massachusetts Bay was settled, “Carolana” is granted to Sir Robert Heath (1630) and assigned to Lord Maltravers; little comes of it. Later Carolina charter under Charles II; Barbadian planters; Fundamental Constitutions; Albemarle and Ashley River settlements; rice and Indian trade; split tendencies toward North and South Carolina.
Chapter XVII — Provinces of New York, New Jersey, and Pennsylvania
After the conquest of New Netherland (1664), commissioners settle the New York–Connecticut boundary. Duke of York’s province; partition of New Jersey among Berkeley and Carteret and later proprietors; Penn’s charter and Holy Experiment; Philadelphia founded; frames of government and early Quaker politics in Pennsylvania and the Jerseys.
Chapter XVIII — Royal Province of New England under James II. Revolution in Maryland and Virginia. Delaware a Separate Province
Massachusetts, charter vacated, hears that Colonel Kirk is named royal governor (1684); Charles II’s death and James II’s Dominion of New England under Andros. Overthrow of Andros at the Glorious Revolution; upheavals in Maryland and Virginia; Delaware’s separation as a distinct proprietary province.
Chapter XIX — New France. The Region of the Great Lakes and the Mississippi
French settlements on Fundy and the St. Lawrence, cotemporaneous with the oldest English colonies. Mountain ridges long bar western exploration; Jesuit missions; fur trade; exploration of the Great Lakes and Mississippi; La Salle, Fort Frontenac, and the strategic design that later collides with English expansion.
Chapter XX — Accession of William III. First Intercolonial War. Massachusetts Charter. Salem Witchcraft
William of Orange’s accession restrains regal power that had threatened popular rights in America as in England (1689), yet is “far from being an unmixed benefit” because it strengthens the Protestant imperial war with France. King William’s War; new Massachusetts charter; Salem witchcraft prosecutions and their political setting.
Chapter XXI — Progress and Conclusion of the First Intercolonial War. Board of Trade and Plantations. Enforcement of Restrictions on Colonial Commerce
While New England and New York suffer war, superstition, and faction, Pennsylvania faces internal trouble under George Keith. Close of the first intercolonial war; creation and activity of the Board of Trade; tightening of Navigation Acts and commercial restrictions that structure later imperial conflict.
Chapter XXII — Settlement of Louisiana. Reign of Queen Anne. Second Intercolonial War. Piracy Suppressed
After Ryswick, France renews efforts to plant at the Mississippi mouth (1698), invited also by Saint-Domingue prosperity. Iberville and Bienville; Queen Anne’s War (second intercolonial war); frontier raids; Port Royal / Acadia; suppression of piracy in American waters.
Chapter XXIII — Reign of George I. Paper Money Schemes. Progress of Louisiana
To hasten Louisiana’s settlement—hardly three hundred inhabitants after twelve years—the province and trade monopoly go to Crozat (1712). Mississippi Company / paper schemes; colonial bills of credit in the English provinces; Burnet and other governors wrestling with assemblies over money and defense under George I.
Chapter XXIV — Designs and Progress of the French. First Twelve Years of George II. Settlement of Georgia
French progress is slow beside the British colonies, yet they still aim at the whole western valley from the lakes to the Gulf (1728). Iroquois no longer the barrier they were; Ohio and Mississippi posts; Oglethorpe and the Georgia trustees; buffer against Florida and experiments in land and slavery policy.
Chapter XXV — Great Britain Attacks the Spanish Colonial System. Third Intercolonial War. Great Revival
European governments make American colonies subservient to the parent state; Spain excludes foreigners with special rigor (from 1737 frame). War of Jenkins’ Ear / King George’s War; Cartagena and Louisbourg threads; domestic “Great Revival” under Whitefield and Wesley and its colonial social effects.
Chapter XXVI — Commencement of the Final Struggle between the French and English for the Country on the Great Lakes and the Mississippi. Fourth Intercolonial War
Thomas Walker and other Virginia surveyors push toward Tennessee and Ohio headwaters (1747). Competing land companies; Washington’s mission and Fort Necessity; Braddock; early disasters of the fourth intercolonial war (French and Indian War) for control of the interior.
Chapter XXVII — Progress and Conclusion of the Fourth Intercolonial War. Accession of George III. The English Masters of the Continent north of the Gulf of Mexico and east of the Mississippi. Local Affairs. Progress of the Colonies
William Pitt forces himself into a chief seat in the British ministry amid popular discontent (1757). Louisbourg, Ticonderoga, Quebec, Montreal; peace settlement that leaves England master east of the Mississippi; accession of George III; local colonial progress and wartime burdens that prefigure taxation disputes.
Chapter XXVIII — Grenville’s Scheme of Colonial Taxation. Passage and Repeal of the Stamp Act
The war that confirmed English possession of North America cost the colonists heavily—Hildreth notes thirty thousand colonial soldiers fallen and large expense (1763 frame). Grenville’s revenue programme; Sugar Act; Stamp Act debates in Parliament and America; congress of 1765; repeal and Declaratory Act.
Chapter XXIX — Townshend’s Scheme of Colonial Taxation. Repeal of the New Taxes except that on Tea. Local Affairs. Territorial Controversies. First Settlements in Tennessee. Kentucky Explored
Despite the claim of power to bind the colonies “in all cases whatsoever,” Stamp Act repeal produces a burst of loyalty (1766). Townshend duties; non-importation; partial repeal leaving the tea tax; Boston Massacre context; Regulator and territorial controversies; first Tennessee settlements and Kentucky exploration—closing the volume on the threshold of the tea crisis of Vol. III.
