In September 1774, a party of British soldiers removes gunpowder from the arsenal at Cambridge, triggering a wave of public agitation. Throughout the countryside, alarms spread; tens of thousands of militia muster and march. Civil government in Massachusetts is effectively obstructed as the royal courts cannot function. Belligerent symptoms multiply. Irving introduces two colorful characters: Israel Putnam, a blunt, courageous Connecticut farmer and veteran of the French and Indian War, famous for his exploits and stories; and General Charles Lee, a eccentric, brilliant former British officer who has cast his lot with the American cause. A general election in Massachusetts produces a new Provincial Congress; John Hancock is chosen as its president. The Congress adjourns from Salem to Concord for safety. It sends a remonstrance to Gage, who finds himself in impossible perplexities — forced to maintain British authority with insufficient troops in a hostile country. Generals Artemas Ward and Seth Pomeroy are appointed to lead the Massachusetts forces. Committees of Safety and of Supplies are formed to coordinate military preparations. Restlessness spreads throughout the land. In Virginia, “independent companies” of volunteer militia spring up, drilling and arming themselves. Mount Vernon takes on a military tone: Washington drills the Fairfax Independent Company, and his guests are increasingly military men — Major Horatio Gates (a former British officer of German birth who settled in Virginia), and the eccentric General Charles Lee, who travels with his pack of dogs and whose peculiarities provide endless anecdotes. Washington attends the Virginia Convention at Richmond in March 1775. Patrick Henry delivers his “Give me liberty or give me death” speech, which Irving recounts with dramatic power. Washington, rising to speak, states his military intentions: he is ready to take up arms in defense of American liberty.
Chapter 37 — Infatuation in British Councils — Colonel Grant, the Braggart — Coercive Measures — Expedition against the Military Magazine at Concord — Battle of Lexington — The Cry of Blood through the Land — Old Soldiers of the French War — John Stark — Israel Putnam — Rising of the Yeomanry — Measures of Lord Dunmore in Virginia — Indignation of the Virginians — Hugh Mercer and the Friends of Liberty — Arrival of the News of Lexington at Mount Vernon — Effect on Bryan Fairfax, Gates, and Washington
Irving describes the “infatuation” in British councils — the conviction that the Americans would not fight. Colonel Grant, one of Braddock’s veterans and a notorious braggart, voices this contempt publicly, boasting that he could march from one end of America to the other with five thousand regulars. The coercive measures continue. In April 1775, Gage dispatches an expedition to seize the military stores collected by the Massachusetts Provincial Congress at Concord. The result is the Battle of Lexington and Concord (April 19, 1775). Irving narrates the events: the night march, the confrontation on Lexington Green, the “shot heard round the world,” the bloody retreat of the British under incessant fire from the aroused Massachusetts countryside. The cry of blood spreads through the land. Old soldiers of the French War — John Stark of New Hampshire, Israel Putnam of Connecticut — seize their muskets and rally the yeomanry. In Virginia, Lord Dunmore, emulating Gage, removes gunpowder from the Williamsburg magazine, triggering an explosion of indignation. Hugh Mercer and the “Friends of Liberty” arm themselves. The news of Lexington reaches Mount Vernon late in April. It has a profound effect on those gathered there: Bryan Fairfax, still hoping for reconciliation, is crushed; Gates, the former British officer, recognizes that civil war is inevitable; and Washington, in his quiet, determined way, resolves his course. He will lead the Virginia forces to the defense of Boston. The die is cast.
Chapter 38 — Enlisting of Troops in the East — Camp at Boston — General Artemas Ward — Scheme to Surprise Ticonderoga — New Hampshire Grants — Ethan Allen and the Green Mountain Boys — Benedict Arnold — Affair of Ticonderoga and Crown Point — A Dash at St. Johns
While the southern colonies arm themselves, events race forward in the north. The Massachusetts Provincial Congress hurries to enlist troops, establishing a camp at Cambridge under General Artemas Ward. A bold scheme is hatched in the New Hampshire Grants (present-day Vermont) to surprise the strategically vital British forts at Ticonderoga and Crown Point, which guard the water route to Canada. Ethan Allen and his Green Mountain Boys — rough, independent frontier fighters who have already defied New York’s claims to the Grants — organize the expedition. They are joined by Benedict Arnold, a Connecticut militia captain of restless ambition and military genius, who arrives with a commission from the Massachusetts Committee of Safety. The two forceful personalities clash, but Allen leads the assault, bursting into the commandant’s bedchamber at Ticonderoga early on May 10, 1775, demanding surrender “in the name of the Great Jehovah and the Continental Congress!” The fort falls without a fight. Crown Point is captured the next day. A cavalry dash at St. Johns captures its garrison. The green cannon of Ticonderoga — more than a hundred pieces of artillery — will soon prove crucial to the American cause.
Chapter 39 — Second Session of Congress — John Hancock — Petition to the King — Federal Union — Military Measures — Debates about the Army — Question as to Commander-in-Chief — Appointment of Washington — Other Appointments — Letters of Washington to his Wife and Brother — Preparations for Departure
The Second Continental Congress convenes in Philadelphia in May 1775. John Hancock presides. Congress adopts a petition to the king (the Olive Branch Petition) affirming American loyalty and seeking redress — a last attempt at reconciliation that will be rejected. It also begins to assume the powers of a federal union, authorizing the raising of armies, the issuance of currency, and the conduct of war. The critical question is who shall command the Continental Army. The debates are intense: John Hancock covets the position; others argue for General Charles Lee or Artemas Ward. But John Adams rises and, in a carefully prepared speech, nominates Washington — a Virginian whose appointment will bind the South to a struggle centering on New England. The choice is unanimous. Washington is appointed commander-in-chief on June 15, 1775. He accepts the command but refuses any salary, asking only that his expenses be paid. Other general officers are appointed: Ward, Lee, Schuyler, Putnam, and others. Washington writes letters to his wife Martha and to his brother John Augustine — the letter to Martha expresses his deep anxiety and his sense of duty, his hope that he will return safely, and his trust in Providence. Preparations for departure are made. He purchases books on military tactics, arranges his affairs, and prepares to ride north.
Chapter 40 — More Troops Arrive at Boston — Generals Howe, Burgoyne, and Clinton — Proclamation of Gage — Nature of the American Army — Scornful Conduct of the British Officers — Project of the Americans to Seize upon Breed’s Hill — Putnam’s Opinion of It — Sanctioned by Prescott — Nocturnal March of the Detachment — Fortifying of Bunker’s Hill — Break of Day, and Astonishment of the Enemy
While Congress debates, the military situation around Boston escalates. More British troops arrive under Generals Howe, Burgoyne, and Clinton — the latter two famously declaring that they would “soon show the Yankees what they were about.” Gage issues a proclamation threatening to treat captured rebels as traitors. The American army, camped around Boston, is a motley collection of militia regiments, poorly armed, badly supplied, and lacking any common organization. The British officers treat them with open scorn. The Americans resolve to seize the heights overlooking Boston — the Charlestown peninsula. The plan is to fortify Bunker’s Hill, but Colonel Prescott, on the night of June 16-17, leads his detachment to Breed’s Hill instead, closer to the British positions. Putnam, consulted, expresses doubts about the exposed position but defers. The men work through the night, digging redoubts and entrenchments under the silent stars. At daybreak, the British look out from Boston to see a formidable fortification raised overnight where there had been only an empty hill. General Howe exclaims in astonishment: the Americans have done in one night what the best engineers in Europe would have thought possible only in a fortnight.
Chapter 41 — Battle of Bunker’s Hill
The Battle of Bunker Hill (June 17, 1775) is described in full detail. The British, under General Howe, land at Charlestown and form for battle on the beach. The American position is held by Prescott, Putnam, Stark, and their men — farmers and mechanics who have never faced regulars in pitched battle. The British advance in perfect order, their bright uniforms making them targets against the green hillside. The Americans are ordered to hold their fire until they can see the whites of the enemy’s eyes. When they fire, the front ranks of the British are shattered. The troops waver, fall back, and re-form for a second advance. Again the deadly volleys tear through them. It is not until the third assault, when the American powder runs out, that the British carry the redoubt by bayonet. The Americans retreat, fighting as they go. The British “victory” is a Pyrrhic one: over a thousand casualties, including a large proportion of officers. The battle proves to the colonies and the world that American militia can stand against British regulars. It also proves to Washington that he will need a disciplined army — raw courage alone will not win a war.
Chapter 42 — Departure from Philadelphia — Anecdotes of General Schuyler — Of Lee — Tidings of Bunker’s Hill — Military Councils — Population of New York — The Johnson Family — Governor Tryon — Arrival at New York — Military Instructions to Schuyler — Arrival at the Camp
Washington departs Philadelphia on June 21, 1775, traveling north to take command of the army. He is accompanied by Generals Schuyler and Lee, and his aides. Irving relates anecdotes of the characters: Schuyler, a New York patrician of Dutch descent, wealthy, cultivated, and a capable military organizer; Lee, the eccentric English soldier of fortune whose caustic wit and peculiar habits provide a constant counterpoint. News of Bunker Hill reaches Washington in New York, where he receives the first official tidings. He holds military councils, assessing the strategic situation. New York’s population is deeply divided between patriots and loyalists; the powerful Johnson family (Sir William Johnson’s heirs) commands the allegiance of the Mohawk Valley. Governor Tryon, though nominally still in office, has lost the confidence of the patriots and is living aboard a British ship in the harbor. Washington issues military instructions to Schuyler for the defense of New York and the projected invasion of Canada. Finally, he arrives in Cambridge, Massachusetts, on July 2, 1775. The following day, under the great elm tree at Cambridge Common, he formally takes command of the Continental Army.
Chapter 43 — Washington Takes Command of the Armies — Sketch of General Lee — Characters of the British Commanders, Howe, Clinton, and Burgoyne — Survey of the Camps from Prospect Hill — The Camps Contrasted — Description of the Revolutionary Army — Rhode Island Troops — Character of General Greene — Washington Represents the Deficiencies of the Army — His Apology for the Massachusetts Troops — Governor Trumbull — Craigie House, Washington’s Head-Quarters
Washington takes command of the heterogeneous army assembled around Boston. Irving offers a sketch of General Lee, whose intellectual gifts and military experience are balanced by his erratic personality and overweening ambition. The British commanders are characterized: Howe, brave and competent but indolent; Clinton, able but cold and touchy; Burgoyne, brilliant, theatrical, and inclined to underestimate his foes. Washington surveys the American camps from Prospect Hill, taking stock of his army. The contrast between the two sides is stark: the British, well-fed, well-clothed, well-disciplined, secure in fortified Boston; the Americans, ragged, half-starved, poorly armed, but burning with the spirit of liberty. Irving describes the Revolutionary Army in detail — regiments from Massachusetts, Connecticut, New Hampshire, and Rhode Island, each with its own character. Among them, the Rhode Island troops under the command of General Nathanael Greene stand out for their discipline. Greene, a young Quaker-born ironmonger who has educated himself in military science, will become Washington’s most trusted general. Washington prepares a comprehensive report to Congress, representing the deficiencies of the army with unflinching honesty — lack of powder, arms, tents, clothing, and organization. He offers an apology for the Massachusetts troops, explaining that their lack of discipline stems from their democratic habits and their belief in independence, not from any defect of courage. He corresponds with Governor Trumbull of Connecticut, one of the most reliable supporters of the Revolution. Washington establishes his headquarters at the Craigie House (the Vassall House) in Cambridge, a fine mansion that will serve as the nerve center of the Continental Army.
Chapter 44 — Questions of Military Rank — Popularity of Putnam — Arrangements at Head-Quarters — Colonel Mifflin and John Trumbull, Aides-de-Camp — Joseph Reed, Washington’s Secretary and Confidential Friend — Gates as Adjutant-General — Hazardous Situation of the Army — Strengthening of the Defences — Efficiency of Putnam — Rapid Changes — New Distribution of the Forces — Rigid Discipline — Lee and his Cane — His Idea as to Strong Battalions — Arrival of Rifle Companies — Daniel Morgan and his Sharp-Shooters — Washington Declines to Detach Troops to Distant Points for their Protection — His Reasons for so Doing
One of Washington’s earliest challenges is the question of military rank: the officers of the various New England regiments have different commissions, and precedence disputes erupt immediately. Putnam, the blunt, beloved Connecticut general, is immensely popular with the troops and the public. Washington organizes his headquarters, appointing Colonel Thomas Mifflin as one of his aides-de-camp, along with John Trumbull (the future painter of the Revolution). He takes Joseph Reed, a Philadelphia lawyer, as his secretary and confidential friend — a relationship that will prove crucial. Gates is installed as adjutant-general, bringing order to the army’s administration. The situation of the army is hazardous: the powder supply is desperately short; if the British sallied in force, the siege might collapse. Washington sets about strengthening the defences, extending the entrenchments, building redoubts, and connecting the various camps. Putnam’s energy and efficiency are invaluable in overseeing this work. A new distribution of the forces is made, creating three divisions under Ward, Lee, and Putnam. Washington insists on rigid discipline — orders are issued against swearing, drunkenness, and plundering. Lee, who has a habit of carrying a cane and delivering oracular pronouncements, confides his strategic philosophy: “Strong battalions are the best negotiators — strong battalions, and nothing else.” Rifle companies from Virginia, Maryland, and Pennsylvania arrive — among them Daniel Morgan’s company of Virginia sharp-shooters, expert marksmen in their distinctive hunting shirts who prove invaluable as skirmishers and snipers. Washington resists calls to detach troops to protect distant points, explaining his strategic rationale: the army must remain concentrated; dispersed, it would be destroyed in detail.
Chapter 45 — Washington’s Object in Distressing Boston — Scarcity and Sickness in the Town — A Startling Discovery — Scarcity of Powder in the Camp — Its Perilous Situation — Economy of Ammunition — Correspondence between Lee and Burgoyne — Correspondence between Washington and Gage — The Dignity of the Patriot Army Asserted
Washington’s strategic object is to distress the British in Boston — to cut off supplies, harass foraging parties, and make the occupation so costly and uncomfortable that Howe will be forced to evacuate the town. The British, cooped up in Boston, suffer from scarcity of fresh provisions and from sickness — smallpox and dysentery are rife. A startling discovery is made in the American camp: the army has barely thirty-six rounds of powder per man, and the total supply in the entire siege lines amounts to only about ninety-three barrels — enough for a few hours of fighting. Washington’s perilous situation is revealed starkly: if the British knew, they could march out and destroy the American army. He takes desperate measures, enforcing strict economy of ammunition — no firing without orders, no wasted volleys. The gunners are forbidden to fire at British sentries, tempting though the targets may be. A correspondence ensues between General Lee and General Burgoyne — a witty, literary exchange, with Burgoyne condescending and Lee defiant. More weightily, Washington and Gage exchange letters on the treatment of prisoners, with Washington asserting the dignity of the patriot army and protesting the British threat to treat captured Americans as traitors to be hanged. The correspondence establishes Washington’s tone: firm, dignified, unyielding on points of principle.
Chapter 46 — Dangers in the Interior — Machinations of the Johnson Family — Rivalry of Ethan Allen and Benedict Arnold — Government Perplexities about the Ticonderoga Capture — Measures to Secure the Prize — Allen and Arnold Ambitious of Further Laurels — Projects for the Invasion of Canada — Ethan Allen and Seth Warner Honored by Congress — Arnold Displaced by a Committee of Inquiry — His Indignation — News from Canada — The Revolution to be Extended into that Province — Enlistment of Green Mountain Boys — Schuyler at Ticonderoga — State of Affairs There — Election for Officers of the Green Mountain Boys — Ethan Allen Dismounted Joins the Army as a Volunteer — Preparations for the Invasion of Canada — General Montgomery — Indian Chiefs at Cambridge — Council Fire — Plan for an Expedition against Quebec — Departure of Troops from Ticonderoga — Arrival at Isle aux Noix
While the siege of Boston continues, dangers brew in the interior. The Johnson family in the Mohawk Valley — Sir John Johnson and his Loyalist followers — threaten to raise the Indians against the Revolution. The rivalry between Ethan Allen and Benedict Arnold over the laurels of Ticonderoga creates friction with the Continental Congress, which is perplexed about how to handle the capture. Congress eventually honors Allen and his lieutenant Seth Warner, recognizing the Green Mountain Boys as a separate regiment. Arnold, displaced by a committee of inquiry, is indignant — his pride stung, his ambition burning. News from Canada suggests that the province might be ripe for revolution. Congress authorizes an invasion of Canada: the Revolution is to be extended into that province. Schuyler is placed in command of the northern department and begins preparations at Ticonderoga. The Green Mountain Boys are enlisted; an election of officers confirms Warner as colonel and leaves Allen dismounted — forced to join as a volunteer, eager to redeem his reputation. General Richard Montgomery, an Irish-born former British officer who has married into the Livingstons of New York, is appointed second-in-command. Indian chiefs come to Cambridge, where a council fire is held, and Washington negotiates for their neutrality or alliance. A bold plan is hatched for a two-pronged invasion: Montgomery will advance by Lake Champlain against Montreal, while a second column, led by Benedict Arnold, will strike through the Maine wilderness directly at Quebec. Troops depart from Ticonderoga and arrive at Isle aux Noix, the assembly point on the Richelieu River.
Chapter 47 — A Challenge Declined — A Blow Meditated — A Cautious Council of War — Preparations for the Quebec Expedition — Benedict Arnold the Leader — Advice and Instructions — Departure — General Schuyler on the Sorel — Reconnoitres St. Johns — Camp at Isle aux Noix — Illness of Schuyler — Returns to Ticonderoga — Expedition of Montgomery against St. Johns — Letter of Ethan Allen — His Dash against Montreal — Its Catastrophe — A Hero in Irons — Correspondence of Washington with Schuyler and Arnold — His Anxiety about Them
Washington declines a personal challenge (likely from a British officer), refusing to engage in affairs of honor while serving as commander-in-chief. But he meditates a blow against the British that will change the course of the war: the expedition against Quebec. A cautious council of war approves the plan. Benedict Arnold is chosen as the leader — the choice reflecting Washington’s recognition of Arnold’s energy, resourcefulness, and daring. Washington gives Arnold detailed advice and instructions, emphasizing the need for secrecy and speed. Arnold’s expedition departs from Cambridge in September 1775. Meanwhile, in the north, General Schuyler advances up the Sorel River, reconnoitres St. Johns, and establishes a camp at Isle aux Noix. Schuyler falls dangerously ill and is forced to return to Ticonderoga, leaving Montgomery in command. Montgomery lays siege to St. Johns, the key to the Montreal approach. Ethan Allen, still smarting from his demotion and eager for glory, decides on his own initiative to dash against Montreal. He attempts to capture the city with a small force of Canadians and Green Mountain Boys — but his attack is badly coordinated; he is surrounded, captured, and thrown into irons, to be sent to England for trial as a traitor. The loss of Allen is a blow to American morale. Washington’s correspondence with Schuyler and Arnold reveals his deep anxiety about both prongs of the Canadian campaign — the supply problems, the lateness of the season, the uncertain loyalties of the Canadian population.
Chapter 48 — British in Boston Send out Cruisers — Depredations of Captain Wallace along the Coast — Treason in the Camp — Arrest of Dr. Church — His Trial and Fate — Conflagration of Falmouth — Irritation throughout the Country — Fitting out of Vessels of War — Embarkation of General Gage for England — Committee from Congress — Conferences with Washington — Resolutions of Congress to Carry on the War — Return of Secretary Reed to Philadelphia
The British in Boston, though besieged, still have naval power. They send out cruisers to ravage the American coast. Captain Wallace, commanding the British armed schooner, terrorizes the towns of Narragansett Bay, plundering and burning. The crisis deepens with the discovery of treason in the American camp: Dr. Benjamin Church, the director-general of the army hospital and a trusted member of the Massachusetts Committee of Safety, is revealed to have been communicating with the British, conveying intelligence through a cipher. Church is arrested, tried, and found guilty; he is imprisoned, his fate a grim warning of the dangers of espionage. In October 1775, the British burn Falmouth (now Portland, Maine), a devastating conflagration that leaves hundreds homeless in the winter cold. The burning galvanizes American resistance and leads to the fitting out of armed vessels — the beginnings of the American navy. General Gage, his health broken by the strain of the siege, embarks for England. A committee from Congress arrives at Cambridge for conferences with Washington, assessing the state of the army and the prospects of the campaign. Congress passes resolutions committing the colonies to carry on the war — the Olive Branch Petition having been rejected by the king. Washington’s secretary Joseph Reed returns to Philadelphia for personal reasons, leaving a gap in Washington’s confidential circle.
Chapter 49 — Measures of General Howe — Desecration of Churches — Three Proclamations — Seizure of Tories — Want of Artillery — Henry Knox, the Artillerist — His Mission to Ticonderoga — Re-enlistment of Troops — Lack of Public Spirit — Comments of General Greene
General Howe, now commanding the British forces in Boston, takes defensive measures — fortifying the town, demolishing buildings to clear fields of fire, and, in civilian complaints, desecrating churches by using them as barracks and stables. He issues three proclamations: one offering pardon to all who will lay down arms and return to allegiance; one threatening the severest penalties against those who persist; and one forbidding trade with the rebels. Loyalists — “Tories” — are seized and imprisoned by the patriots; others flee Boston to the safety of British lines. The critical deficiency in the American camp is artillery — the siege cannot succeed without heavy guns to bombard the British positions. Henry Knox, a Boston bookseller turned artillerist, comes to Washington with a bold proposal: bring the cannon captured at Ticonderoga across the winter wilderness to Boston. Washington approves, and Knox departs on his epic mission. The re-enlistment of troops becomes a desperate struggle: the soldiers’ enlistments expire at the end of 1775, and the army faces the prospect of melting away. Washington appeals to Congress, to the state governments, to the men themselves — but the lack of public spirit, the preference for home and farm over camp and danger, depresses him. General Greene’s comments on these difficulties are recorded: he sees the want of public virtue as the greatest threat to the Revolution.
Chapter 50 — Affairs in Canada — Capture of Fort Chamblee — Siege of St. Johns — Maclean and his Highlanders — Montgomery on the Treatment of Ethan Allen — Repulse of Carleton — Capitulation of the Garrison of St. Johns — Generous Conduct of Montgomery — Maclean Re-embarks for Quebec — Weary Struggle of Arnold through the Wilderness — Defection of Colonel Enos — Arnold in the Valley of the Chaudiere — His Arrival opposite Quebec — Surrender of Montreal — Escape of Carleton — Home-Sickness of the American Troops
The Canadian campaign unfolds on two fronts. Montgomery, having taken command after Schuyler’s illness, captures Fort Chambly with its valuable stores of powder and supplies. He presses the siege of St. Johns, where the British garrison under Major Preston holds out stubbornly. Colonel Maclean and his Highlanders attempt to relieve the fort but are repulsed. Carleton himself leads a force of regulars, militia, and Indians from Montreal to break the siege — and is driven back. Montgomery writes to the captured Ethan Allen with a mixture of sympathy and criticism of his rashness. On November 3, the garrison of St. Johns finally capitulates; Montgomery demonstrates generous and chivalrous conduct toward the defeated. Maclean re-embarks for Quebec. Meanwhile, Arnold’s expedition suffers an ordeal that becomes legendary in American history. Eleven hundred men march into the Maine wilderness in September — by the time they reach the French settlements on the Chaudiere River in November, they are a ragged, starving remnant. They have been forced to eat dogs, shoes, cartridge boxes — anything. The boats proved inadequate, the rivers treacherous, the portages brutal. Supplies spoiled. One of Arnold’s officers, Colonel Enos, turns back with several hundred men — an act of apparent desertion that leaves the remaining force even more desperate. Yet Arnold pushes on, driving his men with fierce energy. They emerge into the valley of the Chaudiere, where French-Canadian peasants feed them. Arnold arrives opposite Quebec on November 9, his force reduced to about six hundred exhausted men. He makes a show of demanding the surrender of the city. Carleton, having narrowly escaped capture when Montreal fell, has arrived in Quebec just ahead of Arnold and prepares the defenses. Surrender of Montreal follows Montgomery’s advance, but Carleton’s escape is a stroke of bad luck for the Americans. The Canadian troops, many of whose enlistments have expired, are afflicted by home-sickness and disease.
Chapter 51 — Washington’s Anticipations of Success at Quebec — His Eulogium of Arnold — Schuyler and Montgomery Talk of Resigning — Expostulations of Washington — Their Effect — Schuyler’s Conduct to a Captive Foe
Washington, following the progress of the Canadian campaign from Cambridge, allows himself to anticipate success at Quebec. He writes a remarkable eulogium of Arnold, praising his “astonishing” march through the wilderness and his determination. But difficulties multiply. Schuyler, frustrated by constant illness, disputes with Congress, and the immense difficulties of the northern command, talks of resigning. Montgomery, too, writes of his desire to resign after the Quebec campaign — he is sick of the service, disappointed by the lack of support from Congress, and disgusted by the indiscipline of the troops. Washington writes urgent, expostulatory letters to both men, begging them to remain at their posts. He appeals to their patriotism, their honor, and their sense of duty — the Revolution cannot succeed without men of their experience and character. His letters have their effect on Montgomery, who promises to see the Quebec campaign through. Schuyler’s conduct to a captured foe — a British officer of the 26th Regiment, Colonel —— — is recounted as an example of the humanity and gentlemanly conduct that Washington has insisted upon. The American treatment of prisoners stands in contrast to British threats to treat them as traitors.
Chapter 52 — Difficulties in Filling up the Army — The Connecticut Troops Persist in Going Home — Their Reception There — Timely Arrival of Spoils in the Camp — Putnam and the Prize Mortar — A Maraud by Americans — Rebuked by Washington — Correspondence of Washington with General Howe about the Treatment of Ethan Allen — Fraternal Zeal of Levi Allen — Treatment of General Prescott — Preparations to Bombard Boston — Battery at Lechmere’s Point — Prayer of Putnam for Powder
The most acute crisis of the siege: filling the army as enlistments expire. The Connecticut troops, their term of service up, persist in going home despite Washington’s desperate appeals. Irving describes their reception in their home towns — initially greeted as heroes, but the novelty soon wears off, and many will re-enlist after a taste of civilian life. A timely arrival of spoils — captured British supply ships — brings much-needed arms, powder, and clothing to the camp. Putnam, ever the practical soldier, captures a valuable brass mortar (the “Prize Mortar”) from a British vessel and presents it to the army. But a maraud by American soldiers, plundering the property of a loyalist, draws Washington’s stern rebuke, demonstrating his determination to maintain discipline even among men he respects. Washington and Howe exchange correspondence on the treatment of Ethan Allen, who has been sent to England in chains. Washington demands that Allen be treated as a prisoner of war rather than a traitor; Howe’s evasive reply underscores the dangerous legal limbo in which captured Americans find themselves. Levi Allen, Ethan’s brother, displays fraternal zeal in trying to secure better treatment for the captive. The treatment of General Prescott, a British prisoner, becomes another point of contention: the Americans treat him well, hoping for reciprocal treatment of their own captured officers. Washington prepares actively to bombard Boston. A battery is constructed at Lechmere’s Point, jutting into the bay within range of the town. But all preparations depend on powder — and Putnam’s prayer for powder, echoed by the entire army, remains unanswered as winter closes in.
Chapter 53 — Mount Vernon in Danger — Mrs. Washington Invited to the Camp — Lund Washington, the General’s Agent — Terms on which he Serves — Instructed to Keep up the Hospitality of the House — Journey of Mrs. Washington to Camp — Her Equipage and Liveries — Arrival at Camp — Domestic Affairs at Head-Quarters — Gayeties in Camp — A Brawl between Round Jackets and Rifle Shirts
Even as Washington commands the Continental Army, his heart remains at Mount Vernon. The estate is in danger — British cruisers on the Potomac could threaten the mansion. Washington invites Mrs. Washington to join him at Cambridge for the winter. He leaves the management of Mount Vernon in the hands of his kinsman Lund Washington, who serves as his agent on carefully defined terms (including a share of the profits). Washington instructs Lund to keep up the hospitality of the house — Mount Vernon must not appear to be deserted — and gives detailed directions about the plantation, the slaves, and the accounts. Mrs. Washington undertakes the journey to Cambridge with considerable equipage — her coach-and-four, her liveried servants — a reminder of the Virginia aristocracy from which she comes. She arrives in camp and establishes domestic affairs at headquarters. Her presence brings a touch of domesticity and elegance to the Craigie House. Despite the gravity of the situation, there are gayeties in camp — dinners, dances, and social gatherings among the officers and their families. A brawl breaks out between the “Round Jackets” (Virginia riflemen in their hunting shirts) and the “Rifle Shirts” (other frontier companies) — a clash of regional pride that Washington handles with firm discipline. The chapter provides a rare glimpse of Washington’s domestic character amid the hardships of war.
Chapter 54 — Affairs in Canada — Arnold at Point Levi — Quebec Re-enforced — Crossing of the St. Lawrence — Landing in Wolfe’s Cove — Arnold on the Heights of Abraham — Cautious Counsel — Quebec Aroused — The Invaders Baffled — Withdraw to Point aux Trembles — Booming of Cannon — Carleton at Quebec — Letter of Washington to Arnold
The volume closes at the end of 1775 with the American forces before Quebec, the siege of Boston ongoing, and the outcome of the Revolution still deeply uncertain.

sources/irving-life-washington-vol2.title: [source] The Life of George Washington — Volume II (Irving, 1899 Desmond)
sources/irving-life-washington-vol2.content:
Irving — The Life of George Washington, Vol. II
Washington Irving (1783–1859) — The Life of George Washington. — Volume II. Extended Annotated Edition. Jazzybee Verlag, Altenmünster, 2014. ISBN: 9783849642174.
This is Volume II of Washington Irving’s five-volume biography of George Washington, first published 1855–1859. This volume covers the early years of the American Revolutionary War, from Washington’s assumption of command at Cambridge (July 1775) through the campaigns of 1776 and the close of that year. Modern “Extended Annotated” introductory material (a biographical primer on Irving) has been stripped; the text is Irving’s original work only.
Scope: Covers July 1775 – December 1776 — Washington takes command of the Continental Army at Cambridge; the Siege of Boston; the invasion of Canada under Montgomery and Arnold; the Declaration of Independence; the Battle of Long Island; the retreat through New York and New Jersey; the victories at Trenton and Princeton; Washington earns the appellation “the American Fabius.”
Chapter-by-Chapter Summary
CHAPTER I — Washington Takes Command at Cambridge
On the 3rd of July, the morning after his arrival at Cambridge, Washington takes formal command of the army drawn up on the Common. Irving describes the review and the ancient elm under which Washington drew his sword as commander-in-chief. Washington’s first task is to assess the raw provincial forces — undisciplined, poorly equipped, and unfamiliar with European tactics — while the British hold Boston and Bunker’s Hill. He writes to Congress requesting supplies, powder, and a reorganization of the medical department.
CHAPTER II — Allaying Discontents Among the Generals
Washington’s justice and impartiality are tested as soon as he takes command, as Irving narrates his handling of precedence disputes among the generals. Major-General Ward’s claims and the rivalry between Connecticut and Massachusetts officers demand delicate diplomacy. Washington insists on merit over seniority, establishing an early precedent for his leadership style. The chapter reveals the sectional jealousies that would plague the army throughout the war.
CHAPTER III — The Siege of Boston Begins
Irving describes how Washington’s great object is to force the enemy out of Boston. His lines cut off the town from the country, but besieging a place defended by a superior naval force presents immense difficulties. The British hold Bunker’s Hill with strong works; their floating batteries and ships of war command the harbor. Washington’s lack of powder (scarcely nine rounds per man) forces him to feign strength while concealing critical shortages from both the enemy and his own officers.
CHAPTER IV — Affairs in Other Quarters
Events elsewhere demand Washington’s superintending care, as Irving recounts. The Northern Department under Schuyler plans the invasion of Canada. Arnold’s expedition through the wilderness of Maine is detailed — the grueling portage between the Kennebec and Dead Rivers, the loss of bateaux, the starvation of men forced to eat their cartridge boxes and moccasins. Meanwhile, Lord Dunmore’s depredations in Virginia and rising tensions in the Carolinas require Washington’s attention, stretching his command across the continent.
CHAPTER V — The Siege Continues
The siege of Boston continues without major action. Irving notes how the British strengthen their lines while Washington grapples with short enlistments, lack of powder, and the militia system. A council of war decides against a direct assault. Washington devises a plan for a night attack on Boston, but his officers advise against it as too risky. He acquiesces, though he later confides to Reed that he believes the enterprise would have succeeded with resolution.
CHAPTER VI — Naval Operations and the Canada Expedition
While the two expeditions threaten Canada from different quarters, war continues along the seaboard. Irving describes how the British in Boston, cut off from supplies, send out foraging parties. Washington commissions armed vessels — the beginning of the American navy. The schooner Hannah captures British transports. The burning of Falmouth (Portland, Maine) by Lieutenant Mowat on October 18, 1775 shocks the colonies: 139 dwellings and 228 stores are destroyed, and the act is viewed as proving British intent to wage a war of terror, pushing public sentiment toward independence.
CHAPTER VII — General Howe Takes Command in Boston
Irving details how General Howe, after taking command in Boston following Gage’s departure, proceeds to fortify the town. He clears houses and throws up redoubts. The Old South Church is desecrated — its pews removed, floor covered with earth, converted into a riding school for Burgoyne’s light dragoons. The North Church is demolished for fuel. Howe issues three proclamations restricting movement from the town. Washington, incensed by the Falmouth burning and Dunmore’s actions, retaliates by ordering the seizure of crown officers as hostages. Henry Knox steps forward, offering to bring artillery from Ticonderoga — the beginning of his legendary feat.
CHAPTER VIII — Dispatches from Canada
Irving recounts the dispatches from Schuyler giving news of the Canada expedition. Chamblee is captured by Montgomery. St. Johns is invested and surrenders after a stout defence by Major Preston. Arnold’s march through the Maine wilderness is described in vivid detail: the carrying-place, the loss of bateaux, the starvation when Colonel Enos turns back with 300 men. Arnold pushes on, reaching the Chaudière River, and emerges at Point Levi opposite Quebec on November 9. The inhabitants marvel that such a march was possible.
CHAPTER IX — Arnold Before Quebec
Arnold’s approach to Quebec. His army is reduced to a handful. Irving describes how he crosses the St. Lawrence and ascends the Plains of Abraham by moonlight, replicating Wolfe’s feat. He summons the town; the garrison fires upon his flag. Arnold awaits Montgomery’s arrival. When Montgomery descends from Montreal, the combined force of about 900 effective men prepares for an assault on the fortress in a driving snowstorm on the last night of 1775.
CHAPTER X — Reorganizing the Army
Irving details the immense difficulty of forming an army under new regulations. The militia system defeats efforts to raise regular regiments. Short enlistments leave Washington without troops as 1776 dawns — his army drops from over 20,000 to fewer than 10,000 men. He writes movingly to Congress and to Reed: “Search the volumes of history through, and I much question whether a case similar to ours is to be found.” The distress of the camp and the “unconquerable desire to return to their homes” among the soldiery are lyrically rendered.
CHAPTER XI — Washington’s Mind Turns to Mount Vernon
Amid the concerns of war, Washington’s thoughts revert to his home on the Potomac. Irving presents his correspondence with his manager Lund Washington: detailed directions for managing the estate, keeping up hospitality to the poor, and his famous instruction to give forty or fifty pounds a year in charity. Mrs. Washington arrives at Cambridge in her carriage with her son and daughter-in-law, bringing domestic grace to headquarters. Irving includes the anecdote of Washington breaking up a brawl between Virginia riflemen and Marblehead sailors by seizing two men by the throat.
CHAPTER XII — The Canadian Invasion Continued
Irving turns from the siege of Boston to the invasion of Canada. Montgomery and Arnold prepare for the assault on Quebec in a snowstorm on December 31, 1775. Montgomery is killed at the first barrier as he cries “Push on, my brave boys, Quebec is ours!” Arnold is wounded in the leg. Morgan and his riflemen fight heroically in the lower town but are forced to surrender. The attack fails; the shattered army retreats three miles from the city. Irving reflects that had Arnold fallen at Quebec, his name would have remained unsullied.
CHAPTER XIII — Lord Dunmore’s Proceedings in Virginia
A vessel captured bearing supplies from Lord Dunmore to Boston reveals his plan to proclaim liberty to indentured servants and slaves, threatening Virginia with a servile war. Norfolk is bombarded and burnt by Dunmore’s fleet. Washington writes that if Dunmore is not crushed before spring, he will become “the most formidable enemy America has.” Lee’s stern policy toward Tories is contrasted with Washington’s more moderate approach.
CHAPTER XIV — British Preparations to Evacuate Boston
Early in January 1776, great activity stirs in Boston harbor. Transports take in supplies for a removal of the army. Sir Henry Clinton sails with a secret expedition to the South. Washington, suspecting New York may be the next target, sends Lee to fortify it. Lee arrives in New York on February 4, puts the city under martial law, seizes Tories, and begins fortifications. His threat to chain Tory friends to houses if the British fire on the city keeps the inhabitants in a fever.
CHAPTER XV — Washington Still Hopeful of Canada
Irving shows Washington still hopeful about Canada despite gathering gloom. He expects tidings that Montgomery and Arnold possess Quebec. Instead, Schuyler’s dispatch announces the failure before Quebec, Montgomery’s death, and Arnold’s wounding. Washington is deeply moved but writes to Schuyler that “we must not despair.” He applies to Massachusetts, New Hampshire, and Connecticut for three regiments to reinforce Canada.
CHAPTER XVI — Schuyler’s Letter on the Canadian Reverse
Schuyler’s letter announces the disaster with manly feeling. He wishes he had no occasion to send such intelligence. Washington’s reply expresses deep sorrow at Montgomery’s fall and concern for the wounded Arnold. Measures are taken to reinforce the army. Schuyler, falsely accused by New Englanders of negligence in forwarding supplies, receives Washington’s unwavering support.
CHAPTER XVII — Winter Siege of Boston
The siege continues through the winter without striking incident. Irving details how the British remain within their works while Washington labors to form a new army. Knox arrives with the artillery from Ticonderoga — fifty cannon, mortars, and howitzers dragged on sledges across frozen lakes and snowy wastes. The arrival is celebrated by christening the huge brass mortar “Congress.” General Putnam’s men construct batteries on Lechmere Point under constant fire. Washington, still eager to attack, proposes an assault when the bay freezes, but his council of war deems it too dangerous.
CHAPTER XVIII — The Occupation of Dorchester Heights
The evening of March 4, 1776 is fixed for the occupation of Dorchester Heights. Irving dramatically narrates how a simultaneous cannonade distracts the enemy while General Thomas leads 1,200 men with 300 wagons of fascines and hay bundles. By dawn, two redoubts frown along the height. Howe exclaims, “The rebels have done more work in one night than my whole army would have done in a month.” A storm prevents Howe’s counterattack. Washington reminds his men it is the anniversary of the Boston Massacre and calls on them to revenge their brethren.
CHAPTER XIX — The British Evacuate Boston
The British fleet bearing the army from Boston disappears from the coast on March 17, 1776. Irving narrates Washington’s entry into the city in triumph. Howe’s retreat is precipitate — cannon spiked, stores destroyed, and the harbor filled with 78 ships carrying 11,000 troops and refugees. Washington writes that “no electric shock” could have struck the Tories with greater consternation. Congress votes a gold medal in Washington’s honor. The question of where the British will strike next looms — New York is the likely target.
CHAPTER XX — Arnold Before Quebec After the Assault
Irving recounts Arnold’s blockade of Quebec after the failed assault. Wounded and crippled, Arnold maintains the siege through the winter with a force that at one point numbers only 500 men. Smallpox ravages the American camp. General Thomas arrives to find the army in a forlorn condition. On May 6, British reinforcements arrive and Carleton sallies forth. The Americans retreat precipitately, abandoning baggage, artillery, and even their sick. The Canadian campaign ends in disaster.
CHAPTER XXI — The Canadian Reverse Reaches Congress
Irving describes how Washington sends General Gates to lay the dispatches before Congress. The news spreads alarm. Congress appoints a committee to confer with Washington, leading to the establishment of a Board of War and Ordnance. Washington’s conferences in Philadelphia result in resolutions for three-year enlistments, a flying camp of 10,000 militia, and the strengthening of the Hudson Highlands.
CHAPTER XXII — Disaster in Canada Continues
Dispatches from Canada remain disastrous. Arnold, commanding at Montreal, establishes a post at the Cedars which is captured by a British and Indian force under Captain Forster. The Americans are compelled to abandon Montreal. The retreat toward the Richelieu and Lake Champlain becomes a rout as Carleton advances. Washington urges reinforcements but has few men to spare.
CHAPTER XXIII — The Close of the Canadian Campaign
Irving narrates the disastrous close of the Canadian campaign. General Thomas dies of smallpox. The army, ravaged by disease and dispirited, evacuates Canada and falls back to Crown Point and Ticonderoga. Washington, though grieved, refuses to despair. He writes that “a manly and spirited opposition only can insure success.”
CHAPTER XXIV — The British Aim at New York and the Hudson
The British aim to seize New York and the Hudson River as the base of operations. Irving details how Washington moves the army from Boston to New York. He fortifies the city and surrounding heights. On June 29, the British fleet under Admiral Howe appears off Sandy Hook — 130 sail. The Declaration of Independence is proclaimed on July 9. Washington has it read to the army, telling his men that “the peace and safety of our country” now depend on their arms.
CHAPTER XXV — First Appearance of Alexander Hamilton
Irving introduces Alexander Hamilton, who first appears in the military ranks as a captain of artillery. His early life, character, and education are sketched. Greene recommends him to Washington’s notice. When Washington sees the skill and science of Hamilton’s fortifications, he invites him to his marquee — beginning the historic partnership.
CHAPTER XXVI — The Declaration of Independence and the British Arrive
The exultation over the Declaration is soon overclouded. Irving describes how British ships stand up the bay. The fleet under Admiral Howe arrives with reinforcements. British forces land on Staten Island, joined by Hessian troops — 4,300 Brunswick troops and nearly 13,000 Hessians hired by the British ministry. The total British force under Howe’s command numbers over 31,000 men. Washington has barely 10,000 fit for duty.
CHAPTER XXVII — Lord Howe’s Efforts at Reconciliation
Lord Howe arrives with powers to treat for peace. Irving recounts his proclamation offering pardon to all who return to their allegiance. When he sends a letter addressed to “George Washington, Esq.,” Washington refuses to receive it — he will not accept a private designation when his public station as commander-in-chief is at issue. Colonel Patterson’s interview with Washington on the subject is described: Washington insists on proper recognition of American rank. His conduct receives the applause of Congress. A conspiracy against Washington’s life — the Tryon plot — is uncovered. Mayor Matthews is arrested, and Hickey, one of Washington’s guards, is executed.
CHAPTER XXVIII — Security of the Hudson
Irving shows Washington anxious to prevent an enemy irruption into the Highlands. Fortifications are erected. A chain and chevaux-de-frise are stretched across the river. General George Clinton commands in the Highlands with prompt energy, calling out militia from their harvest fields. The Phoenix and Rose pass up the Hudson, throwing the river counties into alarm. Local militias muster along the shores.
CHAPTER XXIX — Intelligence from General Lee
Letters from Lee give Washington intelligence of Sir Henry Clinton’s failed expedition to the South. The attack on Sullivan’s Island is detailed: Colonel Moultrie’s heroic defense, the repulse of the British fleet under Sir Peter Parker, the burning of the frigate Actaeon, and the British withdrawal. Lee writes of the “cool courage” of the garrison. The victory raises American spirits at a dark hour.
CHAPTER XXX — General Putnam’s Project
Irving describes Putnam’s mechanical projects to obstruct the Hudson. He constructs chevaux-de-frise by sinking ships filled with stones. Fire-ships are prepared to attack the British fleet. Experiments with a submarine machine (Bushnell’s “American Turtle”) are attempted. Putnam’s vaunted mortar “the Congress” eventually bursts during bombardment.
CHAPTER XXXI — The Battle of Long Island
Irving narrates the Battle of Long Island (August 27, 1776). The British turn the American left flank through the unguarded Jamaica Pass. Stirling’s division makes a heroic stand against overwhelming forces, fighting until surrounded. Stirling surrenders but his sacrifice saves the army from total destruction. The routed Americans retreat to the fortifications at Brooklyn. Washington, who had galloped to the scene, witnesses the disaster from a hilltop and reportedly exclaims, “Good God! What brave fellows I must this day lose!”
CHAPTER XXXII — The Night After the Battle
The night after the battle is weary and sleepless. Irving describes Washington’s decision to retreat from Brooklyn across the East River. Colonel Glover’s Marblehead fishermen man the boats. A providential fog conceals the movement. Washington is among the last to embark. The retreat is one of the most signal achievements of the war, saving the army from destruction.
CHAPTER XXXIII — The British in Possession of Long Island
The enemy now holds Long Island. Irving shows Washington’s distress: “Our situation is truly distressing.” The militia desert in droves — whole regiments at a time. Washington writes that if he could have foreseen such difficulties, no consideration would have induced him to accept command. The British prepare to land on Manhattan while Washington debates whether to abandon New York.
CHAPTER XXXIV — The British Land on Manhattan
Irving details the British landing at Kip’s Bay on September 15. The American militia flee in confusion without firing a shot. Washington, galloping to the scene, is so enraged at the cowardice that he dashes his hat on the ground, exclaims “Are these the men with whom I am to defend America!” and snaps his pistols at the fugitives. An aide seizes his bridle and hurries him away. The army retreats to Harlem Heights.
CHAPTER XXXV — The Fortified Camp
The main body assembles on Harlem Heights. Irving recounts the skirmish of September 16, when the British advance is met by Knowlton’s rangers and Weedon’s Virginians. Knowlton is killed, but the Americans drive the enemy back — their first success in the campaign. Washington, who had been stung by the British bugles sounding “like a fox-chase,” is heartened. The army fortifies its position from Harlem to King’s Bridge.
CHAPTER XXXVI — Lee Delays His March
Irving describes the critical delay of General Lee in marching from the South. Washington sends urgent letters. The British threaten to surround the American army on Manhattan. Lee’s slowness is contrasted with his earlier celerity. Washington writes to the President of Congress that he cannot account for Lee’s tardiness.
CHAPTER XXXVII — Washington Decamps from Manhattan
Irving narrates Washington’s evacuation of Manhattan Island. The army marches to White Plains in four divisions. The British land at Throg’s Neck and Pell’s Point, attempting to cut off the retreat. Washington chooses a strong position at White Plains, fortifying Chatterton’s Hill.
CHAPTER XXXVIII — The Battle of White Plains
Howe advances from the shore. Irving describes the Battle of White Plains (October 28): the British carry Chatterton’s Hill after a fierce fight. Washington withdraws to a stronger position. Howe declines to attack and turns toward the Hudson. Washington crosses into New Jersey, leaving garrisons at Fort Washington and Fort Lee.
CHAPTER XXXIX — Intelligence from the Northern Army
Irving recounts Arnold’s naval engagement on Lake Champlain (October 11–13). Arnold fights heroically in the Congress galley, but the American fleet is destroyed. Nevertheless, the delay prevents Carleton from reaching Ticonderoga before winter. The campaign on the lakes saves the Northern department for the year.
CHAPTER XL — Washington Crosses the Hudson
On November 12, Washington crosses the Hudson with the residue of his troops. Irving narrates the dispute over Fort Washington: Greene, on the spot, believes it can be held; Washington’s order was discretionary. On November 16, the British storm the fort. The garrison of 2,000 men is captured. Magaw surrenders. Washington watches from the Jersey shore and is said to have wept at the sight of his men being bayoneted while begging quarter.
CHAPTER XLI — The Capture of Fort Washington
With Fort Washington lost, Fort Lee is untenable. Irving describes Cornwallis crossing the Hudson on November 20 with 6,000 men and climbing the Palisades. Greene is forced to abandon Fort Lee, leaving tents standing and kettles on the fire. The retreat across the Jerseys begins — a harrowing 100-mile march through a hostile or terrified countryside. Washington writes to Congress urging desperate preparations.
CHAPTER XLII — Lee’s Delay and the Retreat
Despite Washington’s repeated orders, Lee does not reach Peekskill until November 30. Irving recounts Lee’s laggard march and his meditations on attacking British posts independently. The army continues its retreat under Cornwallis’s close pursuit. Washington opens a letter from Lee to Reed and discovers Lee’s disparaging comments about “a certain great man” — a revelation that deeply wounds Washington’s trust in his closest aides.
CHAPTER XLIII — General Lee Captured
Irving narrates Lee’s capture at Baskingridge on December 13. Lingering at a tavern three miles from his camp, he is surprised by Colonel Harcourt’s dragoons, guided by a Tory. Lee is carried off in his slippers and blanket coat. Washington’s comment to his brother is the severest he permits himself: “by his own folly and imprudence.” The army is freed from Lee’s troublesome independence.
CHAPTER XLIV — The Hessian Prisoners at Trenton
The army is reduced to a few thousand men. Irving describes Washington’s daring plan to cross the Delaware on Christmas night and surprise the Hessian post at Trenton. The crossing is perilous — the river is choked with ice, the night is stormy. Colonel Rahl, the Hessian commander, is a brave but careless officer who scorns the idea of breastworks. On the morning of December 26, Washington’s forces converge on Trenton from two directions. Rahl is mortally wounded; nearly 1,000 Hessians surrender. Washington writes that “this is a glorious day for our country.”
CHAPTER XLV — Colonel Griffin’s Episode at Trenton
Irving recounts Colonel Griffin’s operations against British posts as a diversion for the Trenton attack. He succeeds in luring Count Donop toward Mount Holly, preventing him from reinforcing Rahl. After Trenton, the Americans drive the Hessians from Bordentown and Burlington. The fugitives spread panic, abandoning sick and stores.
CHAPTER XLVI — Washington’s Masterly Campaign
Irving concludes the volume with Washington’s masterful follow-up to Trenton. Cornwallis, recalled from embarking for England, hastens to Trenton with 8,000 men. On January 2, 1777, he attacks Washington at the Assunpink but is repulsed. Confident of bagging “the fox in the morning,” Cornwallis halts. Washington steals a march in the night, attacks the British rear at Princeton on January 3, and wins a sharp victory. General Mercer is mortally wounded. Washington establishes winter quarters at Morristown. The campaign closes with Washington hailed as “the American Fabius” — a leader who had snatched victory from the jaws of disaster through patience, daring, and strategic genius.

sources/irving-life-washington-vol3.title: [source] The Life of George Washington — Volume III (Irving, 1899 Desmond)
sources/irving-life-washington-vol3.content:
The Life of George Washington — Volume III
Author: Washington Irving
Publisher: Desmond Publishing Co., Boston, 1899
Source: Internet Archive (University of Florida library copy)
OCLC: 7523322
Overview
Volume III covers the pivotal middle years of the American Revolutionary War, from the autumn of 1777 through the summer of 1781. It opens with Sir Henry Clinton’s attempt to relieve Burgoyne, follows the war across multiple theatres — the Hudson Highlands, Pennsylvania, the southern states, and the Virginia coast — and closes with the combined French and American armies marching towards Yorktown. The volume covers the Saratoga campaign, the Battle of Germantown, the winter at Valley Forge, the Conway Cabal, the Battle of Monmouth, the treason of Benedict Arnold, Greene’s southern campaign, and the final concentration of forces that would defeat Cornwallis.
Contents
Chapter I — Sir Henry Clinton’s Hudson Expedition (October 1777)
The volume opens with Sir Henry Clinton’s expedition up the Hudson, launched in October 1777 to relieve Burgoyne. After awaiting reinforcements from Europe — ships that took three months to cross the Atlantic in Dutch bottoms — Clinton assembles between three and four thousand men on board ships-of-war, armed galleys, and flat-bottomed boats at New York. A southern destination is publicly given out, but shrewd observers surmise the real objective. The narrative surveys the weak state of the Hudson Highland defences: Putnam commands only 1,100 Continentals and 400 militia at Peekskill. The Highland forts — Clinton, Montgomery, and Constitution — are poorly garrisoned. Governor George Clinton, the champion of the Highlands, is absent attending the State Legislature at Kingston (Esopus). Putnam sends urgent intelligence to the governor on September 29, warning that the enemy has called in guides from Croton River, ordered hard bread, and drawn the ships up the river. The governor hastens to his post with whatever militia he can collect. The chapter describes the chain, boom, and chevaux-de-frise across the Hudson between Fort Montgomery and Anthony’s Nose — obstructions that had repeatedly given way under the pressure of the tide. Fort Clinton had been recently erected within rifle shot of Fort Montgomery, separated by a deep ravine and stream called Peploep’s Kill. The combined garrison of both forts numbers fewer than 600 men, mostly militia.
The narrative follows Clinton’s plan: a feint at Peekskill deceives Putnam while the main British force marches secretly through the mountains. Forts Montgomery and Clinton are overpowered after a gallant defence. The commanders narrowly escape. The American frigates in the river are set ablaze and explode in a spectacular conflagration. Putnam and Governor Clinton make rallying efforts. A spy is detected through a silver bullet containing a secret message. Esopus (Kingston) is burnt. The British continue their ravaging progress up the Hudson, spreading destruction through the countryside.
Chapter II — Battle of Saratoga — Surrender of Burgoyne (October 1777)
Scarcity grips the British camp. Gates bides his time, refusing to be drawn into a premature engagement. Burgoyne undertakes a foraging movement that leads to the second battle of Saratoga on October 7, 1777. The British and Hessian forces are routed in a fierce engagement. The narrative describes the harrowing experience of the Baroness Riedesel and Lady Harriet Ackland during the battle — the Baroness, with her three small children, taking refuge in the cellar of a house near the battlefield while cannonballs crash overhead. General Simon Fraser is mortally wounded by a marksman from Morgan’s rifle corps; his funeral is conducted under a hail of enemy fire. The British begin a desperate night retreat. In one of the most celebrated episodes of the campaign, Lady Harriet Ackland — wife of the wounded Major Ackland, a British prisoner — makes her way through enemy lines in a small boat on the Hudson to plead for permission to nurse her husband. Washington Irving dwells on her courage and the chivalrous treatment she receives from General Gates. Burgoyne’s situation becomes hopeless at Saratoga. The capitulation is signed on October 17, 1777, and the Convention Army marches out with the honours of war. The conduct of the American troops is marked by discipline and restraint. In a famous scene, General Schuyler — who had been superseded by Gates — shows magnanimous courtesy toward the Baroness Riedesel and generous conduct toward Burgoyne himself, refusing to gloat over his rival’s triumph. The defeated British army is marched down the Hudson. The victory at Saratoga transforms the strategic situation and seals the fate of the British campaign to split the colonies.
Chapter III — Battle of Germantown (October 4, 1777)
Washington advances his army to Skippack Creek, keeping a watchful eye on the British occupation of Philadelphia. The British fleet is active in the Delaware River, where forts and obstructions have been placed to deny the Royal Navy access to the city. Washington meditates a bold stroke against the main British encampment at Germantown. The chapter narrates the Battle of Germantown (October 4, 1777) in full detail: the complex American plan calling for four separate columns converging on the British camp in the early morning fog. The initial advance drives Howe’s pickets back, but confusion in the fog, the failure of General Stephen’s and General Greene’s columns to link up properly, and the stubborn defence of the Chew House (where Colonel Musgrave and a detachment of the 40th Foot barricade themselves and hold out against repeated assaults) cause the American attack to unravel. A friendly fire incident — soldiers mistaking each other for the enemy in the fog — triggers a panic and retreat. Despite the defeat, Washington’s audacity impresses European observers: it is the first time the Americans have taken the offensive against a major British force in a pitched battle.
Chapter IV — Defence of the Delaware Forts (October–November 1777)
Washington establishes his army at White Marsh, north of Philadelphia. He undertakes measures to cut off the enemy’s supplies from the countryside. The narrative focuses on the forts on the Delaware River — Fort Mifflin (on Mud Island) and Fort Mercer (at Red Bank, New Jersey) — which block British supply lines up the river to Philadelphia. Colonel Christopher Greene of Rhode Island commands Fort Mercer. Count Donop, a Hessian colonel of European reputation, leads an assault on Fort Mercer on October 22, 1777. The attack is repulsed with heavy losses. Donop himself is mortally wounded; he dies several days later after receiving compassionate care from the Americans. The chapter details the siege operations, the shelling of Fort Mifflin from British batteries on Province Island, the heroic but doomed defence by the American garrison, and the eventual abandonment of both forts as untenable. The fall of the Delaware forts clears the river for British shipping, solidifying Howe’s hold on Philadelphia for the winter.
Chapter V — The Conway Cabal Begins (Winter 1777–78)
The chapter introduces the intrigues that would become known as the Conway Cabal. General De Kalb is commissioned a major-general in the Continental Army. Thomas Conway, an Irish-French officer who has risen rapidly through lobbying and political connections, makes pretensions to high command that are thwarted by Washington — Conway is made Inspector-General rather than receiving a major-general’s command. This snub fuels resentment. The Conway Cabal takes shape: a faction in Congress and the army — including Conway, General Horatio Gates (the hero of Saratoga), and Thomas Mifflin (Quartermaster-General) — begins manoeuvring to replace Washington as commander-in-chief. Gates is remiss in his correspondence with Washington after Saratoga, failing to send the customary report to his commanding general. He is dilatory in forwarding troops from the victorious northern army to the main army in Pennsylvania. Washington dispatches his young aide-de-camp Alexander Hamilton on a mission to Gates’s headquarters to press for reinforcements. Hamilton finds Gates evasive. James Wilkinson, Gates’s adjutant, is the bearer of dispatches to Congress from the north; he is a tardy traveller whose leisurely journey allows news of the cabal’s machinations to spread. Conway’s correspondence disparaging Washington is detected — a letter falls into Washington’s hands containing Conway’s boast that “no heaven, no earth” can save Washington from being supplanted. Washington’s response is measured but firm; he writes an apology for his army’s condition, declining to dignify the attacks with public notice.
Chapter VI — Fort Mifflin and the Delaware Campaign (November 1777)
Further hostilities on the Delaware continue. Fort Mifflin is attacked repeatedly by British batteries on Province Island and by ships of the Royal Navy. The garrison defends bravely but is gradually reduced under relentless bombardment. The mission of Alexander Hamilton to Gates is described in greater detail; Hamilton also visits the camps of Governor Clinton and Putnam on the Hudson. Putnam is depicted as “on his hobby-horse” — energetic but unreliable in his commands. The narrative details the great difficulties Washington faces in procuring reinforcements from the northern army, as Gates proves uncooperative. The intrigues of the cabal deepen: letters from James Lovell (a Congressional delegate from Massachusetts and ally of the cabal) and Thomas Mifflin to Gates reveal the extent of the conspiracy. The American works at Red Bank (Fort Mercer) are destroyed to prevent their use by the enemy. The British finally gain complete possession of the Delaware River. Washington’s army, unable to challenge Howe in Philadelphia, must contemplate a winter encampment.
Chapter VII — March to Valley Forge (December 1777)
Washington considers the question of an attack on Philadelphia. General Joseph Reed visits headquarters for consultations. The enemy’s works around Philadelphia are carefully reconnoitred. A council of war produces divided opinions — some favour an attack, others caution against it. Lafayette distinguishes himself in a daring reconnaissance exploit and is rewarded with command of a division. Congress modifies the Board of War, placing Gates at its head — a victory for the cabal. Another letter from Lovell to Gates reveals the continuing machinations. Sir William Howe sallies forth from Philadelphia with his army for manoeuvres and skirmishes. Conway is formally appointed Inspector-General. A council of war debates the question of winter quarters. The army begins its dreary march to Valley Forge on December 19, 1777 — a twelve-mile march through mud and freezing cold, many soldiers barefoot and leaving bloody footprints in the snow. At Valley Forge, the troops begin hutting, constructing log cabins in the wooded hills. Washington writes vindicatory letters defending his conduct of the campaign to Congress and to his critics. The chapter closes with a retrospective of the year 1777 — a year of defeats (Brandywine, Germantown, the loss of Philadelphia) offset by the great victory at Saratoga.
Chapter VIII — The Gates-Washington Correspondence (Winter 1777–78)
Gates is in the ascendant, basking in the glory of Saratoga and presiding over the Board of War. The “Conway letter” — in which Conway wrote disparagingly of Washington — becomes the focus of suspicion and acrimony. A consequential correspondence develops between Gates and Washington. Gates attempts to explain away the correspondence, but his explanations are evasive and unsatisfactory. Dr. James Craik, Washington’s long-time friend and physician, sends a warning letter alerting Washington to the plot against him. Anonymous letters circulate, attacking Washington’s character and leadership. A projected expedition to Canada — backed by the Board of War — is launched, with Lafayette given command but with Gates and the Board attempting to control it from behind the scenes. Lafayette finds himself caught between conflicting instructions from Washington and the Board of War; he seeks Washington’s counsel, who advises him wisely.
Chapter IX — Collapse of the Cabal (Spring 1778)
Gates undertakes to explain his role in the Conway correspondence. Washington subjects the explanation to a searching analysis and finds it wanting. The correspondence between the two generals is brought to a close, but the affair has damaged Gates’s standing. Spurious letters — forged or distorted — are published in an attempt to smear Washington. The Canada expedition — the pet project of the Board of War — proves a fiasco. Lafayette, who had been sent north to lead the expedition, encounters nothing but perplexities: inadequate supplies, unreliable troops, and hostile conditions. He is forced to abandon the enterprise. Throughout the crisis, Washington offers Lafayette sage counsel and support. The cabal’s influence wanes as its machinations are exposed and its members turn on each other.
Chapter X — Wilkinson and the Aftermath (Spring 1778)
More trouble erupts over the Conway letter. A correspondence between Lord Stirling and James Wilkinson reveals Wilkinson’s role in spreading gossip and betraying confidences. Wilkinson’s honour is wounded by accusations of duplicity. He has a passage at arms with General Gates, who accuses him of leaking the Conway letter. His seat on the Board of War becomes uncomfortable. Wilkinson determines that Lord Stirling “shall bleed” — a reference to a contemplated duel. His wounded honour is eventually healed through negotiations. Wilkinson seeks an interview with Washington and, in a dramatic turn, shows Washington the full correspondence between Gates and the conspirators. He then denounces Gates and resigns the secretaryship of the Board of War. Cast out of employment, Wilkinson fades from the scene for a time. The chapter closes with Irving’s concluding remarks on the Conway Cabal — a conspiracy that failed because Washington’s integrity, patience, and the trust of his officers and men proved unshakeable.
Chapter XI — Reforms at Valley Forge — Steuben’s Arrival (Winter–Spring 1778)
A committee of arrangement arrives at Valley Forge to work with Washington on army reforms. The camp suffers from severe scarcity of provisions — the army is nearly starved. The enemy, by contrast, revels in Philadelphia, enjoying balls, theatricals, and the famous Mischianza. An attempt is made to surprise Light-Horse Harry Lee; he makes a gallant defence, is praised by Washington, and is promoted. A letter from General Charles Lee (recently exchanged) is received. Burgoyne returns to England in disgrace. Martha Washington arrives at Valley Forge to join her husband for the winter, boosting morale. Bryan Fairfax — a friend of Washington’s from pre-war Virginia — visits the camp. Then comes the pivotal arrival of Baron Friedrich Wilhelm von Steuben, a Prussian officer who had served under Frederick the Great. His character and methods are described: his bluff manner, his theatricality, his skill as a drillmaster. Steuben takes charge of training the army, drilling the ragged Continentals in the manual of arms, bayonet drill, and evolutions. The discipline of the army is transformed. Greene is made quartermaster-general, reluctantly accepting the thankless but crucial administrative post. The army that emerges from Valley Forge in the spring is a professionally trained force — a direct result of Steuben’s labours.
Chapter XII — Winter at Valley Forge — North’s Conciliatory Bills (Winter–Spring 1778)
The fortifications of the Hudson are reviewed. A project to surprise Sir Henry Clinton is contemplated but not executed. General Howe forages in the Jerseys; ships and stores are burnt at Bordentown in a British raid. Plans for the next campaign are debated at headquarters. Gates and Mifflin are placed under Washington’s direct command — a sign that Washington has decisively overcome the cabal. Conway, the catalyst of the conspiracy, falls from power and eventually leaves the service. Lord North’s Conciliatory Bills — a last-ditch British offer to negotiate, proposing to renounce the right to tax the colonies and appoint commissioners to treat — arrive in America, sent to Washington by Governor Tryon. Washington forwards them to Congress, which resolves to reject any terms that do not acknowledge American independence. Washington sends a firm letter to Tryon. There is rejoicing at Valley Forge when word arrives of the French Alliance. The British in Philadelphia celebrate their own grand fête — the Mischianza, an elaborate tournament and pageant organized by Major John André for the departing General Howe.
Chapter XIII — Lafayette at Barren Hill — British Evacuation of Philadelphia (May–June 1778)
Lafayette is detached from the main army with a small force to keep watch on Philadelphia. He takes a position at Barren Hill, about twelve miles from the city. Sir Henry Clinton — now in command after Howe’s recall — devises a plan to entrap the young Marquis, sending a superior force to cut off his retreat. Washington becomes alarmed for Lafayette’s safety. Lafayette, displaying coolness and tactical skill, extricates his force by a clever stratagem — marching his troops as if to offer battle while secretly withdrawing by a different route, using the cover of woods and ravines. The exchange of General Charles Lee (captured earlier in the war) and Colonel Ethan Allen (captured in 1775 after the failed attack on Montreal) is negotiated. Ethan Allen visits Valley Forge and has an audience with Washington, who forms a measured opinion of the fiery Vermont leader. Preparations begin in Philadelphia for the British evacuation. Washington takes corresponding measures. The Carlisle Peace Commission — the British commissioners sent to treat under Lord North’s Conciliatory Bills — arrives in Philadelphia. They are disappointed to find Congress intransigent on independence. Their proceedings fail utterly, and their manifesto threatening dire consequences is contemptuously received.
Chapter XIV — Battle of Monmouth (June 28, 1778)
Preparations accelerate for the British evacuation of Philadelphia. Washington calls a council of war. General Charles Lee argues vehemently against attacking the British during their march across New Jersey — he believes the American army is not ready for a general engagement. Philadelphia is evacuated on June 18, 1778. Sir Henry Clinton marches his army — a column twelve miles long — across New Jersey toward New York. Washington pursues, calling another council of war. There is a sharp conflict of opinions: some officers favour a partial attack on the British rear; others, following Lee, oppose any attack. Lee’s conduct regarding the command of the advance force is contradictory and evasive — first he refuses the command, then demands it, then seems reluctant to exercise it. The Battle of Monmouth Court House begins on June 28, 1778, in intense heat. Lee’s handling of the attack is hesitant and confused; he orders a retreat at a critical moment, throwing the advance corps into disorder. Washington arrives on the field to find the American troops falling back. In the most famous scene of the battle, Washington rides up to Lee and rebukes him in terms that leave Lee shaken. Washington then personally rallies the troops, reforms the line, and directs the defence, stabilising the situation. The battle ends with the two armies facing each other on the field; Clinton slips away during the night. Both sides claim victory. The subsequent march of the armies continues.
Chapter XV — Lee’s Court-Martial (July–August 1778)
A bitter correspondence between Lee and Washington follows the Battle of Monmouth. Lee writes insulting letters to Washington, demanding satisfaction. Washington responds with icy formality. Lee asks for a trial by court-martial, confident he can vindicate himself. The court-martial is convened, and the evidence is heard. The verdict: Lee is found guilty of disobedience of orders, misbehaviour before the enemy, and disrespect to the commander-in-chief. He is suspended from command for one year. The chapter concludes with Lee’s subsequent history — his vituperative attacks on Washington after his suspension, his writing of pamphlets that damage his own reputation further, and his eventual death in obscurity. The end of Lee’s military career marks the end of a major source of friction within the American high command.
Chapter XVI — Arrival of D’Estaing — Rhode Island Expedition (July–August 1778)
The arrival of the French fleet under the Count d’Estaing — a dozen ships of the line and several frigates — opens a new phase of the war. Washington and D’Estaing exchange cordial correspondence.
