D’Estaing’s plans are ambitious: a combined Franco-American expedition against Newport, Rhode Island, where a British garrison under General Pigot holds the town. Perturbation seizes New York at the news. The French fleet sails for Narragansett Bay. Excitement grips the French crews as they anticipate action. The expedition against Rhode Island begins with General Sullivan commanding the American land forces. Operations proceed by sea and land — the French fleet drives the British ships ashore, and American troops land on the island. But then a violent storm disperses the French fleet, damaging several ships. D’Estaing withdraws to Boston for repairs, infuriating the American troops. The expedition fails. Irritation grows between the allied forces, with accusations of bad faith on both sides. Washington writes a considerate letter to the Count d’Estaing, smoothing over the tensions and preserving the alliance. The French fleet refits at Boston before departing for the West Indies.
Chapter XVII — Indian Warfare — Wyoming — Savannah Captured (Summer–Autumn 1778)
The narrative turns to savage Indian warfare on the frontier. The Valley of Wyoming (in present-day Pennsylvania) is devastated in a brutal massacre — settlers are slaughtered, homes burned, and the valley left desolate. The British and their Indian allies ravage the frontier settlements. In New York, the British undertake counter-movements; Washington responds with his own manoeuvres. British foraging parties range through the countryside. Colonel Baylor’s dragoons are massacred in a surprise night attack at Old Tappan, New Jersey, on September 28, 1778 — the British refusing quarter and bayoneting sleeping men. A British expedition against Little Egg Harbor on the New Jersey coast results in the massacre of Pulaski’s infantry. The Americans retaliate by executing Donop’s Rangers. Admiral Byron arrives from England to command the British fleet and endeavours to trap D’Estaing, but is disappointed as the French admiral eludes him. A British expedition against St. Lucia in the West Indies is launched. A major expedition against Georgia is mounted: Savannah is captured on December 29, 1778, and Georgia is subdued. General Lincoln is sent to command in the Southern Department, tasked with the defence of the South.
Chapter XVIII — Middlebrook Winter Quarters — Canada Expedition Abandoned (Winter 1778–79)
The American army settles into winter cantonments. Washington establishes his headquarters at Middlebrook, New Jersey, a strong defensive position in the Watchung Mountains. A plan of alarm signals for the Jerseys is devised to warn of British incursions. Lafayette’s project for an invasion of Canada — a scheme that has strong backing in Congress — is debated. Washington opposes the expedition vigorously, arguing that the army lacks the resources, the troops are too few, the season is wrong, and the Canadians have shown little enthusiasm for the American cause. Congress eventually abandons the plan. Washington visits Philadelphia, where he finds the war spirit declining, dissensions growing in Congress, and sectional feelings threatening national unity. He makes patriotic appeals to Congress and the country. Plans for the next campaign are developed. An avenging expedition against the Indian tribes is set on foot to repress frontier atrocities. Discontents among the Jersey troops over pay and conditions are appeased by Washington’s personal intervention. The campaign against the Iroquois — the Sullivan-Clinton expedition — is launched and proves successful, destroying Indian settlements and breaking the power of the Six Nations.
Chapter XIX — Stony Point Stormed (May–July 1779)
The enemy turns to predatory warfare. British forces ravage the Chesapeake Bay. Hostilities on the Hudson intensify: Sir Henry Clinton captures Verplanck’s Point and Stony Point, two key positions on opposite sides of the Hudson, fortifying them as bases for further operations. New Haven, Connecticut, is captured and plundered. Fairfield and Norwalk, Connecticut, are burned to the ground by British forces under General Tryon. Washington devises a counter-stroke. On the night of July 15-16, 1779, Brigadier General Anthony Wayne leads a picked force of light infantry in a daring midnight assault on Stony Point. The attack is made with unloaded muskets and fixed bayonets — orders are to rely on cold steel alone. The storming party crosses the flooded causeway under fire, scales the rocky heights, and takes the fort by surprise in a twenty-five-minute action. It is one of the most brilliant American feats of arms of the war. The fort’s guns are spiked and the works demolished before the Americans withdraw. A generous letter from Lee (Henry “Light-Horse Harry” Lee, not Charles Lee) commends Wayne’s exploit.
Chapter XX — Paulus Hook — West Point Fortified (Summer 1779)
An expedition against Penobscot, Maine, by a combined American naval and land force ends in disaster — the Massachusetts ships are trapped and destroyed by a British relief squadron. Major Henry (“Light-Horse Harry”) Lee conducts a night surprise of Paulus Hook (present-day Jersey City) on August 19, 1779, capturing the British garrison in a daring raid. Washington turns his attention to fortifying West Point as the key defensive position on the Hudson — a natural fortress commanding a great bend in the river. His style of living there is described: the daily routine at headquarters, the table at which he entertains officers and distinguished visitors with simple dignity. Sir Henry Clinton receives reinforcements from Europe. The Count d’Estaing arrives on the coast of Georgia with the French fleet. Plans are made in consequence — the French cooperate with General Lincoln in an attempt to recapture Savannah. The French minister visits Washington at his Highland camp. Washington writes to Lafayette. The siege of Savannah fails; d’Estaing is repulsed with heavy losses, including the death of the Polish nobleman Count Casimir Pulaski. Washington sends reinforcements to Lincoln. The army goes into winter quarters. Sir Henry Clinton dispatches an expedition to the South — the opening move of the British southern strategy.
Chapter XXI — The Morristown Winter (Winter 1779–80)
The army suffers terribly at Morristown, New Jersey, during the winter of 1779-80 — the worst winter of the war. The weather is intensely cold, with snowstorms and freezing temperatures exceeding even those of Valley Forge. The currency is in a state of complete derangement — Continental dollars have become nearly worthless. The commissariat is in chaos; supplies cannot be purchased with depreciated paper money. Washington authorizes the impressment of supplies from the surrounding countryside. The people of New Jersey display patriotic conduct, supplying the army despite the hardship to themselves. New York Bay freezes over, allowing the British to move troops and supplies across the ice. Lord Stirling leads an expedition against Staten Island. General Knyphausen launches an incursion into the Jerseys. The church of the Reverend James Caldwell at Elizabethtown is burned by the British — Caldwell’s character as a fighting parson is described. A British foray into Westchester County results in the burning of Young’s House in the valley of the Neperan. The army clings to existence through the brutal winter, its endurance a testament to Washington’s leadership.
Chapter XXII — Arnold in Philadelphia (1778–79)
Benedict Arnold, now military commander of Philadelphia after the British evacuation, is depicted in an unflattering light. His command is characterized by unpopular measures: he fraternizes with the loyalist elite, adopts an extravagant lifestyle far beyond his means, and engages in dubious commercial schemes and speculations. He collides repeatedly with the Pennsylvania Executive Council, which regards him with suspicion. His land project — a scheme to profit from Western lands — embroils him in controversy. Formal charges are sent against him to Congress. He publishes a defiant address to the public defending his conduct. The charges are referred to a court-martial. Amid these troubles, Arnold marries Margaret (“Peggy”) Shippen, the beautiful young daughter of a prominent Philadelphia loyalist-leaning family — a marriage that draws him deeper into the British orbit. The court-martial verdict convicts him on minor charges; Washington issues a public reprimand. Arnold obtains leave of absence from the army, brooding over what he regards as unjust treatment. The seeds of his treason are sown in these months of resentment, debt, and bitterness.
Chapter XXIII — The Southern Campaign Begins — Siege of Charleston (Early 1780)
South Carolina is threatened. The chapter describes the province’s condition and mixed population — wealthy lowcountry planters, upcountry Scots-Irish settlers, and a large enslaved population. Sir Henry Clinton endures a stormy voyage from New York to the South, losing many horses overboard. Lieutenant-Colonel Banastre Tarleton — young, ruthless, and brilliant — is introduced; his character as a cavalry commander is sketched. The British fleet arrives at Tybee Island. Clinton advances upon Charleston, South Carolina’s principal city and port. General Lincoln prepares for defence, aided by Commodore Whipple of the Continental Navy and Governor John Rutledge. Washington writes of his forebodings about the southern theatre. British troops embark from New York to reinforce Clinton. Washington sends De Kalb southward with Continental reinforcements. Washington writes a hopeful letter to Steuben about the prospects of the southern campaign, despite the growing danger.
Chapter XXIV — Currency Crisis — Arnold’s Debt and Difficulties (Winter-Spring 1780)
The evils of the depreciating Continental currency are examined in depth — its collapse is undermining the war effort at every level. Washington proposes military reforms to Congress, but Congress is jealous of military power and suspicious of standing armies. A committee of three is sent to confer with Washington at headquarters. The army’s losses from currency depreciation are to be made good to the troops — a promise that proves difficult to fulfil. Lafayette returns from France with joyful news: a French expeditionary force under Rochambeau is on its way. A scheme for a combined attack on New York is contemplated. Arnold, meanwhile, is beset by debts and difficulties in Philadelphia. He makes overtures to the French minister — seeking money or position — but is rebuffed. Anxious to return to active service and escape his creditors and critics, he seeks a command. A mutiny of the Connecticut troops over their enlistment terms erupts. Washington writes urgently to Joseph Reed, president of Pennsylvania, for aid from the Pennsylvania militia. The good effects of his letter are seen as the mutiny is quelled.
Chapter XXV — Fall of Charleston — Gates’s Southern Command (May 1780)
The siege of Charleston continues. British ships force their way past Fort Moultrie into Charleston Harbor. British troops under General Prevost march up from Savannah to complete the encirclement. Tarleton and his dragoons prove their ferocity in a brush with Colonel Washington (William Washington, a distant cousin of the commander-in-chief) at Monk’s Corner and in an action at Lanier’s Ferry. Charleston is reinforced by General Woodford with Virginia Continentals, but the situation is hopeless. On May 12, 1780, General Lincoln surrenders Charleston and his entire army of over 5,000 men — the worst American defeat of the war. Tarleton’s reputation for brutality is sealed when he overtakes Colonel Buford’s retreating regiment at Waxhaw Creek and, after a brief resistance, refuses quarter, slaughtering over a hundred men — the infamous “Waxhaw Massacre.” Sir Henry Clinton, leaving Cornwallis in command of the South, embarks for New York, believing the southern colonies are effectively subdued.
Chapter XXVI — Knyphausen’s Incursion into the Jerseys (June 1780)
General Knyphausen, the Hessian commander left in charge of New York, launches a marauding expedition into the Jerseys. The British sack Connecticut Farms (present-day Union, New Jersey). The narrative describes the murder of Mrs. Hannah Caldwell, wife of the Reverend James Caldwell — she is shot through a window by a British soldier while holding her infant child. The incident becomes a celebrated atrocity story that galvanizes American resistance. Sir Henry Clinton, arriving back from Charleston, takes personal command. The British burn Springfield, New Jersey, but are checked by American militia and Continentals under General Greene. The Jerseys are evacuated by the British as they fall back to New York.
Chapter XXVII — Gates Appointed to the Southern Command (Summer 1780)
Washington applies to the state legislatures for aid in recruiting the depleted army. The ladies of Philadelphia organize subscriptions to support the soldiers. Amid the crisis in the South, Congress appoints Gates — the hero of Saratoga — to command the Southern Department, passing over Washington’s preferred candidate. The French fleet arrives at Newport, Rhode Island, with the Count de Rochambeau. Preparations begin for a combined movement against New York. Arnold obtains command at West Point — a crucial posting that will prove disastrous. Greene resigns the office of quartermaster-general, exhausted by the thankless administrative burden.
Chapter XXVIII — Battle of Camden (August 16, 1780)
The narrative describes the difficulties of invading North Carolina: the character of its people — hardy, independent, and largely hostile to the British — and its rugged, wooded terrain. Thomas Sumter is introduced — his character, his story, and his role as a partisan leader. His attacks on Rocky Mount and Hanging Rock are described. The slow advance of De Kalb’s Continentals southward is traced. Gates arrives to take command and immediately decides on a bold advance into South Carolina. The army marches through a desolate, sandy region, subsisting on green corn and unripe peaches — many men fall ill. The Battle of Camden (August 16, 1780) is narrated: Gates’s foolish deployment of militia on the left wing against Cornwallis’s best troops; the militia’s immediate flight; the desperate stand of the Continentals under De Kalb, who falls mortally wounded with eleven wounds; Gates’s flight from the field — he rode 60 miles to Charlotte in a single day, his reputation destroyed. Sumter is surprised by Tarleton at the Waxhaws. Washington’s opinion of militia is expressed in his letter to Gates after the disaster. The American cause in the South lies in ruins.
Chapter XXIX — Arnold’s Treason — Negotiations with André (Summer 1780)
The narrative turns to the dramatic central episode of the volume: the treason of Benedict Arnold. His secret correspondence with the enemy through Major John André, Sir Henry Clinton’s adjutant-general, is traced. Arnold’s negotiations with André proceed through intermediaries — Joseph Stansbury, a Philadelphia merchant, and Joshua Hett Smith. The details of the plot emerge: Arnold agrees to surrender West Point — the key fortress of the Hudson — in exchange for £20,000 and a brigadier-general’s commission in the British army. The parting scene with Washington at Arnold’s headquarters is laden with dramatic irony — Washington unsuspectingly confides in a man who is plotting to betray him. The midnight conference on the banks of the Hudson aboard the British sloop Vulture takes place on the night of September 21-22, 1780. André is rowed ashore and meets with Arnold in the darkness among the trees. The return of André by land — against his wishes, as he had wanted to return by water — and the circumstances of his capture near Tarrytown by three militiamen (John Paulding, Isaac Van Wart, and David Williams) on September 23, 1780, are described. The incriminating papers hidden in André’s boot reveal the plot.
Chapter XXX — Arnold’s Flight — Washington’s Response (September 1780)
Washington had travelled to Hartford for an interview with the French officers (Rochambeau and Ternay) to plan combined operations. The return journey is described — Washington had planned to stop at Arnold’s headquarters on his way back. A change of plan delays him. Meanwhile, the captured André is brought to Arnold’s headquarters. Tidings of the capture reach Arnold on the morning of September 24. Arnold hastily excuses himself from the breakfast table, flees to the shore, boards his barge, and escapes down the Hudson to the Vulture. He leaves his wife, Peggy Shippen Arnold, behind. Washington’s arrival at Arnold’s headquarters shortly after the flight — his calm composure in the crisis — is one of the great scenes of the biography. He takes immediate precautions to secure West Point and the other Highland posts. Letters from the traitor are received, attempting to justify his conduct. Mrs. Arnold’s situation is described — her apparent hysterical collapse (which some historians believe was a calculated performance to protect herself). Washington, ever chivalrous, sees that she is safely conducted to her family in Philadelphia.
Chapter XXXI — André’s Trial and Execution (October 1780)
Major John André’s conduct as a prisoner of war is described: his dignity, his charm, his fatalistic acceptance of his fate. He converses with Colonel Benjamin Tallmadge, the head of Washington’s intelligence service, who tells him the story of Nathan Hale — the American spy executed by the British in 1776 — a story that has a profound effect on André. André is held at Tappan, New York. A flurry of correspondence on his behalf ensues: Sir Henry Clinton pleads for his life; General Robertson comes to Tappan under a flag of truce to argue that André was not a spy but a prisoner of war under a flag. Washington refuses the appeal. A board of general officers convenes to try André; they find him guilty of spying and sentence him to death. André is executed by hanging on October 2, 1780. His composure on the scaffold, his remark “I am reconciled to my death, but I detest the mode,” and his placing of the noose around his own neck are described. The three captors are rewarded by Congress. Arnold receives his blood money and a British commission, but his name becomes a synonym for treachery. He issues a proclamation attempting to justify his actions. The after fortunes of Mrs. Arnold are summarized — she eventually reunites with her husband in British-occupied New York and later in England.
Chapter XXXII — Greene Takes Command in the South (Autumn 1780)
Greene assumes command at West Point in the immediate aftermath of the Arnold affair. Insidious attempts are made to shake Washington’s confidence in his other officers — suspicion and paranoia threaten the army’s morale. A plan is devised to entrap Arnold — to capture him from New York and bring him to justice. The character of Sergeant John Champe, who volunteers for the dangerous mission, is described. The plot fails when the boat meant to extract him is delayed. A court of inquiry investigates Gates’s conduct at Camden; his reputation is tarnished but he avoids a formal court-martial. Greene is appointed to the Southern Department — Washington’s best battlefield commander is sent to salvage the situation in the South. Washington’s detailed instructions to Greene are given. Incursions from Canada threaten the northern frontier; the Mohawk Valley is ravaged by British and Indian forces. The state of the army is surveyed — reforms are adopted, including enlistment for the duration of the war and half-pay for officers. The army’s institutional foundation is strengthened.
Chapter XXXIII — Lafayette’s Light Infantry — New York Island Plans (Autumn 1780)
The Marquis Lafayette takes command of a picked corps of light infantry — the elite of the army. He proposes a brilliant stroke against British posts on New York Island, dreaming of decisive action. Preparations for an attack are made. The Marquis of Chastellux, a French general and man of letters, visits the American camp and records his impressions of Washington and the army. The attack on the British posts is ultimately given up as impractical. General Stark forages in Westchester County. Major Benjamin Tallmadge conducts a daring exploit on Long Island, capturing a British officer. The inactivity of the campaigning season frustrates the eager young Frenchman.
Chapter XXXIV — Cornwallis in South Carolina — Ferguson’s Foray — Battle of King’s Mountain (Autumn 1780)
The narrative returns to the South. Cornwallis adopts rigorous measures to subdue South Carolina — confiscations, harsh reprisals, and the mobilization of loyalist militia. Major Patrick Ferguson is sent with a force of loyalists to scour the mountain country between the Catawba and the Yadkin rivers, tasked with protecting Cornwallis’s left flank and recruiting loyalists. Ferguson, a brilliant and inventive officer, finds himself in a hornet’s nest as the backcountry people rise against him. The mountain men — the fierce Scotch-Irish and German settlers of the Appalachian frontier — and the “men from Kentucky” rally under Colonel William Campbell, John Sevier, and Isaac Shelby. They pursue Ferguson to King’s Mountain, a rocky ridge on the border of North and South Carolina. The Battle of King’s Mountain (October 7, 1780) is narrated: the frontiersmen surround the hill, advance from tree to tree, and pick off the loyalists with their long rifles. Ferguson is killed, shot from his horse with his silver whistle still at his lips. The entire loyalist force is killed or captured. Cornwallis orders a retrograde march back into South Carolina, his invasion of North Carolina temporarily halted. The victory sparks new hope in the southern backcountry.
Chapter XXXV — Marion and Sumter — Greene on the Pedee (Late 1780)
The legendary figure of Francis Marion — “the Swamp Fox” — is introduced. His character, his strange by-names, his haunting of the swamps of the Pee Dee and Santee — eluding British pursuit and striking at isolated outposts. Tarleton goes in quest of him but cannot catch him. Sumter operates on the west side of the Santee and has a sharp affair with Tarleton at Blackstock Hill, where the British cavalry is repulsed. Gates is at Hillsborough, but his domestic misfortunes have compounded his military disgrace — he has lost a son. Greene arrives to take command of the shattered southern army. His considerate conduct toward the defeated Gates is a mark of his character; Gates retires to his estate. The condition of Greene’s army is described — a handful of ragged Continentals and unreliable militia. Colonel William Washington (the cavalry commander) employs a clever stratagem at Clermont. Daniel Morgan is detached to the district of Ninety-Six to raise the militia there. Greene posts himself on the Pedee River, establishing a secure base from which to rebuild his army.
Chapter XXXVI — Arnold in Virginia — Pennsylvania Line Mutiny (Winter 1781)
Hostile embarkations from New York signal a new British offensive in the South. Arnold, now a British brigadier-general, is given command of an expedition to Virginia — his commission from Clinton. The country is in a necessitous state, its resources nearly exhausted by four years of war. Washington urgently presses for a foreign loan; Colonel John Laurens is sent as special envoy to France to seek aid in men and money. Meanwhile, grievances of the Pennsylvania Line — over enlistment terms, bounties, and the scandalous injustice that many men who signed up “for the war” had been kept beyond their original three-year terms — come to a head. The Pennsylvania Line mutinies on January 1, 1781, with over 1,300 men marching toward Philadelphia to demand redress. The mutineers negotiate with emissaries from Congress and from Sir Henry Clinton (who attempts to lure them to the British side). An accommodation is reached — the men are discharged or granted furloughs. Washington doubts the wisdom of the conciliatory policy, fearing it will encourage other mutinies. He adopts a rigorous course with other malcontents — executing the leaders of a mutiny in the New Jersey Line — and the policy proves successful. The Articles of Confederation, finally ratified by all thirteen states, come into effect, giving the national government a more solid legal foundation.
Chapter XXXVII — Arnold in Virginia — Steuben Checks the Ravages (January–March 1781)
Arnold’s expedition into Virginia is described as buccaneering in character — he sails up the James River, destroys public stores, burns Richmond (the new state capital), and ravages the countryside. Baron Steuben, commanding in Virginia, attempts to check Arnold’s depredations with a scratch force of militia and new levies. Arnold establishes a strong base at Portsmouth. Congress resolves to form executive departments — a crucial administrative reform. Alexander Hamilton is suggested by Sullivan for the post of Superintendent of Finance. Washington expresses his high opinion of Hamilton’s abilities. But a misunderstanding between Hamilton and the commander-in-chief — a quarrel at headquarters over a trifling matter — leads to Hamilton’s angry resignation as Washington’s aide-de-camp. Washington’s relationship with his brilliant but prickly protégé is strained, though their mutual respect endures.
Chapter XXXVIII — Cowpens (January 17, 1781)
Cornwallis prepares to invade North Carolina. He dispatches Tarleton with a picked force of infantry, cavalry, and light artillery to destroy the American detachment under Daniel Morgan. Morgan, with his mixed force of Continentals and militia, takes a defensive position at Hannah’s Cowpens — a grassy grazing ground in the South Carolina backcountry. The Battle of Cowpens (January 17, 1781) is narrated with full drama: Morgan’s masterful tactical deployment — the skirmishers in front, the militia in the centre instructed to fire two volleys and fall back, the Continentals on the ridge, and the cavalry concealed behind. Tarleton, contemptuous of the Americans, orders a headlong assault. The plan works perfectly: the militia falls back, drawing the British into a trap; the Continentals deliver a devastating volley and countercharge; the cavalry sweeps around the flank. The British force is destroyed — over 800 casualties against only 72 Americans. Tarleton escapes but his reputation is tarnished. Morgan pushes for the Catawba with his prisoners and spoils. Cornwallis, furious, endeavours to intercept him. The rising of the Catawba River — providential for the Americans — slows Cornwallis. Cornwallis halts at Ramsour’s Mills to consider his next move.
Chapter XXXIX — Greene’s Fabian Retreat to the Dan (January–February 1781)
Greene joins Morgan on the Catawba. Confronting Cornwallis’s superior army, Greene adopts the Fabian policy — avoiding battle while wearing down the enemy through manoeuvre and attrition. Cornwallis moves to cross the Catawba. An affair at McGowan’s Ford gives Greene time to retreat. Tarleton surprises the militia at Tarrant’s Tavern. Cornwallis’s advance is checked by the rising of the Yadkin River — another providential flood. A dramatic contest of skill and speed ensues as the two armies race for the Dan River. Greene masterfully manages his retreat, sending his infantry ahead while covering their withdrawal with cavalry and light troops. Cornwallis, encumbered by his baggage train, cannot catch him. Greene crosses the Dan into Virginia, his army intact and Cornwallis’s supply lines stretched to the breaking point. The race to the Dan is one of the finest examples of Greene’s generalship.
Chapter XL — Battle of Guilford Court House (March 15, 1781)
Cornwallis takes post at Hillsborough and issues a grandiloquent proclamation calling on loyalists to rally to the King’s standard. Greene recrosses the Dan into North Carolina. The country is scoured by the partisan bands of Henry Lee and Andrew Pickens. An affair with Colonel Pyle — in which Lee’s Legion, posing as British dragoons, captures or kills Pyle’s loyalist force — demonstrates the ruthless nature of the civil war in the South. Cornwallis manoeuvres desperately to bring Greene to battle. On March 15, 1781, the two armies meet at Guilford Court House. Greene adopts a three-line defensive formation, placing militia in front of the Continentals. The battle is fierce and protracted: the first line of militia fires and retreats; the second line of militia stands briefly but gives way; the third line — the Continental regulars — fights a desperate bayonet and musket duel with the British. Cornwallis, in a controversial act, orders his artillery to fire grapeshot into a melee where British and American troops are locked together. The Americans are forced from the field, but Cornwallis’s army is shattered — it has lost over a quarter of its strength. Greene retreats to Troublesome Creek. Cornwallis, unable to pursue, marches toward Cape Fear to rest and refit. Greene pursues him, brings him to a stand at Deep River, then determines to face about and carry the war back into South Carolina — a stroke of strategic genius. Cornwallis, abandoning the southern interior, marches for Virginia, hoping to link up with other British forces there.
Chapter XLI — Lafayette in Virginia — Operations Against Arnold (Spring 1781)
Arnold remains at Portsmouth, Virginia. Expeditions are sent against him. Washington issues detailed instructions to Lafayette, who is dispatched with a light corps to Virginia to oppose Arnold. Washington goes to Newport for consultations with Rochambeau. The French fleet sails from Newport but is pursued by the British. Lafayette’s expedition to Virginia gets underway. An engagement between the English and French fleets takes place off the Virginia Capes — the French fail to gain a decisive advantage. The expedition against Arnold at Portsmouth fails when the French ships cannot enter the harbour. Washington writes a frank letter to Colonel Laurens about the situation. Measures are taken to reinforce Greene’s southern army. General Phillips takes command at Portsmouth and begins marauding through the Virginia countryside. His depredations are checked by Lafayette, who marches and manoeuvres with energy. Mount Vernon itself is menaced — a British raiding party comes near the estate, and Lund Washington, the General’s cousin and estate manager, supplies them with provisions to prevent destruction. Washington is displeased when he learns of this. Phillips dies of fever, removing a capable British commander.
Chapter XLII — Washington and Rochambeau at Wethersfield (May 1781)
The army’s state remains inefficient, with recruitment lagging far behind requirements. Delancey’s loyalist corps conducts a marauding expedition. Colonel Greene (not Nathanael — this is another officer) is killed in action. The Count de Barras arrives to replace Destouches in command of the French squadron at Newport. More French naval forces are expected from the West Indies. Washington and Rochambeau meet at Wethersfield, Connecticut, in May 1781 for a crucial conference. The plan of combined operations is formulated: the immediate objective is to attack the British posts on New York Island. A financial arrangement by Robert Morris, the new Superintendent of Finance, provides hope of stable funding. A scheme is devised to attack the British works on New York Island and capture Delancey’s Corps. The American and French armies encamp in Westchester County. Reconnoitring expeditions are undertaken to probe the British defences. Washington begins to doubt the feasibility of the New York plan as French naval movements offer alternative possibilities.
Chapter XLIII — Cornwallis and Lafayette in Virginia (Summer 1781)
Movements and counter-movements between Cornwallis and Lafayette in Virginia are described in detail. Cornwallis marches through eastern Virginia, trying to trap the young Marquis. Tarleton and his troopers scour the countryside. Tarleton makes a dramatic dash at the Virginia Legislature, meeting in Charlottesville — lawmakers scatter to escape capture. An attempt is made to surprise Governor Thomas Jefferson at Monticello; Jefferson escapes narrowly, fleeing to Carter’s Mountain. Steuben is outwitted by Simcoe, the bold commander of the Queen’s Rangers. Lafayette is joined by Anthony Wayne with a brigade of Pennsylvania Continentals and by Steuben with Virginia levies. Lafayette now acts on the aggressive. A desperate mêlée between Macpherson and Simcoe’s forces is narrated. Cornwallis is pursued to Jamestown Island. “Mad Anthony” Wayne finds himself trapped in a morass during a sharp engagement; his impetuous valour extricates his men. Lafayette’s alertness prevents disaster. Washington writes his considered opinion of the Virginia campaign, praising Lafayette’s prudence and energy. Cornwallis, following Clinton’s orders and his own inclinations, moves to Yorktown on the Virginia Peninsula, where he fortifies and awaits developments.
Chapter XLIV — Greene’s Campaign in South Carolina (Spring–Summer 1781)
Greene’s retrograde operation in South Carolina — his southward march after the battle of Guilford — unfolds. He appears before Camden. The Battle of Hobkirk’s Hill (April 25, 1781) is fought: Greene’s attack misfires when an American regiment breaks under a British bayonet charge; he is forced to retreat, but Rawdon cannot pursue. Rawdon abandons Camden and falls back toward Charleston. Rapid successes follow for the Americans as the British outposts in the interior collapse. Greene lays siege to the fortress of Ninety-Six, a formidable star fort in the South Carolina backcountry, but is forced to raise the siege when Rawdon marches to its relief. Operations against Lord Rawdon continue. Greene retires to the High Hills of Santee to rest and refit his army in a healthy position. Sumter scours the lower country. Colonel Wade Hampton makes a bold dash to the gates of Charleston. Exploits of Lee and Hampton, and of Captain Armstrong at Quimby Bridge, are described. Actions in the neighbourhood of Charleston continue. Greene’s campaign — a masterpiece of strategic manoeuvre — ends with most of South Carolina’s interior in American hands; the British are bottled up in Charleston, Georgetown, and the coastal enclaves.
Chapter XLV — March to Yorktown — Visit to Mount Vernon (August–September 1781)
Washington is disappointed by the failure of the states to provide promised reinforcements for the campaign against New York. Word arrives that the French fleet under the Count de Grasse is destined for the Chesapeake, not New York. Washington resolves to abandon the proposed attack on New York and instead march the combined Franco-American army to Virginia to trap Cornwallis. Attempts on New York are postponed. The march of the armies to the Chesapeake begins — a masterwork of deception. Washington and Rochambeau march the troops through New Jersey and Pennsylvania, keeping the British in New York guessing as to their destination until it is too late. Stratagems to deceive the enemy are employed: false preparations for an attack on Staten Island, a conspicuous camp left in New Jersey. Arnold, now a British officer, ravages New London, Connecticut — his home state — in a final act of betrayal. Washington arrives in Philadelphia. The combined armies march through the city in a grand spectacle on September 2, 1781. Then Washington, accompanied by Rochambeau, travels by separate route toward the Chesapeake. On September 9, 1781, Washington visits Mount Vernon for the first time in six years — the first time he has seen his beloved home since the start of the war. The chapter describes the emotional homecoming, the crowding of guests at the estate (including the French officers Chastellux and Rochambeau), and the generous Virginian hospitality. On September 12, Washington tears himself away and rides onward to join Lafayette at Williamsburg. Cornwallis is entrenched at Yorktown. The stage is set for the decisive siege. The volume closes with Washington’s army converging on the British position and the combined forces preparing for the climax of the war.

sources/irving-life-washington-vol4.title: [source] The Life of George Washington — Volume IV (Irving, 1899 Desmond)
sources/irving-life-washington-vol4.content:
Irving — The Life of George Washington, Vol. IV
Washington Irving (1783–1859) — The Life of George Washington. — In Four Volumes. Volume IV. Desmond Publishing Co., Boston, 1899.
This is Volume IV (the concluding volume) of Washington Irving’s five-volume biography of George Washington, first published 1855–1859. It covers the period from the Siege of Yorktown (1781) through Washington’s death (1799) — the closing of the Revolutionary War, the formation of the American republic under the Constitution, Washington’s two terms as president, the rise of partisan politics, and his final retirement at Mount Vernon.
The volume contains 456 page-files (OCR’d from the University of Florida library copy), extracted as 25,468 lines (~1.2 MB) of plain text.
Scope: Covers 1781–1799 — the siege and surrender of Yorktown, the dissolution of the Continental Army, Washington’s retirement to Mount Vernon, the framing and ratification of the Federal Constitution, his unanimous election as first President, the establishment of executive departments under Hamilton and Jefferson, the rise of the two-party system, the French Revolution’s impact on American politics, the Genet affair, Jay’s Treaty, the Whiskey Rebellion, Washington’s Farewell Address, the Quasi-War with France, his final appointment as Commander-in-Chief, and his death.
Chapter-by-Chapter Summary
CHAPTER I — The Siege of Yorktown (pp. 13–20)
Irving opens with Cornwallis aroused from his dream of security by the appearance of Count de Grasse’s fleet within the Chesapeake capes on August 28, 1781. Three French ships anchor at the mouth of York River, and 3,300 land forces under the Marquis de St. Simon are transported up James River to join Lafayette. Cornwallis finds his retreat to the Carolinas cut off — York River blocked by French ships, James River filled with transports. He strengthens his works and sends expresses to Clinton. De Grasse, eager to return to the West Indies, urges an immediate attack, but Lafayette wisely waits for Washington and Rochambeau. Admiral Graves arrives with 20 British sail; De Grasse puts to sea with 24 ships. The naval action on September 7 is indecisive, but De Barras arrives with siege artillery, and Graves eventually withdraws to New York. Washington hurries troops forward — “Every day we now lose is comparatively an age” — and on September 14 arrives at Williamsburg.
CHAPTER II — The Surrender of Yorktown (pp. 21–25)
Irving narrates the formal siege operations beginning September 28. The allied armies of 16,000 men — 9,000 French and 7,000 Americans — invest Yorktown. Washington fires the first gun on October 9. The bombardment devastates the British works. On October 14, American and French troops storm Redoubts 9 and 10 in a brilliant night assault led by Hamilton for the Americans and Lafayette’s aide for the French. Cornwallis, his position untenable, attempts an evacuation across the river that fails due to a storm. On October 17, he sends a flag of truce; formal surrender takes place on October 19. The British march out between the French and American lines, their band playing “The World Turned Upside Down.”
CHAPTER III — Aftermath of the Victory (pp. 26–36)
Irving describes the dissolution of the combined armies after Yorktown. Washington hurries to Eltham, where he finds his stepson John Parke Custis dying of camp fever. Custis expires on November 5, leaving four young children whom Washington will raise. Washington at Mount Vernon — his first visit in over six years — is brief. Lafayette sails for France to urge further aid. Washington stimulates Congress to prepare for the next campaign. The case of Captain Asgill, a British officer threatened with execution in retaliation for a murder, is described — Washington is relieved when Congress releases Asgill, sparing Washington a painful duty.
CHAPTER IV — The Close of the War (pp. 37–43)
Irving shows Washington maintaining precautions even as peace rumors circulate. Sir Guy Carleton, replacing Clinton, brings conciliatory news. Discontents arise in the army over back pay and pensions. Colonel Nicola writes an extraordinary letter suggesting Washington become king; Washington’s indignant reply crushes the notion: “No occurrence in the course of the war has given me more painful sensations.” The allied armies join on the Hudson. Congress contemplates reducing the army, heightening officers’ anxieties.
CHAPTER V — The Newburg Address (pp. 44–56)
Irving narrates the Newburg crisis of March 1783. Discontents among officers at Newburg reach a peak. Anonymous addresses circulate in camp urging the army to defy Congress if their grievances are not met. On March 15, Washington calls a meeting of officers. He makes an impassioned address, pausing to put on spectacles and saying, “Gentlemen, you will permit me to put on my spectacles, for I have grown not only gray but blind in the service of my country.” The gesture moves the officers to tears; they pass resolutions of loyalty. Washington’s moral authority saves the republic from a military coup.
CHAPTER VI — News of Peace (pp. 57–65)
Irving recounts the official news of peace in April 1783. Washington issues a proclamation of the cessation of hostilities. The Order of the Cincinnati is formed by officers desiring to perpetuate their association. Washington writes a circular letter to the state governors urging a “more perfect union.” A mutiny in the Pennsylvania Line over pay is suppressed. Washington tours the northern posts on Lake Champlain and the Mohawk Valley, assessing potential for westward expansion.
CHAPTER VII — Washington Resigns His Commission (pp. 66–77)
Irving describes the formal discharge of the army and Washington’s parting address. On November 25, 1783, the British evacuate New York; Washington enters the city in triumph. In Fraunces Tavern on December 4, he bids farewell to his officers — each man steps forward in silence to shake his hand, tears streaming down faces. He then proceeds to Annapolis, where Congress sits, and on December 23 formally resigns his commission. He tells Congress, “Having now finished the work assigned me, I retire from the great theatre of action.” The moment establishes the principle of civilian control of the military.
CHAPTER VIII — Mount Vernon and Domestic Life (pp. 78–81)
Irving paints a picture of Washington’s long-desired retirement at Mount Vernon. He enjoys a soldier’s repose, planning domestic improvements. The Council of Pennsylvania offers him a gift of land and stock, which he declines. He resumes agricultural life, visits his western lands with Dr. Craik, and entertains Lafayette for the last time before Lafayette returns to France. Irving includes recollections of the Fairfax family and Washington’s wistful glances at the ruins of Belvoir.
CHAPTER IX — Rural Life and Schemes of Improvement (pp. 82–95)
Irving describes Washington’s schemes for inland navigation. He refuses shares of stock offered by Virginia for his services but agrees to accept them for public uses such as education. The chapter covers his management of the estate, his tax of letter-writing and sitting for portraits, his ornamental gardening, and the reverential awe he inspired. An account of a visit from Mr. Watson reveals Washington’s festive gaiety, his passion for hunting, and his habit of reading the newspapers at breakfast. The death of General Greene is covered — Washington’s heartfelt regrets and encomiums.
CHAPTER X — The Federal Constitution (pp. 96–106)
Irving shows Washington’s growing doubt about the solidity of the Confederation. Correspondence with John Jay reveals his concern that the Articles of Confederation are inadequate. Shays’ Rebellion in Massachusetts (1786–87) alarms him. He heads the Virginia delegation to the Constitutional Convention in Philadelphia. Elected president of the convention, his presence lends gravitas to the proceedings. The Constitution is hammered out through the summer of 1787 and ratified by the states. Washington writes that the new government is “a little or a great thing according to the wisdom with which it is administered.”
CHAPTER XI — The First Presidency (pp. 107–118)
Irving describes how Washington is universally talked of for the presidency. His letters express genuine reluctance. He is unanimously elected. On April 30, 1789, he takes the oath of office on the balcony of Federal Hall in New York. The inauguration is a solemn ceremony witnessed by crowds. Chancellor Livingston administers the oath; Washington adds “So help me God” and kisses the Bible. Later, in his inaugural address to Congress, he speaks of “the preservation of the sacred fire of liberty and the destiny of the republican model of government.”
CHAPTER XII — Organizing the Government (pp. 119–126)
Irving details the anxious first days of the new government. Washington must create executive departments from scratch. He consults John Jay, Hamilton, James Madison, and Henry Knox. Hamilton is appointed Secretary of the Treasury, Knox Secretary of War. The cabinet begins to take shape. Washington’s position is lonely — he has no constitutional advisers initially. He relies heavily on Hamilton’s energetic mind.
CHAPTER XIII — The President’s Tour and the Death of His Mother (pp. 127–130)
Irving recounts Washington’s journey through the Eastern states in October 1789. John Hancock, Governor of Massachusetts, creates a contest of etiquette over who should pay the first call. Washington visits the scenes of his early military campaigns, the manufacturing establishments of Beverly, and Portsmouth, New Hampshire. He is received everywhere with joy. His mother, Mary Ball Washington, dies on August 25, 1789, at Fredericksburg. Irving sketches her character — a woman of strong mind who had raised Washington in piety and firmness.
CHAPTER XIV — Washington’s Illness and the Death of His Mother (pp. 131–135)
Washington suffers an alarming illness (a malignant carbuncle) that nearly kills him. The Senate rejects one of his nominations for a naval officer in Savannah, and he makes a sensitive vindication of his prerogative. The executive departments are instituted: Treasury (Hamilton), War (Knox), and State (temporarily John Jay). Hamilton is instructed to report a financial plan. The judiciary is organized under Chief Justice John Jay. Edmund Randolph serves as Attorney General. Congress adjourns.
CHAPTER XV — Jefferson and the French Revolution (pp. 136–147)
Irving introduces Thomas Jefferson, who is in Paris as minister, immersed in French politics. The contrast between Jefferson’s enthusiastic support for the French Revolution and Gouverneur Morris’s conservative views is drawn. News of the storming of the Bastille arrives in America, causing popular excitement. Washington maintains a cautious opinion. Hamilton is apprehensive. Jefferson is offered the State Department and, after hesitation, accepts, arriving in New York in March 1790.
CHAPTER XVI — Journey through the Eastern States (pp. 148–161)
Irving details Washington’s journey through the Eastern states, including a contest of etiquette with John Hancock in Boston. Washington records his entry into Boston, his reception, and an address from the Cincinnati Society. He returns to New York, completing the tour that strengthens national unity.
CHAPTER XVII — Northern Tour and Indian Affairs (pp. 162–167)
Washington’s Eastern tour continues. He visits Beverly’s manufacturing establishments, the new State of Rhode Island (which had belatedly ratified the Constitution), and Portsmouth. He boards the French squadron and embarks for New York, then tours Long Island before returning to Mount Vernon.
CHAPTER XVIII — Rhode Island and Mount Vernon (pp. 168–177)
Irving recounts Lafayette at the head of the French Revolution, writing to Washington in enthusiastic terms. Gouverneur Morris provides a different, more skeptical view. Lafayette presents Washington with the key of the Bastille — a symbol of the revolution. Washington visits Rhode Island and Mount Vernon, maintaining a careful silence on French affairs while privately expressing anxiety.
CHAPTER XIX — Frontier War with the Indians (pp. 178–185)
Irving describes frontier difficulties with Indians northwest of the Ohio. General Harmer’s expedition against the Miami towns in 1790 is a failure — Colonel Hardin’s detachment is ambushed, and a second detachment is compelled to retreat. Washington endures long anxiety awaiting the result, which ultimately forces a more serious expedition.
CHAPTER XX — Hamilton’s Financial System (pp. 186–194)
Irving describes Hamilton’s landmark financial arrangements in 1790–1791. Congress moves to Philadelphia — the new temporary capital. Hamilton submits his reports on public credit, proposing the assumption of state debts by the federal government and the creation of a national bank. Jefferson objects on constitutional grounds, beginning the great constitutional debate over implied powers. Two political parties form under Hamilton (Federalist) and Jefferson (Democratic-Republican). Kentucky and Vermont are admitted to the Union. A new expedition under General St. Clair is projected against hostile tribes — Washington issues solemn warnings to St. Clair before his departure.
CHAPTER XXI — Southern Tour and French Affairs (pp. 195–204)
Irving describes Washington’s Southern tour in 1791 — through Virginia, the Carolinas, and Georgia. He visits Savannah and Charleston, where he is greeted with enthusiasm. He writes to Lafayette, who depicts the troubles of a patriot leader. Jefferson’s optimistic view of the French Revolution is contrasted with John Adams’s distrust. The flight and recapture of Louis XVI reaches Washington; he expresses satisfaction when the King accepts the Constitution.
CHAPTER XXII — St. Clair’s Disaster (pp. 205–211)
Irving recounts St. Clair’s disastrous campaign against the Western Indians. On November 4, 1791, St. Clair is surprised by a confederation of Miami, Shawnee, and Delaware warriors near the Wabash River. Over 600 American soldiers are killed and the entire force routed — the worst defeat ever inflicted on the U.S. Army by Native Americans. Washington, dining with guests when the news arrives, controls his emotions until alone, then explodes with rage at St. Clair’s unpreparedness.
CHAPTER XXIII — Washington Contemplates Retirement (pp. 212–221)
Irving shows Washington’s growing weariness with public life. The apportionment bill leads to the first use of the veto power. He asks Madison to prepare a draft of a Farewell Address. Wayne is appointed to succeed St. Clair. Jefferson insists on retiring as Secretary of State at the end of Washington’s first term. Washington is deeply troubled — he cannot spare Jefferson from the divided cabinet.
CHAPTER XXIV — Discord in the Cabinet (pp. 222–228)
Irving details the open warfare between Hamilton and Jefferson. Jefferson suspects Hamilton of monarchical designs; Hamilton considers Jefferson a dangerous visionary. Freneau’s National Gazette attacks the administration. Washington’s healing admonitions to both — urging harmony and warning against party spirit — fail to reconcile them. The excise law meets violent opposition in Pennsylvania. Washington issues a proclamation against the Whiskey rebels.
CHAPTER XXV — Second Term Begins (pp. 229–232)
Irving describes Washington’s unanimous re-election in 1792. He is inaugurated for his second term on March 4, 1793 — his address is brief and solemn, only 133 words. The state of public affairs is gloomy with the French Revolution entering its most violent phase and war between France and England imminent.
CHAPTER XXVI — The French Revolution and Lafayette’s Imprisonment (pp. 233–238)
Irving recounts how Gouverneur Morris, now minister to France, reports the alarming progress of the Revolution. The overthrow of the French monarchy, the September massacres, and the imprisonment of Lafayette shake Washington. He writes a kind letter to the Marchioness Lafayette expressing his concern. Jefferson remains optimistic despite the massacres, but Washington is deeply shocked.
CHAPTER XXVII — Proclamation of Neutrality and the Genet Affair (pp. 239–248)
Irving describes Washington’s entrance upon his second term under gloomy auspices. Louis XVI is executed on January 21, 1793. France declares war on England. Belligerent excitement sweeps America. On April 22, 1793, Washington issues his Proclamation of Neutrality, declaring the United States “friendly and impartial toward the belligerent powers.” Citizen Genet, the new French minister, lands at Charleston and commissions privateers against British shipping before even presenting his credentials. He is greeted with wild enthusiasm in Philadelphia. Jefferson and Hamilton clash over the proper response; Washington calmly steers a middle course.
CHAPTER XXVIII — Genet’s Diplomacy (pp. 249–256)
Genet presents his letter of credence to Washington on May 18, 1793, despite his unwarranted proceedings at Charleston. Irving describes the diplomatic sparring. The British ship Grange is captured by French privateers in Delaware Bay. Washington demands restitution. Genet’s insolent tone — threatening to appeal from the President to the people — shocks the administration. Washington becomes increasingly sensitive to press attacks.
CHAPTER XXIX — The Little Sarah and Genet’s Recall (pp. 257–265)
Irving narrates the crisis of the Little Sarah, a British prize that Genet outfits as a French privateer in Philadelphia. Washington is called to Mount Vernon by the death of his estate manager. In his absence, the cabinet agonizes over what to do. Hamilton and Knox want to seize the vessel by force; Jefferson urges caution. Genet gives evasive assurances; the vessel sails in defiance on July 14. Washington’s fury on his return is described by Jefferson: “The President burst forth into one of those transports of passion beyond his control.” The Democratic Society forms in Philadelphia in imitation of Jacobin clubs. The recall of Genet is determined.
CHAPTER XXX — Genet’s Fall and the Cabinet’s Dissolution (pp. 266–274)
Irving describes the threatened dissolution of the cabinet. The French frigate Ambuscade defeats the British Boston in a single-ship action and returns to New York in triumph. A French fleet arrives. Genet enters New York amid cheering multitudes, tricolor cockades everywhere. He is informed of the measures for his recall and reacts with rage. His popularity quickly declines when it emerges that he threatened to appeal from the President to the people.
CHAPTER XXXI — Neutrality Threatened (pp. 275–280)
Irving details how British impressment of American seamen and seizures of American vessels bound for France endanger neutrality. Congress assembles in December 1793. Washington’s opening speech censures Genet. The Vice-President (Adams) alludes approvingly to the President’s firmness. The administration is in a minority in the House. Jefferson presents his report on commerce and then retires from the cabinet. His parting rebuke to Genet is a model of dignity. Jefferson’s private character of Washington — “his integrity was most pure, his judgment most inflexible” — is quoted.
CHAPTER XXXII — British Spoliations (pp. 281–285)
Irving describes the debate on Jefferson’s report on commercial intercourse. A naval force is proposed to protect against Algerian corsairs. Genet’s recall is followed by the arrival of his successor Fauchet. British captures of American vessels heighten public irritation. An embargo is laid. War with England seems imminent. The partisans of France are in the ascendant. Washington, determined to prevent war, resolves to send a special envoy to the British government.
CHAPTER XXXIII — Monroe Appointed to France and the Whiskey Rebellion (pp. 286–291)
Irving recounts James Monroe’s appointment as minister to France in place of Gouverneur Morris (whose recall the French demanded). Meanwhile, the Whiskey Rebellion erupts in western Pennsylvania — farmers resist the excise tax on whiskey. Washington issues a proclamation on August 7, 1794. When the insurgents persist, he issues a second proclamation and marches with 15,000 militia — the first and only time a sitting president commands troops in the field. The insurgents disperse without bloodshed. Washington denounces “self-created societies” for fomenting the rebellion.
CHAPTER XXXIV — Self-Created Societies and Wayne’s Campaign (pp. 292–296)
Washington’s denunciation of self-created societies is not relished by Congress. Irving describes General Wayne’s campaign against the Indians — the victory at Fallen Timbers on August 20, 1794. Hamilton reports a plan for the redemption of the public debt and retires as Secretary of the Treasury, succeeded by Oliver Wolcott. Knox also resigns, succeeded by Timothy Pickering. The session closes.
CHAPTER XXXV — Jay’s Treaty (pp. 297–307)
Irving details the anxious progress of the Jay Treaty negotiations. Jay’s Treaty arrives for ratification in March 1795. Its terms are unpopular — it secures British evacuation of Western posts and some commercial advantages but says nothing about impressment or neutral rights. The Senate ratifies with a reservation concerning West Indian trade. The treaty is published and met with violent opposition — copies are burned in Boston, New York, and Philadelphia. Washington, despite personal reservations, resolves to ratify, believing it better than no treaty at all.
CHAPTER XXXVI — Randolph’s Resignation (pp. 308–313)
Washington is recalled from Mount Vernon by a mysterious letter from Pickering. Irving describes how an intercepted dispatch from Fauchet, the French minister, implicates Secretary of State Edmund Randolph in questionable conduct — suggesting Randolph had solicited French money. Randolph resigns when confronted. His subsequent vindication is incomplete; he writes a pamphlet bitterly attacking Washington, which he later regrets. Pickering is transferred to State; McHenry becomes Secretary of War. George Washington Lafayette, the general’s son, arrives in America.
CHAPTER XXXVII — The Farewell Address (pp. 314–322)
Irving describes the opening of Congress in December 1795. Washington presents a cheerful summary of events. The French colors — sent in exchange for those Monroe presented — are formally received. The House demands papers related to Jay’s Treaty, and Washington refuses — a landmark assertion of executive privilege. The treaty is ultimately implemented. Monroe is recalled from France; C. C. Pinckney is appointed. France adopts a resentful policy, ordering seizures of American vessels. Washington’s Farewell Address is published in September 1796.
CHAPTER XXXVIII — Last Days of the Presidency (pp. 323–330)
Washington meets Congress for the last time on December 7, 1796. Irving describes his speech recommending a military academy, national university, and gradual naval increase. The Senate’s reply is warm; the House’s more measured. Andrew Jackson votes against the reply, daring to dissent from the universal praise. The French minister Adet publishes an offensive letter attempting to influence the election. John Adams is declared President. Washington writes to Knox on the eve of retirement. Spurious letters from 1776 are republished — Washington denounces them as forgeries. His farewell dinner is an emotional affair.
CHAPTER XXXIX — At Mount Vernon Again (pp. 331–339)
Irving describes Washington’s return to Mount Vernon in March 1797. The influx of visitors is overwhelming. Lawrence Lewis arrives as an aide in entertaining. Washington’s counsel to his granddaughter Nelly Custis on love matters is recounted with charm. Nelly’s romantic episode with the young Carroll of Carrollton is described — Washington’s gentle intercession when she is caught wandering alone in the woods. George Washington Lafayette, the general’s son, arrives from France.
CHAPTER XL — The Quasi-War with France (pp. 340–347)
Irving recounts the XYZ Affair — the degrading treatment of American envoys by Talleyrand’s agents demanding bribes before negotiations could begin. The French Directory refuses to receive C. C. Pinckney. Congress prepares for war. Washington is appointed Commander-in-Chief of the provisional army. He accepts on the condition he need not take the field unless absolutely necessary. He arranges the three major-generals: Hamilton, Pinckney, and Knox. Knox is aggrieved at being ranked below Hamilton, but Washington insists.
CHAPTER XLI — Last Year of Washington’s Life (pp. 348–357)
Washington is taxed anew with the cares of office, organizing the army, corresponding with Lafayette (now released from Olmutz), and managing his estate. A marriage at Mount Vernon — Nelly Custis marries Lawrence Lewis. The appointment of a minister to the French Republic is noted. Washington’s activity on his estate continues despite his sixty-seventh year.
CHAPTER XLII — Washington’s Death (pp. 358–368)
Irving concludes with Washington’s final days. He digests a comprehensive plan for managing his estate, writes to Hamilton approving Hamilton’s plan for a military academy, and rides out in cold rain on December 12, 1799. He develops acute laryngitis. Despite being bled four times, his condition deteriorates. His last words include “I die hard, but I am not afraid to go” and “‘Tis well.” He expires between ten and eleven on the evening of December 14, 1799, aged 67. His funeral is simple and modest at Mount Vernon. His will provides for the emancipation of his slaves after Martha’s death — a final act of moral courage. Congress resolves to shroud the Speaker’s chair in black. The nation mourns.
Appendix

I. Portraits of Washington (pp. 317–333) — A notice of the various portraits and representations of Washington, prepared by H. T. Tuckerman for the illustrated edition, describing works by Peale, Trumbull, Stuart, Pine, Wertmuller, Ceracchi, Houdon, and Crawford.
II. Washington’s Farewell Address (pp. 334–348) — The full text of the Farewell Address.
III. Proceedings of Congress in Consequence of the Death of Washington (pp. 349–357) — The official proceedings, resolutions, and eulogies of Congress.
IV. Washington’s Will (pp. 358–368) — The full text of Washington’s last will and testament.

sources/irving-life-washington-vol5.title: [source] The Life of George Washington — Volume V (Irving, 1899 Desmond)
sources/irving-life-washington-vol5.content:
Irving — The Life of George Washington, Vol. V
Washington Irving (1783–1859) — The Life of George Washington. — Volume V. Extended Annotated Edition. Jazzybee Verlag, Altenmünster, 2014. ISBN: 9783849642204.
This is Volume V (the concluding volume) of Washington Irving’s five-volume biography of George Washington, first published 1855–1859. It covers the period from Washington’s inauguration as first President (1789) through his death (1799) — the establishment of the federal government, the rise of partisan politics under Hamilton and Jefferson, foreign crises with France and Britain, and Washington’s final retirement at Mount Vernon. Modern “Extended Annotated” introductory material (a biographical primer on Irving) has been stripped; the text is Irving’s original work only.
Scope: Covers 1789–1799 — Washington’s unanimous election and inauguration; the organization of the executive departments under Hamilton, Jefferson, and Knox; the creation of the federal judiciary; Hamilton’s financial system and the assumption of state debts; the location of the permanent capital; the rise of the Federalist and Republican parties; the French Revolution and its American repercussions; the Genet affair; the Whiskey Rebellion; Jay’s Treaty; the Farewell Address; Washington’s retirement to Mount Vernon; the Quasi-War with France; his appointment as Commander-in-Chief; his death and the provisions of his will.
Includes appendix material: Portraits of Washington (by H. T. Tuckerman); the full text of Washington’s Farewell Address; and the full text of Washington’s last will and testament.
Chapter-by-Chapter Summary
CHAPTER I — Washington Begins His Administration
Irving describes how the eyes of the world are upon Washington at the commencement of his administration. He must create the government from the ground up. The inauguration is held on April 30, 1789, on the balcony of Federal Hall in New York — Chancellor Livingston administers the oath before an immense crowd. In his inaugural address, Washington speaks of “the preservation of the sacred fire of liberty” as his guiding motive. He is acutely aware of the precedent his actions will set for all future presidents.
CHAPTER II — The President’s Household
Irving details how, the moment the inauguration is over, Washington perceives he is no longer master of himself or his home. The pressure for patronage begins immediately. Washington deliberately establishes formal etiquette for the presidential household — his weekly levees, his carriage, his manner of receiving visitors. Mrs. Adams’s description of his reception at the presidential mansion is quoted, noting his dignity and reserve. He maintains the distance necessary to preserve the respect due to the office.
CHAPTER III — Mrs. Washington’s Journey to New York
On May 17, 1789, Mrs. Washington sets out from Mount Vernon accompanied by her grandchildren Eleanor Custis and George Washington Parke Custis. Irving recounts her journey — she is received with honors along the route, including military escorts and addresses from local dignitaries. Her arrival and reception at the seat of government mark the establishment of a proper style for the President’s family. The social life of the presidential household is described, with Washington’s niece acting as hostess.
CHAPTER IV — Organizing the Departments
Irving shows Washington calling upon the heads of departments to furnish papers and documents respecting their duties. The Treasury, War, and State departments are established. The President’s cabinet begins to take shape with Hamilton as Treasury Secretary, Knox as War Secretary, and John Jay temporarily handling foreign affairs. The question of titles for the President — “His Highness” is proposed — is ultimately settled by Congress with the simple “President of the United States.”
CHAPTER V — The Cabinet Takes Shape
Irving describes how the Department of State still needs a head. John Jay is appointed the first Chief Justice of the Supreme Court. Washington offers the State Department to Thomas Jefferson, then minister to France. Jefferson hesitates, consulting his friends. After long deliberation, he accepts, though Irving notes his reluctance to leave the exciting political scene in Paris where the French Revolution is unfolding.
CHAPTER VI — Washington’s Eastern Tour
In October 1789, Washington embarks on a tour through the Eastern states. Irving describes his journey through Connecticut, Massachusetts, and New Hampshire — his reception by the people, his visit to the scenes of his early military campaigns, the manufacturing establishments of Beverly. The contest of etiquette with Governor John Hancock in Boston provides a notable episode: Hancock, suffering from gout, refuses to call on the President first; Washington stands on protocol; eventually Hancock relents.
CHAPTER VII — Trumbull and the Historical Paintings
Irving recounts how Colonel John Trumbull, Washington’s former aide-de-camp and now an eminent historical painter, arrives from England. Trumbull proposes a series of historical paintings of the Revolution. Washington sits for his portrait. The chapter includes their correspondence about the paintings, which will eventually adorn the Capitol Rotunda.
CHAPTER VIII — The First Congress Under the Constitution
Congress reassembles on January 4, 1790. Irving describes Washington’s address opening the session — he recommends attention to public credit, a naval force, Indian affairs, and the militia system. Hamilton’s epochal Report on Public Credit is presented on January 14, proposing that the federal government assume state debts and fund the national debt at par. The report sparks the great debate that will define early American politics.
CHAPTER IX — The Assumption of State Debts
Irving describes the long and angry debates over the assumption of state debts. Southern states, many of which had already paid their debts, oppose assuming the debts of northern states. A compromise is effected through Thomas Jefferson’s agency: in exchange for southern votes for assumption, the permanent capital will be located on the Potomac. The bill passes, and the seat of government is moved to Philadelphia for ten years before moving to the new federal city.
CHAPTER X — Affairs in France
Irving shows Washington’s attention often called from domestic affairs to the unfolding French Revolution. Lafayette, now at the head of the Revolution, writes enthusiastic letters full of hope. Gouverneur Morris, in Paris, reports a different view — he foresees the violence to come. Washington maintains a cautious silence in public but expresses anxiety in private correspondence.
CHAPTER XI — Indian Depredations on the Frontier
Irving recounts the frequent Indian depredations on the frontier settlements northwest of the Ohio. Washington authorizes offensive operations. General Harmer’s expedition against the Miami towns in 1790 is a failure — Colonel Hardin’s detachment is ambushed, and a second detachment is forced to retreat with heavy losses. Washington endures long anxiety awaiting the result.
CHAPTER XII — The Seat of Government Moves to Philadelphia
Congress reassembles at Philadelphia in December 1790. Washington’s residence at the new seat is established. His opening speech recommends attention to the national debt, the militia, and post roads. The creation of a national bank is proposed by Hamilton. Jefferson raises constitutional objections — the first major debate over implied powers. Washington requires written opinions from his cabinet, and Hamilton’s masterful defense of the bank’s constitutionality convinces Washington to sign the bill.
CHAPTER XIII — Washington’s Southern Tour
In March 1791, Washington sets out on a 1,887-mile tour through the Southern states. Irving describes his route through Virginia, North Carolina, South Carolina, and Georgia. He visits Savannah, Augusta, and Charleston, noting the condition of the Southern country. The tour is a triumphal progress, strengthening the bonds of union. He returns to Philadelphia in July.
CHAPTER XIV — Autumn at Mount Vernon
Irving recounts how Washington snatches a few weeks of autumn at Mount Vernon. He instructs a new agent in the management of the estate, supervises agricultural improvements, and enjoys the joy of being home after the cares of office. His passion for farming and his careful attention to every detail of the plantation are evident.
CHAPTER XV — The Apportionment Bill
A bill for apportioning representatives among the states is introduced. Irving describes how the bill gives an additional fraction to certain states in a manner Washington considers unconstitutional. He consults his cabinet and, convinced the bill violates the Constitution, exercises the first presidential veto on April 5, 1792. The veto establishes an important precedent for executive power.
CHAPTER XVI — Washington Considers Retirement
Irving recounts Jefferson’s painful letter expressing his desire to retire from the cabinet. Washington is deeply troubled — he cannot spare Jefferson, and the cabinet is already dangerously divided between Hamilton and Jefferson. Washington urges Jefferson to remain. He himself begins to consider retirement at the end of his first term.
CHAPTER XVII — Second Term Begins
Washington consents to be a candidate for re-election after a painful conflict of feelings. Irving notes there is no opposition — the electoral vote is unanimous. He is inaugurated on March 4, 1793, in Philadelphia. His address is brief and solemn, only a few sentences. The state of public affairs is gloomy: the French Revolution has entered its most violent phase, and war between France and England is imminent.
CHAPTER XVIII — Gouverneur Morris in France
Irving describes Gouverneur Morris’s appointment as minister plenipotentiary to the French court. His diplomatic correspondence from Paris details the progress of the French Revolution — the imprisonment of the king, the September massacres, the execution of Louis XVI. Morris’s gloomy dispatches contrast sharply with the enthusiastic reports of other observers. Washington’s anxiety for Lafayette, now imprisoned in Olmutz, is acute.
CHAPTER XIX — The French Revolution and American Neutrality
Irving shows Washington beginning his second term under gloomy auspices — a divided cabinet, increasing party exasperation, and a threatened abatement of his popularity. The execution of Louis XVI shocks the world. France declares war on England. On April 22, 1793, Washington issues his Proclamation of Neutrality, declaring the United States “friendly and impartial toward the belligerent powers.” The proclamation is met with fierce opposition from pro-French partisans.
CHAPTER XX — The Genet Affair Begins
Irving recounts the arrival of Citizen Genet as French minister in April 1793. Genet lands at Charleston and, before presenting his credentials, commissions privateers against British shipping, sets up French consular courts to adjudicate prizes, and appeals to the American people over the head of their government. He arrives in Philadelphia on May 18 and presents his letter of credence to a cold and wary Washington. The cabinet is divided on how to respond — Jefferson is sympathetic, Hamilton hostile.
CHAPTER XXI — The Little Sarah Crisis
Irving details the crisis of the Little Sarah in June–July 1793. While Washington is briefly at Mount Vernon, the French minister outfits the British prize Little Sarah as a French privateer in Philadelphia. Governor Mifflin is determined to prevent her departure. Jefferson urges delay until the President returns. Genet gives an evasive assurance, and the vessel sails in defiance on July 14. Washington’s fury on his return is vividly recorded by Jefferson — he bursts out that he had rather be in his grave than in his present situation. The Democratic Society of Philadelphia is formed in imitation of Jacobin clubs.
CHAPTER XXII — The Cabinet Threatens to Dissolve
Irving describes how Washington, already annoyed by managing a divided cabinet, is now threatened with its dissolution. Hamilton announces his intention to retire. Jefferson does the same. Washington calls on Jefferson at his country residence, picturing his “deep distress” at being deserted. Their remarkable private conversation is recorded: Washington denies any monarchical inclinations and declares no man would oppose such a change more decidedly than himself. A compromise keeps Jefferson until January 1794. Genet visits New York and receives a hero’s welcome — the Ambuscade has just defeated the Boston in a single-ship action. But when Genet’s threat to appeal from the President to the people becomes known, his popularity collapses.
CHAPTER XXIII — British Spoliations and Neutrality Endangered
Irving details how British measures endanger neutrality in 1793. British cruisers are instructed to detain all vessels bound to France with provisions. American seamen are impressively pressed into British service. The Western posts are held in violation of the peace treaty. The hostilities of the Indians continued, attributed by many to British influence. Congress assembles in December 1793. Washington’s opening speech urges defense preparations and warns against foreign entanglements. Jefferson’s report on commercial intercourse is presented.
CHAPTER XXIV — Public Affairs Grow More Complicated
Irving shows public affairs becoming more complicated. Events in Europe are gloomy. The debate on Jefferson’s commercial report becomes heated — Fisher Ames and William Giles clash. Genet’s machinations continue — he sends emissaries to Kentucky to recruit for an expedition against Spanish Louisiana. British captures of American vessels heighten public irritation to fever pitch. Washington, determined to avoid war, resolves to send a special envoy to England. Hamilton recommends John Jay for the mission.
CHAPTER XXV — Genet Recalled and Monroe Appointed
Irving recounts the recall of Genet by the French government in February 1794 — his successor Fauchet arrives. James Monroe is appointed minister to France in place of Gouverneur Morris. Washington writes a warm letter of support to Morris despite the recall. Monroe is received in Paris with enthusiasm — the Convention decrees the French and American flags be entwined in the hall. The news of Genet’s successor pacifies the immediate crisis, but French-American relations remain strained.
CHAPTER XXVI — The Whiskey Rebellion
Irving describes the insurrection in Western Pennsylvania against the excise law in the summer of 1794. The insurgents fire upon the federal marshal, attack the inspector’s house, and compel a surrender. Washington issues a proclamation on August 7. When the insurgents persist, he calls out 15,000 militia — the largest army ever assembled in America to that date — and marches in person to Carlisle and Bedford. The insurgents disperse without a shot fired. Washington denounces “self-created societies” for fomenting the rebellion — a bold step that incurs lasting enmity. Hamilton reports a plan for the redemption of the public debt and retires as Treasury Secretary, succeeded by Oliver Wolcott. Knox also resigns, succeeded by Timothy Pickering.
CHAPTER XXVII — Jay’s Treaty
Irving describes Washington’s anxious watch over the mission of John Jay to England. Jay’s Treaty arrives for ratification in March 1795. Washington studies it closely — some provisions are satisfactory, others not. On the whole he considers it the best treaty attainable. The Senate ratifies on June 24 with a reservation concerning West Indian trade. When an abstract of the treaty is published, the country explodes in opposition — treaty copies are burned in Boston, New York, and Philadelphia. Washington resolves to ratify despite the clamor, writing that he will not substitute the opinions of others for his own conviction. The treaty is signed on August 18, 1795.
CHAPTER XXVIII — Washington at Mount Vernon
Irving shows Washington trying to enjoy Mount Vernon while constant political crises summon him back to Philadelphia. A mysterious letter from Pickering brings him hurrying back — an intercepted dispatch from French Minister Fauchet appears to implicate Secretary of State Edmund Randolph in soliciting French money. Washington confronts Randolph, who resigns in anger. Randolph publishes a vindication attacking Washington, which he later deeply regrets. Pickering is transferred to State; McHenry becomes War Secretary. George Washington Lafayette, the general’s son, arrives from France.
CHAPTER XXIX — The President’s Speech at the Opening of Congress
Irving describes Washington’s speech at the opening of Congress in December 1795 — a cheerful summary of events. Wayne’s victory at Fallen Timbers (August 1794) has led to the Treaty of Greenville, ending the Indian war. Treaties with Algiers and Morocco secure peace. Washington receives the colors of France.
